definition: Two people or things, or a small number of people or things (usually around two or three).
examples: ["I'll be ready to leave in a couple of minutes.", "A couple of my friends are coming over for dinner tonight."]
usage_notes: In informal American English, 'of' is often dropped before nouns (e.g., 'a couple minutes'), but using 'a couple of' is standard and grammatically correct.
collocations: ["a couple of days", "a couple of times", "a couple of weeks", "a couple of hours", "a happy couple"]

definition: A term used after a time to show that it is between midnight and noon.
examples: ["My morning alarm goes off every day at 6:30 a.m.", "The train to Chicago departs at 9:00 a.m. sharp."]
usage_notes: Usually written in lowercase with periods (a.m.), though uppercase (A.M.) is also common. Do not use 'in the morning' together with 'a.m.' as it is redundant.

definition: To leave someone or something behind completely, often with no intention of returning.
examples: ["The villagers had to abandon their homes due to the approaching wildfire.", "He decided to abandon the project after realizing it was too expensive."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'to' when leaving a plan or idea (e.g., 'abandon a plan to do something'). When used with people, it implies leaving them in a difficult or vulnerable position.
collocations: ["abandon a ship", "abandon a plan", "abandon hope", "abandon a child", "hasty abandonment"]

definition: To leave someone or something behind completely, often with no intention of returning.
examples: ["The villagers had to abandon their homes due to the approaching wildfire.", "He decided to abandon his old car after it broke down for the third time."]
usage_notes: It is often followed by the preposition 'to' or 'for' in specific contexts, or a direct object when referring to places, people, or plans.
collocations: ["abandon a ship", "abandon a plan", "abandon hope", "abandon an attempt"]

definition: The physical, mental, or financial power, skill, or means to do something.
examples: ["She has a remarkable ability to solve complex mathematical problems quickly.", "His ability to speak three languages fluently helped him get the job.", "The new software will improve our ability to communicate with international clients."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the pattern 'ability to + verb' (e.g., 'ability to swim'). Do not use 'ability of doing' something.
collocations: ["natural ability", "ability to pay", "demonstrate an ability", "best of my ability", "physical ability"]

definition: Having the power, skill, means, or opportunity to do something.
examples: ["She was able to finish the project ahead of schedule.", "Will you be able to come to the party tonight?"]
usage_notes: Most commonly used in the pattern 'be able to + verb'. It functions as a modal-like expression for ability, especially in tenses where 'can' cannot be used (e.g., future 'will be able to' or present perfect 'have been able to').

definition: On the subject of, concerning, or approximately a certain number or amount.
examples: ["We talked about our plans for the upcoming weekend.", "The journey takes about two hours by train."]
usage_notes: When used to mean 'approximately', it is commonly followed by numbers or time. It is also frequently paired with verbs like 'think', 'talk', and 'know'.
collocations: ["about to do", "how about", "what about", "think about", "care about", "just about"]

definition: In or to a higher position than something else, or more than a particular amount or level.
examples: ["The birds were flying high above the trees.", "Temperatures remained above average all week."]
usage_notes: 'Above' is commonly used as a preposition or an adverb. Avoid confusing it with 'over', which often implies movement across or direct contact, whereas 'above' usually means higher up without touching.
collocations: ["above average", "above all", "listed above", "from above", "above the law"]

definition: In or to a foreign country or countries.
examples: ["She decided to study abroad to improve her Spanish.", "Many people like to travel abroad during the summer holidays."]
usage_notes: 'Abroad' is an adverb, so you do not use 'to' before it (e.g., say 'go abroad', not 'go to abroad').

definition: The state of being away from a place or not being present where you are expected to be.
examples: ["Her frequent absence from school started to affect her grades.", "In the absence of a clear plan, the team decided to wait for further instructions."]
usage_notes: Often used in the phrase 'in the absence of something' or followed by the preposition 'from' (e.g., 'absence from work').
collocations: ["absence of mind", "prolonged absence", "leave of absence", "in the absence of", "excused absence"]

definition: Not present in a place, such as school, work, or a meeting.
examples: ["Several students were absent from class today because of the flu.", "He has been absent from work for three consecutive days."]
usage_notes: When used as an adjective, it is usually followed by the preposition 'from' (e.g., absent from school). The stress is on the first syllable for the adjective (/ˈæbsənt/), but on the second syllable when used as a reflexive verb (/æbˈsɛnt/).
collocations: ["absent from work", "absent from school", "conspicuously absent", "mark someone absent"]

definition: Complete, perfect, or total; not limited or restricted in any way.
examples: ["You must tell the truth with absolute honesty.", "The ruling monarch had absolute power over the kingdom."]
usage_notes: Often used for emphasis before a noun (e.g., 'absolute beginner', 'absolute silence'). Avoid using comparative modifiers like 'more' or 'most' with 'absolute', as its meaning is already complete.

definition: Used to express complete agreement or to emphasize that something is completely true.
examples: ["Do you agree with the new policy? Absolutely!", "I am absolutely certain that I locked the front door."]
usage_notes: Often used as a strong one-word answer meaning 'yes'. When modifying adjectives, it is used with non-gradable (extreme) adjectives (e.g., 'absolutely terrifying', not 'absolutely scary').

definition: To take in liquid, gas, light, or heat gradually; or to fully understand and remember new information.
examples: ["Plants absorb water and nutrients from the soil through their roots.", "It takes time to absorb all the information during the first week of a new job."]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive voice when describing someone who is highly focused on something, using the pattern 'be absorbed in' (e.g., 'She was completely absorbed in her book').
collocations: ["absorb water", "absorb information", "absorb knowledge", "be fully absorbed in", "absorb the cost"]

definition: The cruel, violent, or unfair treatment of someone, or the incorrect or improper use of something (such as a substance or power).
examples: ["The organization works to prevent the abuse of power by government officials.", "He was hospitalized due to a long history of substance abuse."]
usage_notes: The word can be used as a noun (pronounced /əˈbjuːs/) or as a verb (pronounced /əˈbjuːz/). Common grammar patterns include 'abuse of power/authority' and 'substance abuse'.
collocations: ["substance abuse", "abuse of power", "verbal abuse", "physical abuse", "child abuse"]

definition: Relating to education, schools, colleges, or scholarship rather than practical or technical skills.
examples: ["She has a strong academic background and excels in research.", "The university offers a wide range of academic programs."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective (e.g., 'academic performance') or a noun referring to a teacher or researcher at a college or university.

definition: A distinctive way of pronouncing a language, especially one associated with a particular country, area, or social class.
examples: ["She speaks English with a strong French accent.", "He grew up in Boston, but he has lost most of his regional accent."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'accent' with 'dialect'. An accent refers only to pronunciation, while a dialect includes different vocabulary and grammar rules.
collocations: ["strong accent", "foreign accent", "regional accent", "speak with an accent", "lose one's accent"]

definition: To agree to take something that is offered, or to believe that something is true or correct.
examples: ["She decided to accept the job offer from the new company.", "It took him a long time to accept that he had made a mistake."]
usage_notes: Often confused with 'except'. Remember that 'accept' is a verb meaning 'to receive', while 'except' usually means 'excluding'. Common grammar pattern: 'accept an offer' or 'accept that [clause]'.
collocations: ["accept an offer", "accept a challenge", "accept responsibility", "accept an apology", "widely accepted"]

definition: Satisfactory or good enough for a particular purpose or standard.
examples: ["The quality of your work is fully acceptable for this project.", "We need to find a solution that is acceptable to both sides."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'to' (acceptable to someone) or 'for' (acceptable for a purpose).

definition: The right, opportunity, or ability to use, enter, or contact something.
examples: ["You need a password to gain access to the database.", "The building has wheelchair access at the rear entrance."]
usage_notes: As a noun, 'access' is uncountable and is almost always followed by the preposition 'to' (e.g., 'access to the internet'). As a verb, it is transitive and does not use 'to' (e.g., 'I cannot access the file').
collocations: ["gain access", "have access to", "internet access", "restricted access", "easy access"]

definition: An unexpected event that typically results in damage, injury, or harm, or anything that happens by chance without being planned.
examples: ["He was injured in a car accident on his way to work.", "I met my old friend by accident at the supermarket."]
usage_notes: Use the preposition 'in' for events (e.g., 'in an accident') and 'by' for unintentional actions (e.g., 'by accident').
collocations: ["car accident", "by accident", "traffic accident", "tragic accident", "prevent an accident"]

definition: Happening by chance or unexpectedly, rather than on purpose.
examples: ["I made an accidental mistake on the form and had to fill it out again.", "The discovery of penicillin was completely accidental."]
usage_notes: Mainly used as an adjective before a noun or after a linking verb like 'was' or 'seems'. The adverb form is 'accidentally'.

definition: By chance or by mistake, without intending to do so.
examples: ["I accidentally deleted the important email from my inbox.", "She accidentally bumped into an old friend at the supermarket."]
usage_notes: A common spelling mistake is writing 'accidently' without the 'al'. It is often used to apologize for or explain unintended actions.

definition: A place to live, stay, or work in, such as a hotel room, apartment, or house.
examples: ["The tour price includes hotel accommodation and all meals.", "It can be difficult to find affordable accommodation in major cities."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'accommodation' is uncountable when referring to places to stay (e.g., 'some accommodation'). In American English, it can be countable ('accommodations'). A common spelling mistake is forgetting the double 'c' or double 'm'.

definition: To go somewhere with someone as a companion, or to exist or occur together with something else.
examples: ["The singer was accompanied on the piano by her sister.", "Children under the age of twelve must be accompanied by an adult."]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive voice ('be accompanied by'). In music, it means to play an instrument while someone else sings or plays the main melody.
collocations: ["be accompanied by", "accompany a friend", "accompany a song", "accompany on the piano"]

definition: As stated by or reported by someone or something; or in a way that agrees with a system, rule, or plan.
examples: ["According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow afternoon.", "The students were arranged in groups according to their reading levels."]
usage_notes: Always follow this phrase with a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase, never a full clause with a subject and verb. Avoid saying 'according to me' when expressing your own opinion; use 'in my opinion' or 'I think' instead.
collocations: ["according to the report", "according to experts", "according to the law", "according to plan", "according to sources"]

definition: A record of money kept in a bank, or a personal profile used to access a service or website. It can also mean a spoken or written description of an event.
examples: ["I opened a new savings account at the local bank yesterday.", "She gave a detailed account of what happened during the meeting."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with prepositions: 'open an account', 'account for' (explain/cause), or 'on account of' (because of).
collocations: ["bank account", "user account", "create an account", "detailed account", "account for"]

definition: To explain the reason for something, or to form a particular amount or part of a total.
examples: ["How do you account for the sudden change in the weather?", "Online sales account for over forty percent of the company's total revenue."]
usage_notes: This phrasal verb is often followed by a noun or a gerund. It is widely used in both academic contexts (to explain something) and business contexts (to represent a percentage or portion).
collocations: ["account for a large portion", "account for the difference", "account for the delay", "account for a majority"]

definition: Correct, exact, and free from errors.
examples: ["The weather forecast was surprisingly accurate this week.", "Please make sure all the information in your report is accurate before sending it."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'information', 'description', or 'data'. The opposite is 'inaccurate'. Do not confuse it with 'precise', which means detailed, though they are often synonyms.

definition: In a way that is correct, exact, and without any mistakes.
examples: ["The report accurately describes the current financial situation.", "She was able to accurately predict the outcome of the experiment."]
usage_notes: It is an adverb that modifies verbs or adjectives. Common patterns include 'accurately describe', 'accurately predict', or 'accurately reflect'.

definition: To say that someone has done something morally wrong, illegal, or unkind.
examples: ["He was accused of stealing the company's confidential data.", "Are you accusing me of lying?"]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive voice. The standard preposition pattern is 'accuse someone of [noun/doing something]'. Do not use 'accuse someone for'.
collocations: ["accuse someone of a crime", "falsely accuse", "stand accused of", "accuse someone directly"]

definition: To successfully bring about or reach a desired objective, level, or result by effort, skill, or courage.
examples: ["She worked hard for many years to achieve her dream of becoming a doctor.", "The team played exceptionally well to achieve a victory in the final minutes of the game."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with abstract nouns like 'goals', 'success', or 'results'. Avoid using it for simple physical actions (e.g., write 'I reached the station', not 'I achieved the station').
collocations: ["achieve a goal", "achieve success", "achieve a target", "achieve results", "difficult to achieve"]

definition: something very good and difficult that you have succeeded in doing, especially through hard work, skill, or effort.
examples: ["Winning the championship was a remarkable achievement for the young team.", "Learning to speak a new language fluently is a major achievement."]
usage_notes: It is a countable noun when referring to specific successes, but can be uncountable when referring to the general state of succeeding (e.g., 'a sense of achievement').
collocations: ["sense of achievement", "major achievement", "academic achievement", "outstanding achievement", "crowning achievement"]

definition: A chemical substance, usually a liquid, that contains hydrogen and can react with other substances to form salts; it often has a sour taste and can burn skin or damage materials.
examples: ["Lemon juice contains citric acid, which gives it a sour taste.", "Be careful when handling the battery, as it contains a strong acid that can burn your skin."]
usage_notes: In everyday English, 'acid' can refer to the chemical substance or be used as an adjective meaning 'sour' or 'sharp' (e.g., 'an acid remark'). In slang, it can also refer to the hallucinogenic drug LSD.

definition: To accept, admit, or recognize the truth, existence, or reality of something, or to confirm that you have received something.
examples: ["She refused to acknowledge that she had made a mistake.", "Please acknowledge receipt of this email by replying to it."]
usage_notes: Often followed by a gerund (verb-ing) or a 'that' clause. In professional contexts, it is frequently used to confirm the receipt of messages or documents.
collocations: ["acknowledge receipt", "acknowledge a mistake", "acknowledge the fact that", "publicly acknowledge", "fail to acknowledge"]

definition: To obtain or buy something for yourself, or to learn and develop a new skill, habit, or quality.
examples: ["She managed to acquire a rare copy of the book at an auction.", "It takes years to acquire a deep understanding of a foreign language."]
usage_notes: Often used in formal, academic, or business contexts instead of 'get' or 'buy'. It is commonly used with abstract nouns like 'knowledge', 'skills', or 'habits'.
collocations: ["acquire a skill", "acquire knowledge", "acquire a habit", "acquire assets", "acquire a taste for"]

definition: From one side of something to the other side, or on the opposite side of something.
examples: ["She walked across the street to meet her friend.", "There is a lovely bakery just across the river."]
usage_notes: Commonly used as a preposition (e.g., 'across the bridge') or an adverb (e.g., 'run across'). Avoid confusing it with the verb 'cross'; we say 'walk across the road' but 'cross the road'.
collocations: ["across the street", "across the country", "across the world", "run across", "come across"]

definition: To do something, take action, or behave in a particular way; it can also mean to perform a role in a play, movie, or show.
examples: ["We need to act quickly to solve this problem before it gets worse.", "She has wanted to act in movies since she was a child."]
usage_notes: Often followed by 'on' (to act on advice) or 'like/as' (to act like a professional). As a noun, it refers to a single thing that is done.
collocations: ["act quickly", "act of kindness", "act as a guide", "put on an act", "act responsibly"]

definition: The process of doing something, typically to achieve an aim, deal with a problem, or make something happen.
examples: ["The government needs to take immediate action to help the homeless.", "I prefer action movies because they are exciting and fast-paced."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the phrase 'take action'. It is usually an uncountable noun when referring to doing things in general, but can be countable when referring to specific deeds or legal proceedings.
collocations: ["take action", "course of action", "action plan", "direct action", "legal action"]

definition: Busy doing physical or mental activities; energetic and lively.
examples: ["She plays tennis and goes running, so she is very active.", "The volcano is still active and could erupt at any time."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe a lifestyle ('an active lifestyle') or participation ('take an active role'). It is the opposite of 'passive' or 'inactive'.

definition: In a way that involves taking action, making an effort, or participating directly, rather than waiting for things to happen.
examples: ["She is actively looking for a new job in the tech industry.", "The school actively encourages students to participate in extracurricular activities."]
usage_notes: This adverb is often used before verbs to show that someone is putting conscious effort into an action, rather than just letting it happen passively.

definition: Something that you do for enjoyment, work, or to achieve a particular goal, or the state of being active and moving.
examples: ["The outdoor center offers a wide range of activities, including kayaking and climbing.", "There was a lot of activity in the office as everyone prepared for the big meeting."]
usage_notes: The word can be countable (e.g., 'leisure activities') or uncountable when referring to general movement or busy behavior (e.g., 'there was sudden activity').
collocations: ["outdoor activity", "leisure activity", "physical activity", "economic activity", "flurry of activity"]

definition: A person whose profession is acting on the stage, in movies, or on television.
examples: ["He is a talented actor who has starred in several award-winning movies.", "She decided to become an actor after performing in her high school play."]
usage_notes: While 'actress' was traditionally used for women, 'actor' is now commonly used as a gender-neutral term for both men and women.

definition: A female actor; a woman who plays a character in a movie, play, or television show.
examples: ["She won an award for being the best actress in a leading role.", "The young actress rehearsed her lines diligently before the audition."]
usage_notes: While 'actress' specifically refers to a woman, the gender-neutral term 'actor' is increasingly used for both men and women in modern English.

definition: Existing in fact or reality; real rather than imagined, planned, or guessed.
examples: ["The actual cost of the repair was much higher than the original estimate.", "I know she looks young, but what is her actual age?"]
usage_notes: A common mistake is using 'actual' to mean 'current' or 'present' due to false friends in other languages (like 'actuel' in French or 'actual' in Spanish). In English, 'actual' only means 'real' or 'factual'.

definition: Used to refer to what is real or true, or to emphasize a fact, especially when it is surprising or different from what people might expect.
examples: ["I thought the test would be difficult, but it was actually quite easy.", "Did you actually see the movie, or did you just read the review?"]
usage_notes: Often used to politely correct someone, to introduce a surprising fact, or to show contrast. In spoken English, it is sometimes used as a filler word.

definition: A short form of the word 'advertisement', which is a picture, short film, or piece of text that tries to persuade people to buy a product or service.
examples: ["I saw an interesting ad for a new smartphone on TV last night.", "Many websites display annoying pop-up ads that block the content."]
usage_notes: 'Ad' is an informal abbreviation of 'advertisement' (or 'advert' in British English). It is highly common in everyday speech and casual writing, but 'advertisement' is preferred in formal business reports or academic writing.
collocations: ["run an ad", "classified ad", "online ad", "TV ad", "ad campaign"]

definition: To change your behavior or ideas in order to deal with a new situation, or to change something so that it is suitable for a new use.
examples: ["It took the children a few months to adapt to their new school.", "The company had to adapt its marketing strategy to appeal to younger customers."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'to' (e.g., 'adapt to a new environment'). Do not confuse with 'adopt' (to take up or start using something) or 'adept' (highly skilled).
collocations: ["adapt to change", "quickly adapt", "adapt to a new environment", "adapt a recipe", "highly adaptable"]

definition: To put something together with something else so as to increase the size, number, or amount.
examples: ["If you add four and five, you get nine.", "Please add some salt to the soup to give it more flavor."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the preposition 'to' (e.g., 'add something to the mixture'). In mathematics, it is the opposite of 'subtract'.
collocations: ["add value", "add fuel to the fire", "add up the numbers", "add to the list"]

definition: To seem reasonable, logical, or consistent; or to increase gradually to a significant amount.
examples: ["His story about where he was last night just doesn't add up.", "All of these small expenses add up to a lot of money over time."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. When it means 'to make sense', it is usually used in negative sentences (e.g., 'it doesn't add up'). When it means 'to accumulate', it is often followed by the preposition 'to'.
collocations: ["doesn't add up", "add up to a total", "small things add up", "add up the numbers"]

definition: To result in a particular total amount, or to lead to a particular result or explanation.
examples: ["All these small expenses add up to a lot of money over time.", "His stories don't quite add up to a believable explanation."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. When used to mean 'result in a total', it is followed by a noun (usually a number or amount). It is inseparable, meaning you cannot put the object between 'add up' and 'to'.
collocations: ["add up to a total of", "add up to nothing", "add up to a significant amount", "add up to a big difference"]

definition: The act of adding something to something else, or a person or thing that is added.
examples: ["The new baby is a wonderful addition to their family.", "In addition to his salary, he receives a monthly bonus."]
usage_notes: Often used in the transitional phrase 'in addition (to)', which is used to introduce extra information in writing and formal speech.
collocations: ["in addition to", "a welcome addition", "latest addition", "make an addition"]

definition: Extra or added to what already exists.
examples: ["The hotel charges an additional fee for using the spa.", "If you need additional information, please do not hesitate to ask."]
usage_notes: Often used in formal, business, or academic contexts instead of the simpler word 'more'. It usually comes before a noun.

definition: To direct one's attention or efforts toward solving a problem; or, the details of where a place is located.
examples: ["We need to address the issue of climate change immediately.", "Please write your home address on the shipping form."]
usage_notes: As a verb, it is often used in formal or professional contexts (e.g., 'address a problem'). Note that the noun can be pronounced with stress on the first syllable (/ˈædrɛs/) or the second syllable (/əˈdrɛs/).
collocations: ["address an issue", "address a problem", "change of address", "mailing address", "public address"]

definition: Good enough or sufficient for a specific need or requirement, though not necessarily outstanding.
examples: ["The old heater is adequate for a small room, but it cannot warm the entire house.", "She proved that her skills were more than adequate for the job."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe something that meets a minimum standard. It can sometimes carry a slightly negative or neutral tone, implying something is 'just okay' but not excellent.
collocations: ["adequate funding", "adequate preparation", "adequate resources", "more than adequate", "prove adequate"]

definition: In a way that is enough or satisfactory for a particular need or purpose.
examples: ["The school was not adequately prepared for the sudden increase in student enrollment.", "Make sure you are adequately hydrated before starting the long run."]
usage_notes: It is the adverb form of 'adequate'. It is often used before past participles (e.g., adequately funded, adequately prepared) and carries a neutral, slightly formal tone.

definition: To change something slightly to make it fit, work better, or be more suitable; or to become accustomed to a new situation.
examples: ["You can adjust the height of the chair by pulling this lever.", "It took her a few months to adjust to living in a new city."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'to' when meaning 'to get used to' (e.g., 'adjust to the climate'). When meaning 'to alter slightly', it is a transitive verb that takes a direct object.
collocations: ["adjust to", "make adjustments", "adjust the volume", "adjust the settings", "readjust"]

definition: A feeling of deep respect, approval, and warm approval for someone or something.
examples: ["I have a lot of admiration for her courage and determination.", "The teacher looked at the student's artwork with genuine admiration."]
usage_notes: Often used with the prepositions 'for' (admiration for someone) or 'in' (to look in admiration). It is a noun; the verb form is 'admire'.
collocations: ["deep admiration", "express admiration", "win the admiration of", "mutual admiration", "filled with admiration"]

definition: To respect and warm-heartedly approve of someone or something, or to look at something with pleasure and appreciation.
examples: ["I really admire my teacher for her patience and dedication.", "We stopped for a moment to admire the beautiful sunset over the mountains."]
usage_notes: Often used in the pattern 'admire someone for something'. It is a stative verb when expressing respect, meaning it is rarely used in the continuous (-ing) form in that context.
collocations: ["deeply admire", "admire from afar", "admire someone's courage", "greatly admire"]

definition: To agree or confess that something is true, especially when you are reluctant to do so; or to allow someone to enter a place.
examples: ["He was brave enough to admit his mistake in front of the whole team.", "The museum ticket allows you to admit one person."]
usage_notes: Often followed by a gerund (verb + -ing) or a 'that' clause, for example: 'She admitted making a mistake' or 'She admitted that she was wrong'. Avoid using an infinitive (not 'admitted to make').
collocations: ["admit defeat", "admit a mistake", "grudgingly admit", "admit to a hospital", "refuse to admit"]

definition: To legally take another person's child into your own family and bring them up as your own; or to start using a new method, plan, or attitude.
examples: ["They decided to adopt a child after trying to conceive for several years.", "The company plans to adopt a new policy regarding remote work next month."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'adopt' with 'adapt' (which means to change or adjust to new conditions). 'Adopt' is a transitive verb, so it always requires a direct object.
collocations: ["adopt a child", "adopt a policy", "adopt an approach", "adopt a pet", "adopt a lifestyle"]

definition: A person who is fully grown and developed, or someone who has reached the legal age of maturity.
examples: ["Children must be accompanied by an adult at the swimming pool.", "Now that you are eighteen, you are legally an adult."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun ('an adult') or as an adjective ('adult education', 'adult life'). In US English, it is sometimes pronounced /ˈæd.ʌlt/.
collocations: ["young adult", "adult life", "responsible adult", "adult education", "consent of an adult"]

definition: To move forward, make progress, or develop; it can also refer to money paid before the usual time or progress made in a particular field.
examples: ["We need to decide how to advance our plans for the new project.", "The company gave her a cash advance to cover her travel expenses."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a verb (to advance), a noun (an advance in technology), or an adjective (advance planning). Note the common prepositional phrase 'in advance', which means beforehand.

definition: Being at a high level of progress, development, or difficulty.
examples: ["She is taking an advanced English course to prepare for her university studies.", "The hospital uses advanced technology to detect diseases early."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe courses of study, technology, or skills. It is the opposite of 'beginner' or 'basic'.

definition: A condition, circumstance, or feature that puts you in a better, more favorable, or more successful position than others.
examples: ["Having a college degree gave her a significant advantage when applying for the job.", "One of the advantages of living in a big city is the excellent public transportation system."]
usage_notes: Often used with the prepositions 'of' (e.g., 'the advantage of working from home') or 'over' (e.g., 'to have an advantage over your competitors'). Note the common idiom 'take advantage of', which can mean to use an opportunity well, or to exploit someone unfairly.
collocations: ["take advantage of", "competitive advantage", "unfair advantage", "huge advantage", "to someone's advantage"]

definition: An exciting, unusual, and sometimes dangerous experience or activity.
examples: ["Our trip through the Amazon rainforest was a real adventure.", "The children are always looking for adventure in the backyard."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a countable noun ('an adventure') or an uncountable noun ('looking for adventure'). It can also be used as a verb meaning to go somewhere risky, though this is less common.
collocations: ["sense of adventure", "outdoor adventure", "go on an adventure", "spirit of adventure"]

definition: A short form of the word 'advertisement', which is a public notice, picture, or video promoting a product, service, or event.
examples: ["I saw an interesting advert for a new smartphone on TV last night.", "They placed an advert in the local newspaper to find a new assistant."]
usage_notes: This is a British English term. In American English, the word 'ad' is much more commonly used instead of 'advert'.

definition: To tell the public about a product, service, or event in order to encourage people to buy, use, or attend it.
examples: ["The company decided to advertise their new smartphone on television and social media.", "They are advertising for a new marketing manager in the local newspaper."]
usage_notes: Can be used with 'for' when looking to hire someone or find something (e.g., 'advertise for a roommate'). Note the spelling difference: 'advertise' is standard in both US and UK English, unlike some words where UK English uses '-ise' and US uses '-ize'.
collocations: ["advertise a product", "advertise heavily", "advertise for a job", "advertise online"]

definition: A picture, short film, or text that tries to persuade people to buy a product, use a service, or apply for a job.
examples: ["I saw an advertisement for a new smartphone on television.", "The company placed an advertisement in the local newspaper to hire a new manager."]
usage_notes: Often shortened to 'ad' (informal) or 'advert' (mainly British English). Note the difference in US pronunciation (/ˌædvərˈtaɪzmənt/) and UK pronunciation (/ədˈvɜːtɪsmənt/).

definition: The business or activity of creating advertisements to persuade people to buy products, services, or ideas.
examples: ["The company spent millions of dollars on television advertising last year.", "She decided to pursue a career in digital advertising after graduating."]
usage_notes: Note that 'advertising' is an uncountable noun (e.g., 'a lot of advertising', not 'an advertising'). To talk about a single item, use 'an advertisement' or 'an ad'.

definition: An opinion or recommendation given to someone about what they should do in a particular situation.
examples: ["She asked her teacher for advice on how to study for the exam.", "My uncle gave me some good financial advice before I bought my first car."]
usage_notes: Advice is an uncountable noun. Do not say 'an advice' or 'advices'. Instead, use 'a piece of advice' or 'some advice'. Do not confuse with the verb 'advise'.
collocations: ["give advice", "take advice", "ask for advice", "a piece of advice", "good advice", "expert advice"]

definition: To give someone a recommendation or suggestion about what they should do in a particular situation.
examples: ["The doctor advised him to get more rest and drink plenty of fluids.", "I would strongly advise against making a decision before reading the full report."]
usage_notes: Commonly confused with the noun 'advice' (with a 'c'). 'Advise' is the verb form (ends in a /z/ sound). Common patterns include 'advise someone to do something' or 'advise someone against something'.
collocations: ["strongly advise", "advise someone to", "advise against", "expertly advise", "legal advise"]

definition: An event, matter, or public concern; it can also refer to a secret sexual relationship between two people, especially when at least one of them is married.
examples: ["The mayor's involvement in the financial scandal became a public affair.", "She discovered that her husband was having an affair with a co-worker."]
usage_notes: When referring to a romantic relationship, it is almost always used with the verb 'have' (e.g., 'to have an affair'). In the plural form ('affairs'), it often refers to personal or business matters, such as 'financial affairs'.
collocations: ["have an affair", "a public affair", "foreign affairs", "state of affairs", "current affairs"]

definition: To produce a change or influence in someone or something.
examples: ["The bad weather will affect our travel plans this weekend.", "How you sleep can directly affect your mood the next day."]
usage_notes: Often confused with 'effect'. 'Affect' is usually a verb (to influence), while 'effect' is usually a noun (a result).

definition: A gentle feeling of liking, fondness, or caring for someone or something.
examples: ["She showed deep affection for her old dog by taking him on slow daily walks.", "He held a lot of affection for the small town where he grew up."]
usage_notes: Usually an uncountable noun, but can be used in the plural ('affections') to refer to romantic feelings or love.
collocations: ["show affection", "deep affection", "mutual affection", "feel affection for", "win someone's affection"]

definition: To have enough money or time to be able to buy or do something.
examples: ["I would love to buy that car, but I can't afford it right now.", "We can't afford to waste any more time on this project."]
usage_notes: Usually used with 'can', 'could', or 'be able to' in negative sentences or questions. When followed by another verb, use the to-infinitive form (e.g., 'afford to buy', not 'afford buying').
collocations: ["can afford", "can't afford to", "afford the cost", "afford a luxury"]

definition: Feeling fear, worry, or anxiety about something bad that might happen.
examples: ["Don't be afraid to ask questions if you don't understand.", "She was afraid of the dark when she was a young child."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by 'of' + noun/gerund (afraid of dogs) or 'to' + verb (afraid to speak). In polite conversation, 'I'm afraid...' is often used to mean 'I am sorry to say...'. Note that 'afraid' is rarely used directly before a noun.
collocations: ["afraid of the dark", "afraid to fail", "I'm afraid that...", "nothing to be afraid of"]

definition: Later in time than something else, or behind someone or something in place or order.
examples: ["We went for a walk after dinner.", "The letter 'B' comes after 'A' in the alphabet."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a preposition, conjunction, or adverb. A common mistake is using 'after' instead of 'in' when referring to a future time period (e.g., say 'I will return in an hour,' not 'after an hour').
collocations: ["after all", "day after day", "one after another", "shortly after", "named after"]

definition: The period of time between midday (noon) and evening.
examples: ["I usually feel a bit tired in the afternoon, so I drink some tea.", "Are you free this afternoon to go for a walk?"]
usage_notes: We use the preposition 'in' when referring to this time of day (e.g., 'in the afternoon'), but we use 'this' or 'yesterday' without a preposition (e.g., 'this afternoon').
collocations: ["this afternoon", "in the afternoon", "afternoon tea", "good afternoon", "late afternoon"]

definition: At a later time; after something else has happened.
examples: ["We had a quick lunch and went for a walk afterwards.", "She was tired during the meeting, but felt much better afterwards."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'afterwards' is the standard form, while 'afterward' (without the 's') is more common in American English, though both are widely understood. It is an adverb and cannot be followed directly by a noun; use 'after' instead (e.g., 'after the game', not 'afterwards the game').

definition: One more time; once more, or returning to a previous place, state, or position.
examples: ["Could you please say that again? I didn't hear you.", "It was great to see her again after so many years."]
usage_notes: Often placed at the end of a sentence. In spoken English, 'then again' is commonly used to introduce a contrasting thought.
collocations: ["once again", "again and again", "never again", "then again", "try again"]

definition: In opposition to, in contact with, or as a protection from something.
examples: ["The local residents are voting against the new highway proposal.", "He leaned his bicycle against the wooden fence."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with verbs of physical contact (lean, press) or verbs of opposition (fight, argue, vote). Avoid using 'against' when 'to' or 'with' is required by the verb.
collocations: ["against the law", "against the rules", "lean against", "fight against", "against all odds"]

definition: The number of years someone has lived or something has existed, or a specific period of time in history.
examples: ["She started learning how to play the piano at a very young age.", "We are currently living in the digital age, where information is easily accessible."]
usage_notes: When asking about someone's age, use 'How old are you?' rather than 'What is your age?' in informal spoken English.
collocations: ["at the age of", "old age", "digital age", "middle age", "look your age"]

definition: Having lived or existed for a long time; old, or of a specified age.
examples: ["The cheese is aged for two years to develop a strong flavor.", "He volunteered at a community center helping aged members of the neighborhood."]
usage_notes: When used to mean 'very old', it is pronounced as two syllables (/ˈeɪ.dʒɪd/), as in 'the aged'. When used to state a specific age (e.g., 'a child aged ten') or referring to food/wine, it is pronounced as one syllable (/eɪdʒd/).

definition: A business or organization that provides a specific service, often acting on behalf of another person or group; it can also mean the ability of an individual to make their own choices and take action.
examples: ["She decided to hire an advertising agency to help promote her new brand.", "The program aims to give young people a sense of agency over their own lives."]
usage_notes: In business contexts, it usually refers to a service organization (like a travel agency). In academic, philosophical, or sociological contexts, it refers to the capacity of individuals to act independently.
collocations: ["travel agency", "government agency", "advertising agency", "sense of agency", "employment agency"]

definition: A person or business that acts on behalf of another person or group, or a representative who manages affairs like business or travel.
examples: ["We hired a real estate agent to help us sell our house.", "The secret agent gathered important information for the government."]
usage_notes: Countable noun. Often followed by the preposition 'for' (e.g., an agent for the company).
collocations: ["real estate agent", "travel agent", "FBI agent", "literary agent", "insurance agent"]

definition: Behaving in an angry or violent way towards others, or using very strong and forceful methods to achieve success.
examples: ["The dog became aggressive whenever anyone approached its food bowl.", "The company launched an aggressive marketing campaign to win new customers."]
usage_notes: While 'aggressive' often has a negative meaning related to anger or violence, in business and sports it can be positive, meaning 'highly energetic, assertive, and determined to win'.

definition: In the past, measuring back from the present time.
examples: ["I graduated from college five years ago.", "The train left just a few minutes ago."]
usage_notes: Always placed after the measurement of time (e.g., 'three days ago', NOT 'ago three days'). It is used with the simple past tense, not the present perfect.
collocations: ["a long time ago", "a moment ago", "years ago", "not long ago", "centuries ago"]

definition: To have the same opinion as someone else, or to say yes to a suggestion or plan.
examples: ["I completely agree with your decision to move to a new city.", "They agreed to meet at the coffee shop at two o'clock."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by 'with' (for people or opinions) or 'to' (for actions or proposals). Avoid saying 'I am agree'; the correct form is 'I agree'.
collocations: ["agree with someone", "agree to do something", "agree on a plan", "completely agree", "agree to disagree"]

definition: A decision or arrangement shared by two or more people, groups, or organizations, or the state of sharing the same opinion.
examples: ["After hours of negotiation, the two companies finally signed a written agreement.", "We are in complete agreement about where to go for our summer vacation."]
usage_notes: Often used with the prepositions 'on' (agreement on a topic) or 'with' (in agreement with someone). It can be countable (an agreement/agreements) or uncountable (reach agreement).
collocations: ["reach an agreement", "sign an agreement", "written agreement", "in agreement", "mutual agreement"]

definition: In front, further forward in space or time, or making progress toward a goal.
examples: ["Go straight ahead for two blocks, and the library will be on your right.", "We need to plan ahead if we want to finish the project on time."]
usage_notes: Often paired with 'of' (e.g., 'ahead of schedule', 'ahead of us'). Used as an adverb or adjective, but usually follows the verb or noun it modifies.
collocations: ["straight ahead", "look ahead", "plan ahead", "ahead of time", "ahead of schedule"]

definition: Help or support given to someone, often in the form of money, food, or services, especially during a difficult situation.
examples: ["The organization sent emergency aid to the victims of the earthquake.", "A dictionary is a useful aid when you are learning a new language."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'aid' is more formal than 'help'. As a noun, it can refer to the assistance itself (uncountable) or a helpful device/tool (countable, e.g., 'visual aids').
collocations: ["first aid", "foreign aid", "humanitarian aid", "financial aid", "with the aid of"]

definition: To point a weapon or object at a target, or to direct your efforts toward achieving a specific goal.
examples: ["She aims to finish her degree by the end of next year.", "He carefully took aim before shooting at the target."]
usage_notes: When used as a verb meaning 'intend,' it is typically followed by an infinitive ('aim to do something'). As a noun, it often pairs with 'achieve' or 'reach'.
collocations: ["take aim", "main aim", "aim to achieve", "aim at a target"]

definition: The invisible mixture of gases that surrounds the Earth, which people and animals breathe.
examples: ["It was a hot day, so we went outside to get some fresh air.", "Balloons float because they are filled with gas that is lighter than air."]
usage_notes: When referring to the atmosphere we breathe, 'air' is an uncountable noun and does not take a plural form.

definition: Any vehicle that is able to fly through the air, such as an airplane, helicopter, or glider.
examples: ["The airport has a large hangar used for maintaining commercial aircraft.", "The military deployed several aircraft to assist with the rescue mission."]
usage_notes: The word 'aircraft' is the same in both singular and plural forms. Do not say 'aircrafts'.
collocations: ["commercial aircraft", "military aircraft", "aircraft carrier", "board the aircraft", "unmanned aircraft"]

definition: A place where aircraft regularly take off and land, equipped with facilities for passengers and goods.
examples: ["We arrived at the airport two hours before our flight.", "Her plane lands at the international airport tonight."]
usage_notes: Remember to use the preposition 'at' when talking about being located inside or near an airport (e.g., 'I am at the airport').
collocations: ["international airport", "airport terminal", "head to the airport", "airport security"]

definition: A device that makes a loud noise to warn people of danger or to wake them up; or a sudden feeling of fear or worry that something bad might happen.
examples: ["I set my alarm for 6:00 AM so I wouldn't miss the train.", "The sound of the smoke alarm made everyone run out of the building."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a noun and a verb (e.g., 'The news alarmed her'). In everyday conversation, 'alarm' often refers to an 'alarm clock'.
collocations: ["set an alarm", "sound the alarm", "false alarm", "alarm system", "cause alarm"]

definition: Feeling worried, frightened, or anxious that something dangerous or unpleasant might happen.
examples: ["She was alarmed by the sudden increase in her electricity bill.", "Local residents are alarmed at the prospect of a new highway being built through the forest."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the prepositions 'by' or 'at' (e.g., 'alarmed by the news'). It can also be followed by a to-infinitive (e.g., 'alarmed to hear') or a 'that' clause.
collocations: ["alarmed by", "alarmed at", "growing alarmed", "deeply alarmed", "alarmed to find"]

definition: Causing worry, fear, or surprise because something is dangerous or getting worse.
examples: ["The doctor noticed an alarming rise in the patient's blood pressure.", "It is alarming how fast the ice caps are melting."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe news, statistics, rates, or trends that cause deep concern.

definition: Drinks such as beer, wine, or whiskey that can make people drunk; or a chemical substance used in medicine and industry for cleaning or sterilizing.
examples: ["The doctor advised him to avoid drinking alcohol while taking the medication.", "Rubbing alcohol is commonly used to clean minor cuts and disinfect surfaces."]
usage_notes: The word 'alcohol' is an uncountable noun. When referring to drinks, we say 'some alcohol' or 'bottles of alcohol', but not 'an alcohol'.

definition: Containing alcohol, or relating to a person who is unable to control their drinking of alcohol.
examples: ["Would you prefer an alcoholic drink or a fruit juice?", "He has been a recovering alcoholic for over five years."]
usage_notes: The word can be used as an adjective (e.g., 'alcoholic beverages') or as a noun to refer to a person (e.g., 'he is an alcoholic'). When referring to people, it is often sensitive, and terms like 'person with alcohol use disorder' are sometimes preferred in medical contexts.

definition: Living and not dead, or full of life, energy, and activity.
examples: ["Doctors worked hard to keep the patient alive.", "The streets came alive with music and dancing during the festival."]
usage_notes: 'Alive' is usually used after a verb (like 'be', 'keep', or 'stay') rather than directly before a noun. Use 'living' or 'live' before a noun instead (e.g., 'a living person', not 'an alive person').
collocations: ["stay alive", "keep alive", "come alive", "alive and well", "buried alive"]

definition: The whole quantity, amount, or number of something; every single one of a group.
examples: ["She ate all the apples in the basket.", "All of the students passed the final exam."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a determiner, pronoun, or adverb. When followed by a noun, 'all' or 'all of' can often both be used (e.g., 'all the people' or 'all of the people').
collocations: ["all day", "all over", "all the time", "all of a sudden", "first of all"]

definition: Satisfactory, acceptable, or uninjured; it is also used to express agreement or to check if someone is safe or needs help.
examples: ["Is everything all right, or do you need some help?", "The movie wasn't amazing, but it was all right."]
usage_notes: Always write as two words ('all right') in formal writing. The single-word spelling 'alright' is common in informal contexts, but often considered incorrect in standard written English.
collocations: ["turn out all right", "feel all right", "all right with me", "do all right"]

definition: Joined together or working in partnership with another country, group, or organization to achieve a common purpose.
examples: ["The two companies formed an allied network to expand their market reach.", "Allied forces worked together to provide humanitarian aid to the region."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective (e.g., 'allied nations') or as the past tense of the verb 'ally' (often followed by 'with' or 'to').

definition: To give permission for someone to do something, or to let something happen.
examples: ["My parents don't allow me to stay out past midnight.", "The new rules allow students to use calculators during the exam."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the pattern 'allow someone to do something' (active) or 'be allowed to do something' (passive). Avoid using a gerund directly after a person, such as 'allow him doing'.
collocations: ["allow access", "allow time", "not allowed to", "allow for the possibility"]

definition: To consider or include something when making a plan, calculation, or judgment.
examples: ["You should allow for traffic delays when planning your trip to the airport.", "The budget needs to allow for unexpected expenses."]
usage_notes: Always followed by a noun or gerund (-ing form). Often used when preparing for potential future problems or changes.
collocations: ["allow for extra time", "allow for unexpected costs", "allow for delays", "allow for growth"]

definition: A person, group, or country that agrees to help and support another, especially in a war or for a shared purpose.
examples: ["The two countries became strong allies during the conflict.", "She has been a valuable ally in my fight for better working conditions."]
usage_notes: When used as a verb, it is pronounced /əˈlaɪ/ (e.g., 'to ally oneself with someone'). As a noun, the stress is on the first syllable.

definition: Very nearly, but not completely.
examples: ["I'm almost finished with my homework.", "It took almost an hour to get there."]
usage_notes: Place 'almost' directly before the word it modifies (e.g., 'almost ready', 'almost finished'). Avoid using 'very' before 'almost'.

definition: Without any other people present, or feeling isolated without help or support.
examples: ["She enjoys sitting alone in the park to read a book.", "He managed to fix the entire car all by himself, completely alone.", "You are not alone in feeling nervous about the upcoming exam."]
usage_notes: 'Alone' is typically used as an adjective after a verb (e.g., 'he was alone'), not directly before a noun. To describe feeling sad about being by yourself, use 'lonely' instead.
collocations: ["leave me alone", "all alone", "feel alone", "stand alone", "fly alone"]

definition: Moving in a constant direction on or beside a path, road, or line, or being together with someone.
examples: ["We took a pleasant walk along the riverbank.", "Do you mind if I come along to the movie?"]
usage_notes: Often used as a preposition (walk along the road) or an adverb (bring someone along). Common in phrasal verbs like 'get along' or 'go along'.
collocations: ["all along", "along the way", "go along with", "come along", "get along with"]

definition: Next to or together with something or someone.
examples: ["A new highway was built alongside the old railway line.", "She worked alongside famous scientists during her research project."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a preposition (followed directly by a noun, e.g., 'alongside the road') and an adverb (e.g., 'the boat pulled alongside'). It is often used metaphorically to mean working together in cooperation.

definition: In a voice that can be heard clearly, rather than silently in your mind.
examples: ["She read the story aloud to her younger brother.", "I accidentally said my thoughts aloud during the quiet meeting."]
usage_notes: Often confused with 'out loud', which means the same thing but is slightly more informal. 'Aloud' usually follows verbs related to speaking or reading, such as 'read', 'think', or 'say'.

definition: A set of letters or symbols in a fixed order used to represent the basic sounds of a language when writing.
examples: ["The English alphabet consists of twenty-six letters.", "Young children often learn the alphabet by singing a song."]
usage_notes: Countable noun. Often used with 'the' when referring to the full set of letters of a specific language.

definition: Arranged in the order of the letters of the alphabet, from A to Z.
examples: ["The files are kept in alphabetical order by the last name of each client.", "Please arrange the books on the shelf alphabetically."]
usage_notes: Most commonly used in the phrase 'in alphabetical order'.

definition: In the order of the letters of the alphabet, from A to Z.
examples: ["The students' names are listed alphabetically on the roster.", "Please arrange the files alphabetically by last name."]
usage_notes: Often used with verbs of organizing, such as 'arrange', 'sort', 'list', or 'organize'. The adjective form is 'alphabetical'.
collocations: ["arranged alphabetically", "listed alphabetically", "sorted alphabetically", "alphabetically by name", "in alphabetical order"]

definition: Before the present time, or earlier than the time expected.
examples: ["I have already finished my homework, so I can go out to play.", "Is it 9:00 PM already? Time flies!"]
usage_notes: Often used with the present perfect tense (e.g., 'have already done'). Be careful not to confuse 'already' (one word meaning 'by this time') with 'all ready' (two words meaning 'completely prepared').

definition: In addition; too; besides.
examples: ["She speaks French, and she also speaks Spanish.", "I am tired, and I am also very hungry."]
usage_notes: In a sentence, 'also' usually goes before the main verb, but after the verb 'to be' or auxiliary verbs (e.g., 'I also like it' vs. 'I am also here'). It is rarely used at the very end of a sentence in standard English; 'too' or 'as well' are preferred there.
collocations: ["not only... but also", "also known as", "but also", "also referred to as"]

definition: To change or modify something, usually in a small or limited way.
examples: ["She had to alter her travel plans because of the bad weather.", "The tailor will alter the jacket so that it fits him perfectly."]
usage_notes: Often confused with 'altar' (a table or structure used in religious ceremonies). It is a formal or semi-formal synonym for 'change'.
collocations: ["alter plans", "alter behavior", "significantly alter", "alter clothes", "alter the course"]

definition: A choice or possibility that is different from the current option, or describing something that is available as another choice.
examples: ["We decided to look for an alternative route to avoid the heavy traffic.", "If the main plan fails, do you have a viable alternative?"]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a noun (e.g., 'an alternative') and an adjective (e.g., 'an alternative plan').

definition: Used to introduce a different option, choice, or possibility from the one previously mentioned.
examples: ["We could take the train to the airport. Alternatively, we can hire a taxi.", "You can pay the full amount now or, alternatively, pay in three monthly installments."]
usage_notes: It usually appears at the beginning of a sentence or clause, followed by a comma, to propose another idea.

definition: Used to introduce a statement that makes the main statement seem surprising or unexpected; in spite of the fact that.
examples: ["Although it was raining heavily, they decided to go for a walk in the park.", "She decided to buy the car, although it was more expensive than she had planned."]
usage_notes: Do not use 'but' in the same sentence when you start with 'although' (e.g., say 'Although it was cold, he went out,' not 'Although it was cold, but he went out'). It is more formal than 'though'.
collocations: ["although some might argue", "although it is true that", "although not entirely", "although necessary"]

definition: Completely, or including everyone or everything to give a total.
examples: ["That makes fifty dollars altogether.", "I am not altogether sure that this is the best idea."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'altogether' (meaning completely or in total) with 'all together' (meaning all people or things gathered in one place).

definition: At all times, on every occasion, or continuously without stopping.
examples: ["She always drinks a cup of coffee before starting her workday.", "The sun always rises in the east."]
usage_notes: Placed before the main verb, but after the verb 'to be' or auxiliary verbs (e.g., 'She is always late', 'I have always liked him'). When used with the present continuous tense (e.g., 'He is always complaining'), it often expresses annoyance.

definition: To surprise someone very much or fill them with wonder.
examples: ["Her ability to speak five languages fluently never fails to amaze me.", "The magician's incredible tricks amazed the entire audience."]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive form ('to be amazed by/at something') or as a participle adjective ('amazing' or 'amazed').
collocations: ["never cease to amaze", "continue to amaze", "amaze the world", "utterly amaze"]

definition: Extremely surprised and impressed by something unexpected or remarkable.
examples: ["I was amazed by how quickly she learned to play the piano.", "We stood there in silence, amazed at the breathtaking view of the mountains."]
usage_notes: Usually followed by the prepositions 'at', 'by', or a 'that'-clause. Do not confuse with 'amazing', which describes the thing causing the feeling.
collocations: ["absolutely amazed", "amazed at the difference", "amazed to see", "amazed by the news"]

definition: Causing great surprise, wonder, or admiration; extremely good or impressive.
examples: ["The view from the top of the mountain was absolutely amazing.", "She did an amazing job on her final presentation."]
usage_notes: Very common in everyday spoken English. Often intensified with adverbs like 'absolutely' rather than 'very'.
collocations: ["an amazing idea", "look amazing", "absolutely amazing", "an amazing experience"]

definition: A strong desire and determination to achieve success, power, or a specific goal.
examples: ["Her ambition is to become a top surgeon and lead her own research team.", "He lacked the ambition needed to advance in his corporate career."]
usage_notes: Usually a positive quality showing drive, but can sometimes imply being overly ruthless if someone has 'too much ambition'. Common prepositions include 'ambition for' something or 'ambition to do' something.
collocations: ["achieve an ambition", "burning ambition", "fuel someone's ambition", "career ambition", "personal ambition"]

definition: A specialized vehicle equipped to treat and transport sick or injured people to a hospital in an emergency.
examples: ["Someone called an ambulance immediately after the accident occurred.", "You must pull over to the side of the road when you hear an ambulance siren."]
usage_notes: Countable noun. Often used with verbs like 'call', 'send', or 'ride in'. In emergencies, people usually say 'call an ambulance'.
collocations: ["call an ambulance", "ambulance siren", "ambulance crew", "ride in an ambulance"]

definition: In the middle of, surrounded by, or included within a group of three or more people or things.
examples: ["She felt comfortable standing among her close friends.", "The house was hidden among a dense grove of oak trees."]
usage_notes: Use 'among' when referring to three or more distinct items or a collective group. Use 'between' when referring to two distinct items.
collocations: ["among others", "among the best", "divide among", "popular among", "scattered among"]

definition: The total quantity or measure of something, especially things that cannot be counted individually.
examples: ["He spent a large amount of money on his new car.", "A small amount of rain fell during the night."]
usage_notes: Use 'amount' with uncountable nouns (e.g., amount of water, amount of time). Use 'number' with countable nouns (e.g., number of people, number of books).
collocations: ["large amount", "small amount", "amount of money", "amount of time", "total amount"]

definition: To add up to a total quantity, or to be equivalent to something in impact or meaning.
examples: ["The total expenses for the trip amount to over five hundred dollars.", "Her silence on the matter amounts to an admission of guilt."]
usage_notes: Often used in business or math contexts to talk about totals, or in general contexts to mean 'equal to' or 'be the same as'. It is usually followed by a noun or a gerund (-ing form).
collocations: ["amount to a total of", "amount to the same thing", "amount to nothing", "amounts to a refusal"]

definition: To entertain someone or make them smile or laugh.
examples: ["The magician's tricks continued to amuse the young children.", "I brought a book to keep myself amused during the long flight."]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive voice as 'be amused' or with the pattern 'amuse yourself'. Do not confuse 'amused' (feeling entertained) with 'amusing' (causing entertainment).
collocations: ["amuse oneself", "be easily amused", "seem amused", "keep someone amused"]

definition: Finding something funny, entertaining, or enjoyable.
examples: ["She had an amused smile on her face as she watched the puppy chase its tail.", "He was quietly amused by his friend's silly mistake."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'by' or 'at' (e.g., 'amused by the story'). Do not confuse with 'bemused', which means confused.
collocations: ["easily amused", "amused smile", "look amused", "be amused by", "mildly amused"]

definition: Causing laughter or providing entertainment; funny and enjoyable.
examples: ["She told an amusing story about her first day at work.", "I found the movie quite amusing, even though the plot was simple."]
usage_notes: It is an adjective usually applied to stories, situations, or people. While it means funny, it often implies light, mild entertainment rather than hilarious laughter.
collocations: ["amusing story", "amusing anecdote", "find something amusing", "quite amusing", "mildly amusing"]

definition: To study or examine something in detail, breaking it down into parts, in order to understand it or find relationships.
examples: ["The researchers need to analyse the blood samples before they can make a diagnosis.", "We spent hours trying to analyse the sales data to find out why profits dropped."]
usage_notes: 'Analyse' is the standard British English spelling, whereas 'analyze' is the standard American English spelling. It is a transitive verb, meaning it is followed directly by an object.
collocations: ["analyse data", "analyse results", "carefully analyse", "analyse a situation", "analyse trends"]

definition: The detailed study or examination of something in order to understand it better or draw conclusions.
examples: ["The scientist published a detailed analysis of the experiment's results.", "A quick analysis of the market showed that demand for electric cars is growing."]
usage_notes: The plural form is 'analyses' (pronounced /əˈnæləsiːz/). Common verb form is 'analyze'.
collocations: ["detailed analysis", "data analysis", "conduct an analysis", "final analysis", "critical analysis"]

definition: Belonging to a period of history that is thousands of years in the past, or very old.
examples: ["Archaeologists discovered the ruins of an ancient city buried under the desert.", "My grandfather loves telling stories about his ancient car."]
usage_notes: When referring to history, 'ancient' usually means the period before the fall of the Western Roman Empire. In informal speech, it is often exaggerated to mean anything very old.

definition: A conjunction used to connect words, phrases, or clauses that belong together.
examples: ["I bought apples and oranges at the store.", "She sat down and started to read her book."]
usage_notes: In fast speech, 'and' is often unstressed and pronounced as /ən/ or /n/ (e.g., 'rock 'n' roll'). Avoid starting too many sentences with 'and' in formal writing.
collocations: ["black and white", "bread and butter", "on and on", "more and more"]

definition: A strong feeling of being annoyed, upset, or hostile because of something wrong or unfair.
examples: ["She tried to hide her anger when she heard the unfair decision.", "He spoke in anger and later regretted the words he used."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both an uncountable noun ('feel anger') and a verb ('to anger someone'). A common prepositions to use with the noun is 'in' (e.g., 'said in anger').
collocations: ["extreme anger", "express anger", "manage anger", "outburst of anger", "shake with anger"]

definition: The space between two lines or surfaces that meet, measured in degrees, or a particular way of looking at a situation.
examples: ["The two roads meet at a sharp angle.", "Try looking at the problem from a different angle."]
usage_notes: Can be used literally in geometry and design, or figuratively to mean 'perspective' or 'approach'.
collocations: ["right angle", "sharp angle", "different angle", "camera angle", "from every angle"]

definition: In a manner that shows strong feelings of annoyance, displeasure, or hostility.
examples: ["He slammed the door angrily after the argument.", "She glared angrily at the person who cut in line."]
usage_notes: It is an adverb that modifies verbs showing actions done in anger (e.g., 'mutter angrily', 'reply angrily'). Do not confuse it with the adjective 'angry'.

definition: Feeling or showing strong displeasure, resentment, or hostility because of something wrong, unfair, or hurtful.
examples: ["He was very angry with his sister for breaking his favorite mug.", "The customers became angry when they were told the flight was delayed by five hours."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the prepositions 'at' or 'with' for people (e.g., 'angry with him'), and 'about' or 'at' for situations (e.g., 'angry about the decision').
collocations: ["get angry", "angry with someone", "angry about something", "look angry", "make someone angry"]

definition: A living creature that can move around and react to its surroundings, but is not a human, plant, or fungus.
examples: ["The zoo is home to many different kinds of wild animals.", "Dogs and cats are two of the most popular domestic animals."]
usage_notes: In everyday speech, 'animal' usually excludes humans, though scientifically humans are animals. It can also refer to mammals specifically, as opposed to birds, fish, or insects.

definition: The joint that connects the foot with the lower leg.
examples: ["She twisted her ankle while running down the stairs.", "The ice water came up to my ankles."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with verbs like 'sprain', 'twist', or 'break'.

definition: A date that is remembered or celebrated because a special event happened on that date in a previous year.
examples: ["We are going out to a nice restaurant to celebrate our wedding anniversary.", "Today marks the 10th anniversary of the company's founding."]
usage_notes: Often used with ordinal numbers (e.g., '5th anniversary', '50th anniversary'). For a 50th anniversary, the term 'golden anniversary' is commonly used.
collocations: ["wedding anniversary", "celebrate an anniversary", "mark an anniversary", "annual anniversary"]

definition: To make something known publicly or officially.
examples: ["The company will announce its new product line tomorrow morning.", "They happily announced their engagement to family and friends."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'that' (announce that...) or with a direct object (announce a decision). Note the pattern 'announce something to someone' rather than 'announce someone something'.
collocations: ["officially announce", "announce a decision", "announce a plan", "announce a winner", "proud to announce"]

definition: To make someone feel slightly angry, impatient, or irritated.
examples: ["The constant dripping of the faucet began to annoy her.", "It really annoys me when people talk loudly on their phones during the movie."]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive voice as 'be annoyed' (e.g., 'I was annoyed by his behavior') or as an adjective 'annoying' to describe the thing causing the irritation.
collocations: ["annoy someone intensely", "begin to annoy", "easily annoyed", "annoy the neighbors"]

definition: Slightly angry, irritated, or bothered by someone or something.
examples: ["She was annoyed with him for arriving late to the meeting.", "I get really annoyed when people talk loudly on the phone during a movie."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the prepositions 'with' or 'at' when referring to a person, and 'by' or 'about' when referring to a situation (e.g., 'annoyed with him', 'annoyed by the noise').
collocations: ["annoyed with someone", "annoyed by something", "get annoyed", "look annoyed", "slightly annoyed"]

definition: Causing irritation, slight anger, or nuisance.
examples: ["It is really annoying when people talk loudly on their phones during a movie.", "He has an annoying habit of interrupting others while they speak."]
usage_notes: 'Annoying' describes the thing or person that causes irritation, while 'annoyed' describes the feeling a person has.

definition: Happening or done once every year, or relating to a period of one year.
examples: ["The company holds its annual meeting every spring.", "Sunflowers are annual plants that complete their lifecycle in one season."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'annual' (happening once a year) with 'biennial' (happening every two years) or 'perennial' (lasting for many years). It can be used as an adjective or as a noun (meaning a plant that lives for one year).

definition: Once every year or every twelve months.
examples: ["The company publishes its financial report annually.", "We hold an annually organized festival every October."]
usage_notes: It is an adverb. The adjective form is 'annual'. Do not confuse 'annually' (once a year) with 'biannually' (twice a year).

definition: One more person or thing of the same type, or a different one.
examples: ["Would you like another cup of coffee?", "That plan didn't work, so we need to try another one."]
usage_notes: 'Another' is used with singular countable nouns. Do not use it directly with plural nouns (use 'other' or 'more' instead).

definition: To say, write, or do something in reaction to a question, letter, phone call, or situation.
examples: ["She raised her hand to answer the teacher's question.", "I tried calling him twice, but nobody answered the phone."]
usage_notes: When used as a verb, do not use 'to' before the object (e.g., say 'answer the question', not 'answer to the question'). As a noun, it is followed by 'to' (e.g., 'the answer to the question').
collocations: ["answer a question", "answer the phone", "answer a call", "correct answer", "short answer"]

definition: A prefix meaning opposed to, against, or preventing something.
examples: ["The doctor prescribed an antibiotic to help fight the bacterial infection.", "She joined an anti-war protest in the city center."]
usage_notes: When attached to a proper noun (e.g., anti-American) or to avoid double vowels (e.g., anti-inflammatory), a hyphen is typically used. In many common words, it is written as a single word without a hyphen (e.g., social becomes antisocial).

definition: To expect or predict that something will happen, and often to prepare for it in advance.
examples: ["We anticipate a full recovery for the patient after a few weeks of rest.", "The company did not anticipate such a high demand for its new product."]
usage_notes: Often followed by a noun, a gerund (-ing form), or a 'that' clause. Avoid using a full infinitive (to + verb) directly after 'anticipate'.

definition: A feeling of worry, nervousness, or unease about something with an uncertain outcome.
examples: ["He felt a wave of anxiety before giving his presentation to the team.", "Deep breathing exercises can help reduce anxiety during stressful situations."]
usage_notes: Uncountable when referring to the general feeling, but can be countable ('anxieties') when referring to specific worries or fears.

definition: Feeling worried, nervous, or uneasy about something with an uncertain outcome. It can also mean being very eager or wanting to do something very much.
examples: ["She felt anxious about her upcoming job interview.", "He was anxious to start his new job as soon as possible."]
usage_notes: When meaning 'worried', it is usually followed by 'about' (e.g., anxious about the test). When meaning 'eager', it is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., anxious to leave).
collocations: ["feel anxious", "anxious about", "anxious to do something", "anxious thought", "anxious wait"]

definition: In a manner that shows nervousness, worry, or unease about something that may happen.
examples: ["She waited anxiously by the phone for the test results.", "The passengers looked anxiously out the window as the storm grew worse."]
usage_notes: This is an adverb derived from the adjective 'anxious'. It is commonly followed by prepositions like 'about', 'for', or verbs of waiting and watching.

definition: Used to refer to one or some of a thing or number of things, no matter how much or how many, especially in negative statements and questions.
examples: ["Do you have any questions about the assignment?", "I don't have any money left in my wallet."]
usage_notes: Typically used in questions and negative sentences, while 'some' is preferred in positive affirmative sentences.
collocations: ["any time", "any longer", "at any rate", "hardly any", "any moment"]

definition: Any person; used in questions, negative statements, and conditional sentences to refer to an unspecified person.
examples: ["Is anybody home?", "I didn't see anybody I knew at the party."]
usage_notes: "Anybody" and "anyone" are interchangeable, but "anybody" is slightly more informal. It is grammatically singular, so it takes a singular verb (e.g., "Does anybody know?"), but is often referred to with plural pronouns (e.g., "Does anybody have their keys?").

definition: Any person; used in questions, negative statements, and conditional sentences, or to mean 'any person at all' in positive sentences.
examples: ["Does anyone know where the library is?", "Anyone can join the club, regardless of their age."]
usage_notes: Written as one word. Do not confuse with 'any one' (two words), which refers to one specific person or thing from a group.
collocations: ["anyone else", "hardly anyone", "is anyone there", "anyone who wants"]

definition: Used to refer to a thing, no matter what kind, especially in questions, negative statements, or conditional sentences.
examples: ["Is there anything I can do to help you?", "I haven't eaten anything since breakfast."]
usage_notes: Use 'anything' in questions and negative sentences, but use 'something' in positive statements. 'Anything' can also mean 'it doesn't matter which thing' in positive sentences (e.g., 'You can choose anything you want').
collocations: ["anything else", "hardly anything", "do anything", "if anything", "anything at all"]
