definition: Used to change the subject, return to an earlier topic, or to indicate that something is true despite other facts.
examples: ["It was raining, but we went for a walk anyway.", "Anyway, as I was saying before we were interrupted, the meeting is at two o'clock."]
usage_notes: Often used as a transition word in spoken English. Be careful not to confuse it with 'anyways', which is considered informal or non-standard.

definition: In, at, or to any place. It is often used in questions, negative statements, or to mean 'it doesn't matter where'.
examples: ["I can't find my keys anywhere in the house.", "You can sit anywhere you like."]
usage_notes: 'Anywhere' is a single word. Avoid writing it as 'any where'. In British English, 'anyplace' is sometimes used informally, but 'anywhere' is standard in all dialects.

definition: Separated by a distance in time, space, or relation; not together.
examples: ["The two houses were built about fifty yards apart.", "We had to take the old clock apart to see what was wrong with it."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'from' (e.g., 'apart from') to mean 'except for' or 'in addition to'. It is also commonly paired with verbs like 'take' (take apart) and 'fall' (fall apart).

definition: Except for, or in addition to; used to show that someone or something is not included in a statement, or to introduce an extra point.
examples: ["Apart from a few minor spelling mistakes, your essay was excellent.", "Apart from the high price, the hotel was absolutely perfect."]
usage_notes: This phrase can mean both 'excluding' (except for) and 'including' (in addition to), depending on the context. It is synonymous with 'aside from' in American English.
collocations: ["apart from that", "apart from the fact that", "apart from anything else", "apart from a few"]

definition: A set of rooms for living in, usually on one floor of a building containing other similar sets of rooms.
examples: ["She lives in a modern two-bedroom apartment in the city center.", "They are looking to rent a cheap apartment near the university."]
usage_notes: In British English, the word 'flat' is much more commonly used instead of 'apartment'.
collocations: ["rent an apartment", "studio apartment", "apartment building", "spacious apartment", "furnished apartment"]

definition: To say that you are sorry for doing something wrong or causing a problem.
examples: ["I want to apologize for being late to the meeting.", "She apologized to her friend after they had an argument."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'to' for the person being addressed (apologize to someone) and 'for' for the reason (apologize for something). In British English, it is often spelled 'apologise'.
collocations: ["apologize sincerely", "apologize for the delay", "apologize to someone", "publicly apologize", "demand an apology"]

definition: Easy to see or understand, or seeming to be true although it may not actually be so.
examples: ["It became apparent that she was not going to change her mind.", "Their apparent success was actually the result of a lot of hidden debt."]
usage_notes: Often used before a noun to mean 'seeming' (e.g., 'his apparent wealth'), or after a verb like 'become' or 'be' to mean 'obvious' (e.g., 'it is apparent that...').
collocations: ["become apparent", "for no apparent reason", "apparent discrepancy", "heir apparent", "apparent ease"]

definition: Used to say that something seems to be true based on what you have heard, read, or seen, even though you are not completely sure.
examples: ["Apparently, the meeting has been postponed until next Thursday.", "I thought they were married, but apparently they are just good friends."]
usage_notes: It is often placed at the beginning of a sentence to introduce a piece of information you learned from someone else. It can sound slightly informal or conversational, but it is also common in written English.

definition: To make a serious, urgent, or formal request for help, mercy, or a change in a decision; or to be attractive and interesting to someone.
examples: ["The charity made an urgent appeal for donations to help the flood victims.", "The idea of working from home doesn't appeal to everyone."]
usage_notes: When meaning 'to be attractive,' it is followed by the preposition 'to' (e.g., 'it appeals to me'). In legal contexts, it can be used as a verb or a noun to describe challenging a court decision.
collocations: ["appeal to someone", "make an appeal", "lose its appeal", "broad appeal", "lodge an appeal"]

definition: To start to be seen, or to give the impression of being or doing something.
examples: ["A small boat suddenly appeared on the horizon.", "She tried to appear calm, but she was actually very nervous."]
usage_notes: Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'He appears to be lost') or a 'that' clause. In the sense of 'to seem', it is a linking verb and is followed by an adjective, not an adverb.
collocations: ["appear to be", "suddenly appear", "appear in public", "make an appearance"]

definition: The way that someone or something looks on the outside, or the act of coming into sight or public view.
examples: ["She was very professional in her dress and general appearance.", "The famous author made a brief appearance at the local bookstore."]
usage_notes: The word can refer to physical looks (countable or uncountable) or the act of showing up (countable). Common verbs used with it include 'keep up' (to maintain a good social image) and 'make' (to show up).
collocations: ["physical appearance", "make an appearance", "personal appearance", "keep up appearances", "sudden appearance"]

definition: A round fruit with red, green, or yellow skin and crisp white flesh.
examples: ["She took a bite of a juicy red apple.", "My grandmother bakes a delicious apple pie every autumn."]
usage_notes: Countable noun. Often used in common idioms like 'the apple of my eye' (someone highly cherished) or 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away'.
collocations: ["apple pie", "bite an apple", "rotten apple", "apple juice", "crisp apple"]

definition: A formal request for something such as a job, position, or permission, or a computer program designed for a specific purpose.
examples: ["She submitted her job application yesterday morning.", "You can download the new language learning application on your phone."]
usage_notes: Often shortened to 'app' when referring to software. When referring to a formal request, it is usually followed by the preposition 'for' (e.g., application for a visa).
collocations: ["job application", "submit an application", "software application", "application form", "written application"]

definition: To make a formal request for something, such as a job or admission to a school; or to put something into use or action.
examples: ["She decided to apply for a job at the local library.", "You need to apply the cream to the affected area twice a day."]
usage_notes: When requesting a job or position, use the preposition 'for' (apply for a job). When referring to the organization receiving the request, use 'to' (apply to a college).
collocations: ["apply for a job", "apply to college", "apply a rule", "apply pressure", "apply online"]

definition: To officially choose someone for a job, position, or responsibility.
examples: ["The board decided to appoint her as the new CEO of the company.", "The president has the power to appoint federal judges."]
usage_notes: Often used in the passive voice (e.g., 'he was appointed') and commonly followed by the preposition 'as' or an infinitive verb (e.g., 'appointed to lead').
collocations: ["appoint a committee", "appoint a successor", "be appointed as", "newly appointed"]

definition: A formal agreement to meet someone at a specific time and place, usually for business or medical reasons.
examples: ["I have a doctor's appointment tomorrow morning at nine o'clock.", "She called the office to schedule an appointment with her lawyer."]
usage_notes: Use 'make', 'schedule', or 'book' an appointment. Use the preposition 'with' for people (e.g., an appointment with the doctor) and 'for' for times or reasons (e.g., an appointment for a checkup).
collocations: ["make an appointment", "schedule an appointment", "cancel an appointment", "doctor's appointment", "by appointment only"]

definition: To recognize the full value of something, or to be grateful for something someone has done.
examples: ["I really appreciate all the help you gave me with my project.", "Over time, you will learn to appreciate the art and culture of this city."]
usage_notes: When expressing gratitude, 'appreciate' is usually followed by a noun or a gerund (e.g., 'I appreciate your advice' or 'I appreciate you helping me'). Avoid using a 'to-infinitive' directly after it.
collocations: ["greatly appreciate", "appreciate the effort", "appreciate the value", "would appreciate it if"]

definition: To come near to something or someone in distance, time, or quality; or a particular way of thinking about or dealing with something.
examples: ["As winter approaches, the weather is getting much colder.", "We need to adopt a new approach to solve this customer problem."]
usage_notes: When used as a verb meaning 'to come near', do not use 'to' after it (e.g., say 'approach the building', not 'approach to the building'). When used as a noun, it is often followed by 'to' (e.g., 'an approach to learning').
collocations: ["a new approach", "cautious approach", "approach a problem", "slowly approach", "direct approach"]

definition: Suitable, acceptable, or correct for a particular situation, person, or purpose.
examples: ["Please wear clothes that are appropriate for a job interview.", "The teacher took appropriate action to stop the bullying."]
usage_notes: The adjective is pronounced with a short 'it' sound at the end (/ət/). Note that 'appropriate' can also be a verb meaning to take something for one's own use, which is pronounced with a long 'ate' sound (/eɪt/).

definition: The feeling that someone or something is good or acceptable, or official permission to do something.
examples: ["The manager gave her approval for the new project proposal.", "He showed his approval with a warm smile and a nod."]
usage_notes: Often used with the verbs 'give', 'get', 'receive', or 'win'. The preposition 'of' usually follows when expressing a positive opinion (e.g., 'approval of the plan').
collocations: ["final approval", "seek approval", "seal of approval", "win approval", "prior approval"]

definition: To officially accept a plan, proposal, or request, or to agree that something is good, right, or suitable.
examples: ["The city council voted to approve the budget for the new park.", "My parents don't approve of my decision to quit my job."]
usage_notes: When you agree with an action or behavior, use the pattern 'approve of' (e.g., 'I don't approve of smoking'). When you officially allow something, use 'approve' directly as a transitive verb (e.g., 'The manager approved the request').
collocations: ["approve a request", "approve a budget", "approve of a decision", "officially approve", "fail to approve"]

definition: Showing that you believe someone or something is good, acceptable, or satisfactory.
examples: ["She gave me an approving nod when I finished my presentation.", "The audience responded with approving smiles and warm applause."]
usage_notes: This is the adjective form of the verb 'approve'. It is most commonly used to describe facial expressions, gestures, or tones of voice (e.g., an approving look, an approving murmur).

definition: Close to a particular number, time, or position, but not completely accurate or exact.
examples: ["The approximate cost of the repairs will be around two hundred dollars.", "Can you give me an approximate time of your arrival?"]
usage_notes: The adjective is pronounced with a /mət/ sound at the end, whereas the verb form ('to approximate') is pronounced with a /meɪt/ sound.

definition: Close to a particular number or amount, but not exactly.
examples: ["The journey will take approximately three hours.", "The repair work will cost approximately five hundred dollars."]
usage_notes: Often abbreviated as 'approx.' in writing. It is more formal than 'about' or 'around' and is frequently used in academic, business, and scientific contexts.

definition: The fourth month of the year, coming after March and before May, consisting of 30 days.
examples: ["We are planning to go on vacation in early April.", "April showers bring May flowers."]
usage_notes: In English, the names of months like April must always be capitalized.

definition: A particular part of a place, city, country, or space; it can also refer to a specific field of study or activity.
examples: ["There is a beautiful picnic area near the lake.", "She is an expert in the area of digital marketing."]
usage_notes: When talking about physical space, 'area' is countable. When referring to the size of a surface (e.g., length times width), it is uncountable.
collocations: ["surrounding area", "residential area", "rural area", "area of expertise", "gray area"]

definition: To disagree with someone in an angry, verbal way, or to give reasons in order to support or oppose an idea.
examples: ["My parents rarely argue about money because they plan their budget together.", "The lawyer will argue that his client is completely innocent."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the prepositions 'with' (someone) or 'about' (something). In academic contexts, 'argue' does not mean to fight, but rather to present a logical point of view.
collocations: ["argue with someone", "argue about something", "strongly argue", "argue a case", "start to argue"]

definition: A conversation or discussion in which people disagree, often angrily, or a set of reasons given to support an idea.
examples: ["They got into a heated argument about who should pay for the damage.", "The lawyer presented a strong argument to convince the jury."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the verbs 'have', 'get into', or 'win/lose'. Use the preposition 'with' for the person you disagree with, and 'about' or 'over' for the topic (e.g., 'have an argument with someone about something').
collocations: ["have an argument", "heated argument", "convincing argument", "win an argument", "main argument"]

definition: To happen, occur, or start to exist, especially when referring to problems, difficulties, or opportunities.
examples: ["A new problem has arisen with the computer system.", "If the opportunity arises, you should definitely take it."]
usage_notes: The past tense is 'arose' and the past participle is 'arisen'. It is more formal than 'happen' or 'come up' and is frequently used with abstract nouns like 'problem', 'issue', 'difficulty', or 'opportunity'.
collocations: ["if the opportunity arises", "problems arise", "complications arise", "a conflict arises"]

definition: Either of the two long upper limbs of the human body, reaching from the shoulder to the hand.
examples: ["She held the baby in her arms.", "He stretched out his arm to reach the top shelf."]
usage_notes: The word 'arm' can also be used as a verb meaning 'to provide with weapons'. As a noun, the plural form 'arms' can also refer to weapons in general.
collocations: ["broken arm", "arm in arm", "fold one's arms", "stretch your arms"]

definition: Carrying weapons, especially firearms, or equipped with essential tools, information, or security features.
examples: ["The bank was robbed by two armed men wearing masks.", "Armed with all the facts, she felt confident going into the negotiation."]
usage_notes: Often used with the preposition 'with' when referring to being equipped with information, knowledge, or tools (e.g., 'armed with a laptop').

definition: Weapons, especially those used by the military or police; it can also refer to the plural of the upper limbs of the human body.
examples: ["The country agreed to reduce its export of conventional arms.", "She held the crying baby in her arms."]
usage_notes: When used to mean 'weapons', 'arms' is a plural noun and does not have a singular form with the same meaning (you cannot say 'an arm' to mean a weapon).
collocations: ["bear arms", "arms race", "lay down arms", "open arms", "arms control"]

definition: A large, organized group of soldiers trained to fight on land in wars.
examples: ["He decided to join the army after finishing high school.", "The army was sent to the region to help with the flood relief efforts."]
usage_notes: The word 'army' is a collective noun. In American English, it usually takes a singular verb ('the army is...'), while in British English, it can take either a singular or plural verb ('the army are...').
collocations: ["join the army", "serve in the army", "army officer", "regular army", "standing army"]

definition: In a circle, on all sides of something, or in various places nearby.
examples: ["We sat around the table to eat dinner.", "I'll be around all afternoon if you need any help."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a preposition (e.g., 'around the world') and an adverb (e.g., 'look around'). In British English, 'round' is often used instead of 'around' in many contexts.
collocations: ["all around", "turn around", "look around", "around the corner", "travel around"]

definition: To plan, prepare, or organize something; or to put things into a neat, attractive, or specific order.
examples: ["I need to arrange a meeting with the project manager for next Tuesday.", "She carefully arranged the flowers in a beautiful glass vase."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the infinitive 'to do' (e.g., 'arrange to meet') or the preposition 'for' (e.g., 'arrange for a taxi').
collocations: ["arrange a meeting", "arrange flowers", "arrange in alphabetical order", "arrange for a trip", "make arrangements"]

definition: An agreement or plan made between people, or the specific way in which things are organized and positioned.
examples: ["We have a flexible working arrangement that allows us to work from home twice a week.", "The florist created a beautiful flower arrangement for the dining table."]
usage_notes: Often used with the verbs 'make' (to make arrangements) or 'have' (to have an arrangement). It can be countable when referring to plans, or uncountable when referring to the act of organizing.

definition: To legally seize someone by legal authority and take them into custody, usually because they are suspected of committing a crime; it can also mean to stop or attract attention.
examples: ["The police officer decided to arrest the suspect after finding the stolen goods in his car.", "An unusual sound outside the window managed to arrest her attention."]
usage_notes: Most commonly used as a verb in passive voice ('he was arrested') or as a noun in the phrase 'under arrest'.
collocations: ["under arrest", "place under arrest", "cardiac arrest", "arrest a suspect", "arrest the spread of"]

definition: The act of reaching a place, or the appearance of a person or thing that has come to a destination.
examples: ["We apologized for our late arrival because our train was delayed.", "The hotel staff was ready to welcome the new arrivals."]
usage_notes: It is the noun form of the verb 'arrive'. It is often used with the prepositions 'at' or 'in' (e.g., 'arrival at the airport', 'arrival in London').

definition: To reach a destination or a specific place at the end of a journey.
examples: ["The train is scheduled to arrive at the station at 6:00 PM.", "We finally arrived at the hotel after a very long flight."]
usage_notes: Use 'arrive in' for cities or countries and 'arrive at' for specific buildings or locations. Avoid saying 'arrive to'.

definition: To reach a specific place at the end of a journey, or to reach a decision or agreement after discussion.
examples: ["We arrived at the airport two hours before our flight.", "After much debate, the team finally arrived at a solution."]
usage_notes: Use 'arrive at' for specific locations like buildings or stations, and 'arrive in' for larger areas like cities or countries. It is also commonly used for abstract results like decisions.
collocations: ["arrive at a decision", "arrive at a conclusion", "arrive at the station", "arrive at a compromise", "arrive at the hotel"]

definition: A thin, straight stick with a sharp point shot from a bow, or a symbol used to point in a specific direction.
examples: ["The archer aimed his arrow carefully at the center of the target.", "Follow the painted arrows on the floor to find the emergency exit."]
usage_notes: The word refers both to the physical weapon used in archery and the graphical symbol used for navigation or on computer keyboards.
collocations: ["bow and arrow", "shoot an arrow", "arrow key", "directional arrow", "poisoned arrow"]

definition: The expression or application of human creative skill and imagination, typically in a visual form such as painting or sculpture, producing works to be appreciated primarily for their beauty or emotional power.
examples: ["She decided to study art history at university because she loved visiting museums.", "The gallery is displaying a new exhibition of modern art this month."]
usage_notes: The word 'art' is usually uncountable when referring to the general concept, but it can be countable ('the arts') when referring to various creative fields like music, drama, and literature.
collocations: ["work of art", "modern art", "art gallery", "fine art", "martial arts"]

definition: A piece of writing about a particular subject in a newspaper, magazine, or website; it can also refer to a specific object or item.
examples: ["I read an interesting article about space exploration in the newspaper this morning.", "The shop sells various articles of clothing, including hats and scarves."]
usage_notes: In grammar, the words 'a', 'an', and 'the' are called articles. In legal or formal contexts, it can also mean a specific section of a document.
collocations: ["news article", "feature article", "article of clothing", "scholarly article", "journal article"]

definition: Made or produced by human beings rather than occurring naturally, often as a copy of something natural.
examples: ["The room was filled with artificial light from the lamps.", "She prefers artificial flowers because they never wilt."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe things that mimic nature. It can also describe human behavior that seems insincere or fake.

definition: In a way that is not natural or is created by humans rather than occurring by itself in nature.
examples: ["The price of the product was artificially inflated to make it seem more valuable.", "These flowers were grown artificially in a climate-controlled greenhouse."]
usage_notes: This is an adverb often used to describe things that are manipulated or fake, frequently appearing before adjectives or past participles.

definition: A person who creates art, such as paintings, drawings, sculptures, or music, often as a profession.
examples: ["The artist spent months working on the large oil painting.", "She is a talented makeup artist who works in the film industry."]
usage_notes: While often used for painters, it can also describe musicians (recording artist) or people skilled in specific crafts (makeup artist).

definition: Relating to art or artists, or showing skill and imagination in creating beautiful things.
examples: ["She has a very artistic way of decorating her home.", "The film was praised for its artistic direction and cinematography."]
usage_notes: It can describe both a person's natural ability and the quality of an object or performance.

definition: In a way that shows creative skill or aesthetic beauty.
examples: ["The food was artistically presented on the plate, looking almost too good to eat.", "She is artistically gifted and spends most of her free time painting landscapes."]
usage_notes: This is an adverb used to describe the manner in which an action is performed or how something is arranged to look pleasing.

definition: Used to describe the purpose or role of someone or something, or to indicate that something happens at the same time as another event.
examples: ["She works as a manager at a large tech company.", "The phone rang just as I was leaving the house."]
usage_notes: It can function as a preposition, conjunction, or adverb. It is also commonly used in comparisons with the pattern 'as + adjective + as'.
collocations: ["as soon as", "as well as", "such as", "as if", "as long as"]

definition: Feeling guilty, embarrassed, or sorry because of something you have done or because of a quality you have.
examples: ["He felt ashamed of his behavior at the party last night.", "She was too ashamed to admit that she had made a mistake."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'of' or followed by an infinitive verb. It describes a person's feeling, whereas 'shameful' describes the action itself.
collocations: ["deeply ashamed", "ashamed of yourself", "feel ashamed", "nothing to be ashamed of"]

definition: To one side or out of the way, often to make space or to speak to someone privately.
examples: ["She moved the heavy boxes aside to clear a path.", "The manager pulled me aside after the meeting to discuss my promotion."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with verbs of movement like 'step', 'move', or 'pull'. It can also be used as a noun in theater to describe a character speaking to the audience.
collocations: ["step aside", "pull someone aside", "set aside", "move aside", "aside from"]

definition: Used to indicate an exception to a statement or to introduce additional information related to the topic.
examples: ["Aside from a few scratches, the car is in perfect condition.", "Aside from her regular job, she also volunteers at the local animal shelter."]
usage_notes: Similar in meaning to 'apart from' or 'except for'. It can be used to mean 'excluding' or 'in addition to' depending on the context.
collocations: ["aside from that", "aside from the fact that", "aside from the cost", "aside from the obvious"]

definition: To say something to someone as a question or to request information or help.
examples: ["I need to ask my teacher a question about the homework.", "She asked him for directions to the train station."]
usage_notes: Use 'ask for' when you want someone to give you something, and 'ask' when you want information.
collocations: ["ask a question", "ask for help", "ask for permission", "ask around", "ask out"]

definition: In a state of sleep; not awake.
examples: ["The baby is finally asleep in her crib.", "I fell asleep while watching the movie."]
usage_notes: This word is an adjective usually used after a verb like 'be' or 'fall'. It is rarely used directly before a noun; instead, use 'sleeping'.

definition: A particular part, feature, or side of a situation, idea, or problem.
examples: ["The financial aspect of the project is the most concerning.", "She loves every aspect of her new job, from the tasks to the people."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the preposition 'of'. It is a versatile word used to break down a complex topic into smaller parts.

definition: To help someone by doing part of their work or providing what they need to complete a task.
examples: ["The software is designed to assist users in managing their daily schedules.", "A local charity will assist the family with their medical expenses."]
usage_notes: It is more formal than the word 'help' and is frequently followed by the prepositions 'with' or 'in'.
collocations: ["assist with", "assist in", "offer to assist", "technical assist", "financial assist"]

definition: Help or support given to someone to complete a task or deal with a problem.
examples: ["The shop assistant offered her assistance in finding the right size.", "The charity provides financial assistance to families in need."]
usage_notes: It is more formal than the word 'help' and is usually an uncountable noun.

definition: A person who helps someone else do their job or provides support in a specific task.
examples: ["She works as a personal assistant for a famous writer.", "The shop assistant helped me find the right size of shoes."]
usage_notes: Often used as a job title or followed by 'to' to indicate who the person is helping.

definition: To connect someone or something in your mind with another person or thing, or to spend time with someone as a friend or partner.
examples: ["Most people associate the color red with passion or danger.", "He chose not to associate with his former colleagues after the scandal."]
usage_notes: When used as a verb, it is almost always followed by the preposition 'with'. Note that the verb ends in an 'ate' sound (/eɪt/), while the noun or adjective form ends in a shorter 'it' sound (/ət/).

definition: To connect one thing with another in your mind, or to be related to something else.
examples: ["I always associate the smell of lavender with my grandmother's house.", "There are several health risks associated with a high-sugar diet."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'with'. The word functions as a verb (to connect) or a noun (a colleague or partner).

definition: An official group of people organized for a specific purpose, or a mental connection between ideas, feelings, or objects.
examples: ["She joined a professional association for graphic designers to network with others in her field.", "The smell of lavender has a strong association with my grandmother's house."]
usage_notes: When referring to a connection between things, it is frequently used with the preposition 'with'.
collocations: ["professional association", "trade association", "in association with", "close association", "mental association"]

definition: To accept something as true or as a fact without having any proof.
examples: ["I saw his car outside, so I assumed he was at home.", "Don't just assume that she knows the rules; you should explain them to her."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by a 'that' clause (e.g., 'I assume that...'). Be careful not to confuse it with 'presume', which is used when you have some evidence to support your guess.
collocations: ["assume responsibility", "assume the worst", "safe to assume", "make an assumption", "assume control"]

definition: To tell someone confidently that something is true or will happen, especially to make them feel less worried or doubtful.
examples: ["The manager assured the team that their jobs were safe despite the company's merger.", "I can assure you that we are doing everything possible to resolve the issue quickly."]
usage_notes: This verb is almost always followed by a person (the object) and then a 'that' clause or the preposition 'of'.
collocations: ["assure someone that", "rest assured", "can assure you", "assure the public", "assure success"]

definition: A preposition used to indicate a specific place, time, location, or point in a process.
examples: ["I will meet you at the library at 5:00 PM.", "She is currently sitting at her desk."]
usage_notes: Use 'at' for specific points in time or precise locations. It is often contrasted with 'in' (for enclosed spaces) and 'on' (for surfaces).
collocations: ["at home", "at work", "at night", "at the moment", "at school", "at first"]

definition: The layer of gases surrounding a planet, or the general mood and feeling of a place or situation.
examples: ["The Earth's atmosphere protects us from the sun's harmful radiation.", "The restaurant had a very cozy and friendly atmosphere."]
usage_notes: It can be used in a scientific context (the air) or a social context (the 'vibe' of a room).

definition: The smallest basic unit of a chemical element that can exist, consisting of a nucleus surrounded by electrons.
examples: ["Everything in the universe is made up of tiny atoms.", "Scientists use powerful microscopes to study the structure of an atom."]
usage_notes: While primarily a scientific term, it is occasionally used in literature to describe an extremely small amount of something.
collocations: ["hydrogen atom", "split the atom", "atomic structure", "carbon atom", "subatomic particles"]

definition: To join, fasten, or connect one thing to another.
examples: ["Please attach the document to your email before sending it.", "He used a clip to attach the badge to his shirt."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the preposition 'to'. In a digital context, it refers to adding a file to an email or message.
collocations: ["attach a file", "attach a label", "attach importance to", "firmly attach"]

definition: To fasten, join, or connect one thing to another, or to include a document or file with an email.
examples: ["Please attach the report to your email before you send it.", "You need to attach a recent photo to the application form."]
usage_notes: This verb is almost always used with the preposition 'to'.
collocations: ["attach a file", "attach importance to", "firmly attached", "emotionally attached"]

definition: To use violence to hurt a person or damage a place, or to criticize someone or something very strongly.
examples: ["The soldiers launched a sudden attack on the enemy base.", "The politician came under attack for his controversial new policies."]
usage_notes: This word functions as both a verb and a noun. In medical contexts, it refers to a sudden period of illness, such as a heart attack.
collocations: ["heart attack", "terrorist attack", "launch an attack", "under attack", "cyber attack"]

definition: To try to do something, especially something that is difficult or challenging.
examples: ["She made a final attempt to explain her reasons for leaving.", "The team will attempt to break the world record during the next race."]
usage_notes: It can be used as both a verb and a noun. It is often followed by an infinitive, such as 'attempt to do something'.
collocations: ["make an attempt", "first attempt", "failed attempt", "successful attempt", "attempt to"]

definition: To try to do something, especially something difficult or challenging.
examples: ["She will attempt to break the world record in the marathon next month.", "The team made a final attempt to complete the project before the deadline."]
usage_notes: It can be used as both a verb and a noun. It is slightly more formal than the word 'try'.
collocations: ["make an attempt", "first attempt", "attempt to do", "failed attempt", "successful attempt"]

definition: To be present at an event, meeting, or function, or to go regularly to a place such as a school.
examples: ["Over two hundred people are expected to attend the conference.", "Students must attend at least eighty percent of their classes to pass."]
usage_notes: When 'attend' means to be present, it is a transitive verb and does not take the preposition 'to'. 'Attend to' is a different phrasal verb meaning to deal with or take care of something.
collocations: ["attend a meeting", "attend a wedding", "attend school", "attend a lecture", "attend an event"]

definition: To deal with a task or problem, or to take care of someone's needs.
examples: ["The nurse will attend to your wound in just a moment.", "I have several urgent matters to attend to before I can leave the office."]
usage_notes: This is a formal phrasal verb. It is commonly used in professional, medical, or customer service contexts.
collocations: ["attend to a matter", "attend to needs", "attend to details", "attend to a patient", "attend to business"]

definition: The act of listening to, looking at, or thinking about something or someone carefully.
examples: ["Please pay attention to the safety instructions before we begin.", "The bright colors of the flowers caught her attention immediately."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the verb 'pay'. It can also mean special care or treatment, such as 'medical attention'.
collocations: ["pay attention", "draw attention", "catch someone's attention", "undivided attention", "medical attention"]

definition: A way of thinking or feeling about someone or something, which is often shown in the way you behave.
examples: ["He has a very positive attitude toward his studies.", "If you want to succeed, you need to change your attitude."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'toward' or 'towards'. It can describe both a general mindset and a specific behavior.
collocations: ["positive attitude", "negative attitude", "attitude toward", "change your attitude", "mental attitude"]

definition: A person who is legally qualified to represent someone in a court of law or to give legal advice.
examples: ["She hired an attorney to help her with the business contract.", "The defense attorney argued that there was not enough evidence for a conviction."]
usage_notes: In the United States, 'attorney' is a formal term for a lawyer. It is often used in professional or legal contexts.
collocations: ["defense attorney", "district attorney", "power of attorney", "hire an attorney", "consult an attorney"]

definition: To cause someone or something to move toward a place or to become interested in something.
examples: ["The bright flowers attract many bees to the garden.", "The company is trying to attract new customers with a big sale."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the pattern 'attract someone to something' or in the passive voice 'be attracted to'.
collocations: ["attract attention", "attract interest", "attract customers", "attract investment", "attract a crowd"]

definition: A place that people visit for interest or enjoyment, or a feeling of being drawn to someone or something because of its qualities.
examples: ["The Grand Canyon is a famous tourist attraction in the United States.", "They felt a strong mutual attraction from the moment they met."]
usage_notes: Often used in the phrase 'tourist attraction' to describe landmarks, or in physics to describe forces pulling objects together.

definition: Pleasing or appealing to the senses, especially visually, or having qualities that draw interest and attention.
examples: ["The company offered him a very attractive salary and benefits package.", "She wore an attractive dress that caught everyone's eye at the party."]
usage_notes: While often used to describe physical beauty, it is also frequently used in business to describe deals, prices, or opportunities.

definition: A group of people who gather together to watch or listen to a performance, speech, or presentation.
examples: ["The audience gave the performers a standing ovation at the end of the play.", "The speaker struggled to keep the audience's attention during the long presentation."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'audience' is usually treated as a singular noun, while in British English, it can be used with either singular or plural verbs.
collocations: ["target audience", "live audience", "reach an audience", "address the audience", "captive audience"]

definition: Respected and impressive, especially because of a high position, great age, or historical importance.
examples: ["The university is an august institution with a long history of excellence.", "He felt honored to be invited into such an august group of scientists."]
usage_notes: This is a formal adjective. Note that the stress is on the second syllable, unlike the month 'August' which is stressed on the first.

definition: The sister of your father or mother, or the wife of your uncle.
examples: ["My aunt Sarah is coming to visit us this weekend.", "I have three aunts on my mother's side of the family."]
usage_notes: In many families, 'Aunt' is used as a title before the person's first name, such as 'Aunt Linda'.

definition: A person who writes a book, article, or any other piece of writing.
examples: ["The author of the novel will be signing books at the library tomorrow.", "She is a well-known author of several scientific papers."]
usage_notes: While usually used as a noun, it can also be used as a verb meaning 'to write' (e.g., 'He authored several books').

definition: The power or right to give orders and make decisions, or a person who is an expert in a particular subject.
examples: ["The police have the authority to arrest anyone who breaks the law.", "She is a world-renowned authority on 19th-century literature."]
usage_notes: When referring to an expert, it is often followed by the preposition 'on'. The plural form 'authorities' usually refers to the government or police.
collocations: ["position of authority", "local authorities", "exercise authority", "challenge authority", "authority figure"]

definition: Working by itself without direct human control, or done without conscious thought or effort.
examples: ["The store has automatic doors that open when you walk toward them.", "Blinking is an automatic reaction to keep your eyes moist."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe machines, but can also describe human habits or physical reactions.

definition: In a way that happens by itself without needing a person to operate it, or done without thinking about it.
examples: ["The lights turn off automatically after ten minutes of inactivity.", "I automatically looked at my watch when he asked for the time."]
usage_notes: It can describe both mechanical processes and human habits or reflexes.

definition: The season of the year between summer and winter, characterized by cooler weather and leaves changing color and falling from trees.
examples: ["The leaves turn beautiful shades of red and orange in autumn.", "We harvested the apples in late autumn."]
usage_notes: In American English, the word 'fall' is more commonly used in everyday conversation, while 'autumn' is often seen as more formal or literary.

definition: Ready to be used, bought, or found, or not busy and free to talk to someone.
examples: ["Is this seat available?", "The manager is not available for a meeting right now."]
usage_notes: It can be used before a noun or after a linking verb like 'be'.

definition: A number calculated by adding several amounts together and dividing by the total number of amounts; also, something that is normal or typical.
examples: ["The average age of the students in the class is twenty-two.", "On average, it takes about thirty minutes to get to the city center."]
usage_notes: It can function as a noun, an adjective, or a verb. In everyday conversation, it often describes something that is ordinary or not special.

definition: To stay away from a person, place, or situation, or to prevent something unpleasant from happening.
examples: ["He took a different route to avoid the heavy morning traffic.", "You should avoid eating too much sugar if you want to stay healthy."]
usage_notes: This verb is commonly followed by a noun or a gerund (the -ing form of a verb).
collocations: ["avoid eye contact", "avoid a mistake", "avoid conflict", "avoid the rush", "avoid crowds"]

definition: Not sleeping; conscious and alert.
examples: ["I was still wide awake at midnight.", "The noise from the street kept me awake all night."]
usage_notes: Usually used as an adjective after a verb like 'be', 'stay', or 'keep'. While it can be a verb, 'wake up' is more common in daily speech.
collocations: ["wide awake", "stay awake", "keep someone awake", "fully awake", "half awake"]

definition: A prize or honor given to someone to recognize their achievements, or the act of officially giving such a prize or decision.
examples: ["She won an award for the best actress of the year.", "The committee decided to award the contract to a local building company."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a noun and a verb. As a verb, it often follows the pattern 'award someone something' or 'award something to someone'. Do not confuse it with 'reward', which is given for good behavior or effort rather than an official decision.
collocations: ["win an award", "present an award", "prestigious award", "academy award", "award a contract"]

definition: Knowing about something or being conscious of a situation or fact.
examples: ["She was aware of the potential risks before starting the project.", "Are you aware that the meeting has been rescheduled?"]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'of' or followed by a 'that' clause.
collocations: ["well aware", "fully aware", "become aware", "socially aware", "aware of the fact"]

definition: To or at a distance from a particular place, person, or thing; in or into another place or direction.
examples: ["She turned her face away so he wouldn't see her crying.", "The beach is only a five-minute walk away."]
usage_notes: Often used with verbs of movement (go, run, take) or to indicate distance in space or time (three miles away, two weeks away).

definition: Extremely bad, unpleasant, or of very poor quality.
examples: ["The weather was absolutely awful during our entire vacation.", "I feel awful about forgetting your birthday; I am so sorry."]
usage_notes: In informal speech, 'awful' can also be used as an adverb meaning 'very' (e.g., 'an awful lot of people').
collocations: ["awful weather", "feel awful", "look awful", "awful smell", "an awful lot"]

definition: Used as an intensifier to mean very or extremely, often to emphasize a feeling or a quality.
examples: ["I'm awfully sorry for the misunderstanding.", "It is awfully cold in this room, isn't it?"]
usage_notes: While it comes from the word 'awful,' it is most commonly used in conversation as a synonym for 'very.' It can sound slightly formal or old-fashioned depending on the region.

definition: Feeling or causing embarrassment, or being difficult to handle or deal with because of its shape or size.
examples: ["There was an awkward silence after she asked the personal question.", "The large sofa was very awkward to move up the narrow stairs."]
usage_notes: This word is commonly used to describe both social discomfort and physical difficulty in handling objects.

definition: In a way that is not graceful or that shows you feel embarrassed or uncomfortable.
examples: ["He shifted awkwardly in his seat when they asked him the difficult question.", "The two old friends stood awkwardly in the hallway, unsure of what to say."]
usage_notes: This is the adverb form of the adjective 'awkward'. It is frequently used to describe social interactions that feel forced or embarrassing, as well as physical movements that lack coordination.

definition: A very young child, especially one who has not yet learned to walk or talk.
examples: ["The baby is sleeping peacefully in her crib.", "They are expecting a new baby in the spring."]
usage_notes: While it primarily refers to an infant, it is also commonly used as an informal term of endearment for a romantic partner.
collocations: ["newborn baby", "baby shower", "have a baby", "baby steps", "baby clothes"]

definition: The rear part of the human body from the shoulders to the hips, or the side/part of something that is opposite the front.
examples: ["He was lying on his back looking up at the sky.", "Please write your signature on the back of the check."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun, adjective, adverb, or verb. As an adverb, it often indicates a return to a previous place, state, or time.
collocations: ["back pain", "go back", "at the back of", "back and forth", "get back to"]

definition: To make a copy of digital information so that it is safe if the original is lost or damaged; also, to move backward or to support someone.
examples: ["You should always back up your important files to an external hard drive.", "Can you back up a little bit so I can open the car door?"]
usage_notes: When used as a verb, it is written as two words ('back up'). The noun form is written as one word ('backup').
collocations: ["back up your files", "back up a car", "back up a claim", "back someone up"]

definition: The details of a person's past experience and education, or the part of a scene or picture that is behind the main objects.
examples: ["The interviewer asked several questions about her professional background.", "The mountains in the background of the photograph were covered in snow."]
usage_notes: It can refer to both physical space (behind something) and abstract history (a person's life story or experience).
collocations: ["educational background", "family background", "background noise", "background information", "in the background"]

definition: Directed toward the back or the past, or showing a lack of progress or development.
examples: ["He took a step backward to avoid the puddle.", "The new policy was seen as a backward move for the company."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'backward' is used as both an adjective and an adverb, while 'backwards' is more commonly used as an adverb in British English.

definition: Moving toward the back or in the opposite direction of what is normal.
examples: ["He took a step backward to avoid the puddle.", "She can say the alphabet backward very quickly."]
usage_notes: In US English, 'backward' is used as both an adjective and an adverb. In British English, 'backwards' is the preferred adverbial form.

definition: Very small living things consisting of a single cell that exist everywhere; some can cause disease while others are beneficial to health.
examples: ["Washing your hands with soap helps to kill harmful bacteria.", "The yogurt contains live bacteria that are good for your digestion."]
usage_notes: Bacteria is the plural form of bacterium. In scientific contexts, it takes a plural verb, but in everyday English, it is sometimes treated as an uncountable noun.
collocations: ["harmful bacteria", "beneficial bacteria", "kill bacteria", "spread of bacteria", "bacterial infection"]

definition: Not good in quality, or something that is unpleasant, harmful, or wrong.
examples: ["I have some bad news to tell you.", "The weather was really bad during our vacation."]
usage_notes: It is a very common adjective used to describe many different negative situations. Avoid overusing it by trying more specific words like 'terrible' or 'harmful'.

definition: Easily annoyed or made angry; having a grumpy or irritable disposition.
examples: ["He becomes very bad-tempered when he hasn't had enough sleep.", "The bad-tempered clerk was rude to the customers."]
usage_notes: This adjective can be used before a noun or after linking verbs like 'be' or 'become'.
collocations: ["a bad-tempered person", "become bad-tempered", "increasingly bad-tempered", "a bad-tempered mood"]

definition: In a poor or unsatisfactory way, or to a very great or intense degree.
examples: ["The team played badly and lost the match.", "He wanted to win the competition very badly."]
usage_notes: When used with verbs like 'want' or 'need', it means 'very much'. In informal speech, people sometimes use 'bad' as an adverb, but 'badly' is the correct form in standard English.
collocations: ["behave badly", "want something badly", "badly injured", "badly damaged", "treat someone badly"]

definition: A container made of flexible material like paper, plastic, or cloth, used for carrying or storing items.
examples: ["He carried his groceries home in a reusable cloth bag.", "Don't forget to pack your sleeping bag for the camping trip."]
usage_notes: Commonly used as a noun, but can also be a verb meaning to put something into a bag.

definition: The suitcases and bags that you take with you when you travel, or the past experiences and feelings that influence how you act now.
examples: ["The airline lost my baggage during the flight to London.", "He has a lot of emotional baggage from his previous relationship."]
usage_notes: It is an uncountable noun, meaning it has no plural form. Use 'a piece of baggage' or 'some baggage' instead of 'a baggage' or 'baggages'.
collocations: ["excess baggage", "emotional baggage", "baggage claim", "check your baggage", "carry-on baggage"]

definition: To cook food, such as bread, cakes, or cookies, in an oven using dry heat.
examples: ["I am going to bake a chocolate cake for the party.", "The smell of fresh bread baking filled the entire house."]
usage_notes: While 'bake' is mostly used for flour-based foods, it can also describe cooking vegetables or fish in an oven.
collocations: ["bake a cake", "freshly baked", "bake from scratch", "bake in the oven"]

definition: A state where different things are equal in value or importance, or the ability to remain upright and steady without falling.
examples: ["He struggled to keep his balance while walking across the narrow bridge.", "You need to find a good balance between studying and relaxing."]
usage_notes: Often used as a noun to talk about physical stability or a bank account total, and as a verb meaning to give equal importance to two things.
collocations: ["keep your balance", "lose your balance", "work-life balance", "bank balance", "strike a balance"]

definition: A round object used in games and sports, or a large formal party where people dance.
examples: ["The children were kicking a ball around the park.", "She wore a beautiful long dress to the charity ball."]
usage_notes: In sports, it refers to the equipment. In a social context, it refers to a very formal event. The idiom 'have a ball' means to have a lot of fun.

definition: To officially or legally prohibit something from being done, used, or seen.

usage_notes: It can be used as a verb (to ban something) or a noun (a ban on something).
collocations: ["lift a ban", "impose a ban", "total ban", "travel ban", "ban someone from"]

definition: A group of musicians who play music together, or a thin strip of material used to hold things together or as decoration.

usage_notes: The word can refer to people (musicians) or objects (strips of material). In some contexts, it also refers to a range of radio frequencies or a stripe of color.

definition: A strip of cloth or other material used to cover, protect, or support an injury.
examples: ["The nurse wrapped a clean bandage around his sprained ankle.", "You should change the bandage every day to keep the wound clean."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun (the material itself) or as a verb (the action of wrapping an injury).
collocations: ["apply a bandage", "wrap a bandage", "elastic bandage", "sterile bandage", "remove a bandage"]

definition: A financial institution where people keep, borrow, or exchange money, or the sloping land along the side of a river or lake.
examples: ["I need to go to the bank to deposit this check.", "We sat on the river bank and watched the sunset."]
usage_notes: The word can be a noun (a place) or a verb (to deposit money). It is also used in the idiom 'bank on,' which means to rely on something happening.

definition: A place where alcoholic drinks are served, or a solid, rectangular piece of something like chocolate or soap.
examples: ["We met at a local bar for a drink after work.", "She bought a large bar of dark chocolate."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'to bar' means to officially prevent someone from entering a place or doing something.
collocations: ["chocolate bar", "behind bars", "raise the bar", "bar exam", "snack bar"]

definition: Something bought at a much lower price than its true value, or the act of negotiating the terms of an agreement or price.
examples: ["This designer coat was a real bargain at only fifty dollars.", "The union spent weeks bargaining with the company for better wages."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun to describe a good deal or as a verb meaning to negotiate. The phrase 'into the bargain' means 'in addition to everything else'.

definition: A physical object that blocks a path or a situation that prevents people from doing something or communicating.

usage_notes: Can refer to physical objects or abstract concepts like social or economic obstacles.
collocations: ["language barrier", "trade barrier", "physical barrier", "break down barriers", "barrier to entry"]

definition: The bottom part of an object that supports it, or a main place where a person or organization lives or works.
examples: ["The lamp has a heavy metal base so it does not tip over.", "The company has its main base in London, but they have offices all over the world."]
usage_notes: Commonly used as a verb in the phrase 'based on' to indicate the source or foundation of an idea.

definition: To use a particular fact, idea, or situation as the foundation or starting point for something else.
examples: ["The movie is based on a true story.", "We should base our decision on the facts available to us."]
usage_notes: This phrase is most frequently used in the passive voice (e.g., 'is based on').
collocations: ["based on a true story", "base a decision on", "base a theory on", "firmly based on"]

definition: Located in a particular place, or developed from a specific foundation or source.
examples: ["The tech company is based in San Francisco.", "The movie is based on a true story from the 1920s."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the prepositions 'in' (for location) or 'on' (for a source). In modern internet slang, it can also describe someone who is authentic and unbothered by others' opinions.

definition: Relating to the simplest and most important parts of something, or providing a starting point from which other things develop.
examples: ["The hotel room was very basic, but it was clean and comfortable.", "You need to learn the basic rules of the game before you start playing."]
usage_notes: It can describe something essential or something that lacks luxury. In modern informal slang, it is sometimes used to describe someone who is unoriginal or follows mainstream trends.

definition: Used to emphasize the most important or fundamental point of something, often when simplifying a complex situation.
examples: ["Basically, the plan is to save money by eating at home more often.", "The two phone models are basically the same, except for the camera quality."]
usage_notes: It is very common in spoken English as a filler word, but it should be used sparingly in formal writing to avoid sounding repetitive.
collocations: ["basically the same", "basically true", "basically saying", "basically correct", "basically means"]

definition: The foundation, underlying support, or the main reason why something exists or happens.
examples: ["The two companies decided to work together on a trial basis.", "We meet on a weekly basis to discuss our progress."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'on' (e.g., 'on a daily basis'). The plural form is 'bases' (pronounced /ˈbeɪsiːz/).
collocations: ["on a regular basis", "on the basis of", "legal basis", "scientific basis", "daily basis"]

definition: A large container filled with water for washing your body, or the act of washing yourself in such a container.
examples: ["I like to relax in a hot bath after a long day at work.", "It is time to give the toddler a bath before bed."]
usage_notes: In American English, people usually 'take a bath,' whereas in British English, it is more common to 'have a bath.'
collocations: ["take a bath", "have a bath", "bubble bath", "hot bath", "bath towel"]

definition: A room in a house or public building that contains a toilet and often a sink and a bathtub or shower.

usage_notes: In American English, 'bathroom' is the standard polite term for a room with a toilet, even in public places where there is no bathtub.
collocations: ["use the bathroom", "public bathroom", "bathroom mirror", "clean the bathroom", "master bathroom"]

definition: A device that stores chemical energy and converts it into electricity to power electronic devices like phones, cars, and toys.
examples: ["My phone is about to die because the battery is low.", "This toy requires four AA batteries to work."]
usage_notes: The word 'battery' can also refer to a series of similar things (e.g., 'a battery of tests') or a legal term for physical attack, but its most common everyday use is the electrical device.
collocations: ["dead battery", "rechargeable battery", "battery life", "charge a battery", "battery charger"]

definition: A fight between large groups of people, especially in a war, or a long and difficult struggle to achieve something.
examples: ["The soldiers fought a fierce battle in the mountains.", "She won her long battle against the illness."]
usage_notes: It can be used as both a noun and a verb. It is frequently used metaphorically to describe personal or social struggles.
collocations: ["win a battle", "lose a battle", "uphill battle", "battle for survival", "fierce battle"]

definition: A body of water partially surrounded by land, or a specific area or compartment used for a particular purpose, such as parking or storage.
examples: ["The ship dropped its anchor in the calm waters of the bay.", "Please make sure the delivery truck is parked in the loading bay."]
usage_notes: While most commonly used to describe a coastal feature, it is also frequently used in technical or industrial contexts to describe a designated space.
collocations: ["San Francisco Bay", "loading bay", "keep at bay", "bay window", "parking bay"]

definition: To remain unused, uneaten, or unspent after the rest has been finished or used.
examples: ["There was a lot of food left over after the party, so we packed it into containers.", "If there is any money left over at the end of the month, I put it into my savings account."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb often used in the passive voice. The noun form 'leftovers' (always plural) refers specifically to remaining food from a meal.
collocations: ["food left over", "money left over", "time left over", "nothing left over"]

definition: A sandy or pebbly area along the edge of an ocean, sea, or lake.
examples: ["We spent the whole day relaxing on the beach.", "The children are building a sandcastle on the beach."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the prepositions 'at' or 'on'. Be careful with the long 'e' sound in pronunciation to avoid confusion with a similar-sounding vulgar word.
collocations: ["sandy beach", "go to the beach", "beach towel", "beach resort", "private beach"]

definition: The hard, pointed outer part of a bird's mouth, used for eating, grooming, and defense.
examples: ["The eagle used its sharp, hooked beak to tear its food.", "A woodpecker uses its strong beak to drill holes in tree trunks."]
usage_notes: While primarily used for birds, it is sometimes used informally or humorously to describe a person's large or prominent nose.

definition: A large, heavy mammal with thick fur and a short tail, or a verb meaning to carry a weight or endure a difficult situation.
examples: ["The hikers were careful not to leave food out in case a bear was nearby.", "She had to bear the heavy responsibility of managing the entire team alone."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'bear' is often used in formal contexts or common idioms like 'bear in mind' (to remember) or 'can't bear' (to strongly dislike).

definition: The hair that grows on the lower part of a man's face, including the chin and cheeks.

usage_notes: Commonly used with verbs like 'grow', 'trim', or 'shave'.
collocations: ["grow a beard", "trim a beard", "shave off a beard", "thick beard", "facial hair"]

definition: To defeat someone in a game or competition, or to strike something repeatedly.
examples: ["Our team managed to beat the champions in the final game.", "She had to beat the eggs for several minutes to make the cake fluffy."]

definition: To hurt someone by hitting or kicking them repeatedly, or to describe something that is old and in bad condition.

usage_notes: When used as a verb meaning to attack, it is separable (e.g., 'beat him up'). As an adjective describing an object in poor condition, it is usually hyphenated ('a beat-up car').

definition: Very attractive or pleasing to the senses or the mind.

usage_notes: While often used for physical appearance, it can also describe weather, music, or even a kind action.

definition: In a way that is very attractive, pleasing to the senses, or done with great skill.
examples: ["She sang the song beautifully, and the audience was moved to tears.", "The old house has been beautifully restored to its original condition."]

definition: A quality that gives great pleasure to the senses, especially the sight, or a person or thing that has this quality.
examples: ["The natural beauty of the mountains is incredible.", "She is a real beauty with a very kind heart."]

definition: For the reason that; used to introduce the cause or explanation of something.

definition: Used to introduce the reason for something or to explain why something happened.
examples: ["The outdoor concert was canceled because of the heavy rain.", "She succeeded because of her hard work and dedication."]
usage_notes: This phrase is a preposition and must be followed by a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase. Do not follow it with a full clause (subject + verb); use 'because' instead.

definition: To begin to be something, or to develop into a particular state or condition.

definition: A piece of furniture that you lie on to sleep or rest.

definition: A room in a house or apartment used primarily for sleeping.

definition: The meat from a cow used as food, or informally, a complaint or a disagreement between people.

usage_notes: When referring to meat, it is an uncountable noun. In informal slang, 'to have a beef' means to have a grudge or a problem with someone.

definition: An alcoholic drink made from grain, such as barley, and flavored with hops.

usage_notes: It is often used as a countable noun when ordering a specific serving, such as 'Two beers, please.'

definition: At an earlier time, or in front of someone or something.

collocations: ["before long", "the day before", "never before", "just before", "long before"]

definition: To start doing something or to happen from a particular point in time.
examples: ["The movie will begin at 8:00 PM.", "I want to begin learning how to play the guitar."]
usage_notes: It is often followed by an infinitive ('to do') or a gerund ('doing'). While 'begin' and 'start' are often interchangeable, 'begin' is slightly more formal.
collocations: ["begin a journey", "begin to cry", "begin a career", "begin a new chapter", "begin with"]

definition: The first part or the start of something.

definition: As a representative of someone else or for the benefit and interest of another person or group.

usage_notes: Most commonly used in the prepositional phrase 'on behalf of'. It is often used in formal settings when one person acts for another.

definition: To act or conduct oneself in a specified way, especially in a polite or socially acceptable manner.

usage_notes: When used without an adverb, 'behave' usually means 'to behave well' (e.g., 'Please behave!'). It is often used with reflexive pronouns like 'behave yourself'.

definition: The way that a person or animal acts or conducts themselves, especially toward others or in a particular situation.
examples: ["The teacher praised the students for their excellent behavior during the field trip.", "Scientists are studying the social behavior of elephants in the wild."]
usage_notes: In American English, it is spelled 'behavior', while in British English, it is spelled 'behaviour'. It is often used as an uncountable noun.
collocations: ["good behavior", "human behavior", "antisocial behavior", "behavioral patterns", "change one's behavior"]

definition: At or toward the back of someone or something; also, supporting someone or lagging in progress.
examples: ["The sun disappeared behind the clouds.", "Our team is behind schedule, so we need to work faster."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a preposition (e.g., 'behind the door'), an adverb (e.g., 'fall behind'), or an adjective. Avoid using 'at the back of' when 'behind' is more natural for physical location.
collocations: ["behind schedule", "fall behind", "leave behind", "right behind you", "behind the scenes"]

definition: The feeling of being certain that something is true or exists, or a strong opinion or trust in something.

definition: To accept something as true, genuine, or real, or to have trust and confidence in someone or something.
examples: ["I firmly believe that education can change a person's life.", "Do you believe in ghosts, or do you think there is always a logical explanation?"]
usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'in' when expressing trust in someone's ability or the existence of something (e.g., 'believe in yourself'). It is a stative verb, so it is rarely used in the continuous (-ing) form.
collocations: ["firmly believe", "believe in yourself", "hard to believe", "make believe", "reason to believe"]

definition: To feel sure that something or someone exists, or to trust that someone or something is good, effective, or right.
examples: ["Many children believe in Santa Claus.", "If you want to achieve your goals, you must believe in yourself."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. 'Believe in' something means you trust its existence or value, whereas 'believe' someone means you think they are telling the truth.

definition: A hollow metal object, usually shaped like a cup, that makes a ringing sound when struck.
examples: ["The church bell rang to signal the start of the service.", "She rang the doorbell, but nobody answered."]
usage_notes: Often used in idioms such as 'ring a bell' (sound familiar).

definition: To be in the right, proper, or natural place; also, to be owned by someone or to be a member of a group.
examples: ["I feel like I finally belong in this city.", "Does this blue umbrella belong to you?"]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the preposition 'to' when indicating ownership or membership (e.g., 'belong to a club'). Do not use 'belong' in the progressive/continuous form when expressing ownership (say 'This belongs to me', not 'This is belonging to me').
collocations: ["belong to", "belong together", "a sense of belonging", "belong in"]

definition: To be the property of someone, or to be a member of a particular group, club, or organization.
examples: ["This blue umbrella belongs to me.", "She has belonged to the local swimming club for three years."]
usage_notes: This is a stative verb, meaning it is not usually used in the continuous (-ing) form. You should say 'I belong to' rather than 'I am belonging to'.
collocations: ["belong to a club", "belong to a group", "belong to a category", "belong to someone"]

definition: In a lower position than something else, or further down on a page or list.

usage_notes: Commonly used as a preposition or an adverb to indicate position or level. It is the opposite of 'above'.

definition: A strip of leather, fabric, or other material worn around the waist to support clothes or for decoration.

usage_notes: Can be used as a noun (the accessory) or as a verb meaning to fasten with a belt (e.g., 'belted coat') or to hit something hard.
collocations: ["leather belt", "seat belt", "tighten one's belt", "fasten a belt"]

definition: To change the shape of something into a curve or angle, or to lean your body forward and downward.
examples: ["He had to bend down to pick up his keys off the floor.", "Be careful not to bend the pages of the book."]
usage_notes: The past tense and past participle form is 'bent'. Common phrasal verbs include 'bend over' and 'bend down'.

definition: In or to a lower position than something; under or directly below.
examples: ["We sat in the shade beneath a large oak tree.", "He hid the letter beneath a pile of papers on his desk."]
usage_notes: Beneath is more formal than 'under' or 'below'. It can also be used metaphorically to describe someone's behavior as being unworthy of their social status or dignity (e.g., 'beneath his dignity').
collocations: ["beneath the surface", "beneath the waves", "beneath one's dignity", "directly beneath"]

definition: An advantage or profit gained from something, or a helpful effect that improves a situation.
examples: ["One major benefit of regular exercise is improved sleep quality.", "The new software will benefit the entire team by saving time."]
usage_notes: It can be used as both a noun and a verb. As a verb, it is frequently followed by the preposition 'from'.

definition: To curve something that was straight, or to move your body so that it is not upright.
examples: ["The road begins to bend to the left after the bridge.", "I had to bend down to pick up the coin."]
usage_notes: The past tense and past participle is 'bent'. It can also be used as a noun to describe a curve in a road or pipe.

definition: Next to or at the side of someone or something.
examples: ["She sat beside her friend during the movie.", "The hotel is located right beside the lake."]
usage_notes: Be careful not to confuse 'beside' (next to) with 'besides' (in addition to or except for).
collocations: ["sit beside", "stand beside", "right beside", "beside the point", "beside oneself"]

definition: Of the highest quality, excellence, or standing; better than all others of the same kind.
examples: ["This is the best pizza I have ever tasted.", "She is my best friend and we tell each other everything."]
usage_notes: It is the superlative form of 'good'. It is almost always used with the definite article 'the' when describing a noun.

definition: To risk money on the result of an event, or to state that you are very sure something is true or will happen.
examples: ["I bet ten dollars that our team will win the championship.", "I bet it's going to rain today because the sky is so dark."]
usage_notes: In casual conversation, 'I bet' is often used to mean 'I am sure.' 'You bet' is a common informal way to say 'You're welcome' or 'Certainly.'

definition: Of a higher quality, more effective, or more desirable than something else; it can also mean an improvement in health or well-being.
examples: ["This new laptop is much better than my old one.", "I hope you feel better after you get some rest."]

definition: To risk money or something valuable on the result of a race, game, or event, or to state that you are certain something will happen.
examples: ["He decided to place a bet on his favorite football team.", "I bet that they will arrive late to the party."]
usage_notes: In casual conversation, 'I bet' is frequently used to express agreement or to show that you are sure about a situation.
collocations: ["place a bet", "make a bet", "safe bet", "bet on", "bet against"]

definition: In the middle of two points, objects, people, or times.
examples: ["The small town is located between two large mountains.", "I need to choose between the red shirt and the blue one."]

definition: Further away in the distance than something, or outside the limits, range, or understanding of something.
examples: ["The small village lies just beyond the hills.", "The complexity of the problem was beyond his understanding."]

definition: A vehicle with two wheels that you sit on and move by turning pedals with your feet.
examples: ["I ride my bicycle to work every morning to get some exercise.", "She bought a new mountain bicycle for her weekend trips to the forest."]
usage_notes: In everyday conversation, the word 'bike' is much more common than 'bicycle'.

definition: To offer a specific amount of money for something, especially at an auction, or to make an attempt to achieve a goal.

definition: Large in size, amount, degree, or importance.

usage_notes: In formal writing, 'large' or 'significant' is often preferred over 'big'.

definition: A vehicle with two wheels that you ride by pushing pedals with your feet, or a common short name for a motorcycle.
examples: ["I usually ride my bike to work when the weather is nice.", "He bought a new mountain bike for his weekend trips."]
usage_notes: Bike is an informal and very common word for bicycle. It can also refer to a motorcycle depending on the context.

definition: A document that shows how much money you owe for goods or services, or a piece of paper money.
examples: ["The waiter brought the bill to our table after we finished dinner.", "I need to pay my electricity bill before the end of the month."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'bill' is used for paper currency (e.g., a five-dollar bill), whereas British English uses 'note'. In US restaurants, 'check' is often used interchangeably with 'bill'.

definition: The number 1,000,000,000, which is equal to one thousand million.

definition: A container used for storing things or for throwing away trash.
examples: ["Please throw your empty coffee cup in the trash bin.", "We keep the extra blankets in a plastic storage bin under the bed."]

definition: The scientific study of living things, including plants, animals, and microorganisms.
examples: ["She decided to major in biology because she was fascinated by marine life.", "Our biology teacher showed us how plant cells absorb water under a microscope."]
usage_notes: The word is uncountable, so it is not used in the plural form. When referring to the living organisms of a specific region, you can say 'the biology of...'.

definition: A creature with feathers and wings, usually able to fly, that lays eggs.
examples: ["A colorful bird was singing outside my window this morning.", "Many birds fly south for the winter to find food and warmer weather."]
usage_notes: 'Bird' is a regular countable noun (plural: birds). It appears in common idioms like 'early bird' (someone who gets up early).

definition: The process of being born, or the start of a baby's life outside the mother's body.
examples: ["She gave birth to a healthy baby boy yesterday morning.", "The hospital has a special ward for mothers before and after birth."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the phrase 'give birth to' (someone). It can also be used metaphorically to describe the beginning or creation of something, like 'the birth of a nation'.
collocations: ["give birth", "date of birth", "birth control", "birth certificate", "natural birth"]

definition: The anniversary of the day on which a person was born, often celebrated with gifts, a party, or a cake.
examples: ["We are planning a surprise party for my sister's birthday this weekend.", "He received a lot of cards and presents on his tenth birthday."]
usage_notes: Often used with the verb 'celebrate' or prepositions like 'on' (e.g., 'on my birthday').

definition: A small, flat, crisp sweet cake (in British English) or a small, soft, flaky bread roll typically eaten with savory food (in American English).
examples: ["Would you like a chocolate biscuit with your tea?", "She served warm biscuits with gravy for breakfast."]
usage_notes: Note the regional difference: in the UK, a biscuit is what Americans call a cookie. In the US, a biscuit is a soft, savory bread roll.
collocations: ["chocolate biscuit", "tea and biscuits", "warm biscuits", "biscuits and gravy"]

definition: A small piece, part, or amount of something.
examples: ["Could you wait a little bit while I finish this?", "I'm feeling a bit tired after the long walk."]
usage_notes: Very common in informal speech. Often used as an adverb to mean 'slightly' (e.g., 'a bit cold').
collocations: ["a little bit", "a bit of", "every bit", "not a bit", "a bit tired"]

definition: To use your teeth to cut into or crush something, or the act of doing so.
examples: ["He took a big bite out of the juicy apple.", "Be careful, that dog might bite if it feels threatened."]
usage_notes: The verb is irregular: bite (present), bit (past), bitten (past participle). It can also be used as a noun to refer to a small amount of food or a wound from an insect.
collocations: ["grab a bite", "bite your nails", "bite the bullet", "a quick bite", "mosquito bite"]

definition: Having a sharp, pungent taste that is not sweet, or feeling angry and resentful because of bad experiences or unfair treatment.
examples: ["The coffee was so bitter that I had to add a lot of sugar.", "He felt bitter about being passed over for the promotion despite his hard work."]
usage_notes: This word can describe physical taste, extreme weather (bitter cold), or strong negative emotions.
