collocations: ["bitter taste", "bitter cold", "bitter disappointment", "bitter enemy", "bitter pill to swallow"]

definition: In a way that shows strong negative feelings like anger, resentment, or sadness; also used to describe extreme cold.
examples: ["She was bitterly disappointed when she didn't get the promotion.", "The wind was blowing bitterly across the frozen lake."]
usage_notes: This adverb is most commonly used as an intensifier for negative emotions or harsh weather conditions.

definition: The darkest color, like coal or the night sky, which reflects no light.
examples: ["She wore a elegant black dress to the party.", "The cat was completely black except for its white paws."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective or a noun. In some contexts, it is used figuratively to describe something dark, gloomy, or secret.
collocations: ["pitch black", "black and white", "black coffee", "black tie", "black market"]

definition: The flat, sharp part of a tool or weapon used for cutting, or a single thin leaf of grass.
examples: ["The chef used a stone to sharpen the blade of his favorite knife.", "A single blade of grass was growing through a crack in the concrete."]
usage_notes: While most commonly used for knives and tools, it is also used in anatomy (shoulder blade) and botany (blade of grass).
collocations: ["blade of grass", "razor blade", "shoulder blade", "sharp blade", "saw blade", "fan blade"]

definition: To say or think that someone or something is responsible for something bad that has happened.
examples: ["Don't blame me for your mistakes.", "The police blame the accident on the icy roads."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the patterns 'blame someone for something' or 'blame something on someone'.
collocations: ["take the blame", "lay the blame", "blame someone for", "put the blame on", "share the blame"]

definition: Empty, with nothing written, printed, or recorded on it; or showing a lack of understanding, interest, or expression.
examples: ["Please write your name in the blank space at the top of the page.", "She gave him a blank look, clearly not understanding his question."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective (a blank sheet), a noun (fill in the blanks), or a verb (my mind blanked). In casual conversation, 'to draw a blank' means to be unable to remember something.
collocations: ["blank space", "blank sheet of paper", "blank stare", "fill in the blanks", "draw a blank"]

definition: Unable to see because of injury, disease, or a genetic condition; it can also describe a situation where someone is unable or unwilling to notice or understand something.
examples: ["The guide dog helped the blind man navigate the busy city streets safely.", "She was so focused on her goal that she was blind to the potential risks involved."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective, a verb (meaning to make someone unable to see), or a noun (referring to window coverings). When referring to people, 'blind person' or 'person who is blind' is preferred over 'the blind'.

definition: A solid piece of hard material with flat sides, or the act of stopping something from moving or passing through.
examples: ["The children are building a tall tower out of wooden blocks.", "A large truck is parked in the middle of the street and is blocking traffic."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun for a physical object or a verb meaning to obstruct. In American English, it also refers to the distance between two parallel streets.
collocations: ["writer's block", "city block", "building blocks", "block a shot", "cinder block"]

definition: Having pale yellow or golden-colored hair.
examples: ["She decided to dye her hair blonde for the summer.", "The actor is known for his bright blonde hair and blue eyes."]
usage_notes: Traditionally, 'blonde' is used for females and 'blond' for males, though 'blonde' is often used as a general term in modern American English.

definition: The red liquid that flows through the bodies of people and animals, carrying oxygen and nutrients to all parts of the body.
examples: ["The nurse took a sample of my blood for the medical test.", "He wiped a small drop of blood from his finger after the paper cut."]
usage_notes: It is an uncountable noun. The related verb is 'bleed'.

definition: To move or be moved by a current of air; to force air out of your mouth.
examples: ["A strong wind began to blow from the north.", "Make sure to blow on your soup before eating it so you don't burn your tongue."]
usage_notes: The past tense is 'blew' and the past participle is 'blown'. It can also be used informally as a noun meaning a hard hit or a sudden disappointment.
collocations: ["blow out candles", "blow your nose", "wind blows", "blow a whistle", "blow an opportunity"]

definition: To extinguish a flame by blowing air on it, or to burst or fail suddenly, such as a tire or a fuse.
examples: ["She made a wish and blew out all the candles on her birthday cake.", "The car swerved to the side of the road after the front tire blew out."]
usage_notes: When used for flames, it is a separable phrasal verb (e.g., 'blow it out'). In sports or health, it can refer to a severe injury or a very one-sided victory.
collocations: ["blow out the candles", "tire blow out", "blow out a fuse", "blow out your knee", "a major blowout"]

definition: To explode or be destroyed by an explosion, or to inflate something with air.
examples: ["The terrorists threatened to blow up the bridge.", "We need to blow up these balloons for the party."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb with two distinct meanings: to explode (intransitive or transitive) and to inflate (transitive). It is informal.
collocations: ["blow up a balloon", "blow up a building", "blow up in someone's face", "blow up a photo", "blow up at someone"]

definition: A primary color that is the color of the clear sky or the deep sea; it can also describe a feeling of sadness.
examples: ["The sky was a beautiful shade of bright blue this morning.", "He has been feeling a bit blue since his best friend moved away."]
usage_notes: In informal English, 'blue' is frequently used to describe feeling depressed or sad. The phrase 'out of the blue' means something happened unexpectedly.
collocations: ["bright blue", "feel blue", "out of the blue", "navy blue", "sky blue", "deep blue"]

definition: A flat piece of wood or other hard material used for a specific purpose, or the act of getting onto a ship, aircraft, or vehicle.
examples: ["The teacher wrote the instructions on the board for the students to see.", "Passengers are requested to board the plane through the rear door."]
usage_notes: As a noun, it can refer to a flat surface, a group of people in charge (board of directors), or meals provided with a room. As a verb, it means to enter a large vehicle.
collocations: ["bulletin board", "board meeting", "on board", "board a flight", "surf board"]

definition: A small vessel used for traveling over water.
examples: ["We took a small boat out onto the lake to go fishing.", "The ferry boat carries passengers across the river every hour."]
usage_notes: While 'boat' usually refers to smaller vessels, 'ship' is used for much larger ones that travel on the ocean.
collocations: ["fishing boat", "row a boat", "sail a boat", "speed boat", "get on a boat"]

definition: The entire physical structure of a person or animal, including the skin, bones, and organs.
examples: ["It is important to drink plenty of water to keep your body hydrated.", "The human body is a complex system of organs working together."]
usage_notes: In addition to the physical form, 'body' can also refer to the main part of a text or a large amount of something, like a 'body of water'.

definition: To heat a liquid until it bubbles and turns into steam, or to cook food in water that has reached this temperature.
examples: ["Please boil some water so we can make some tea.", "The soup will start to boil in about five minutes."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a verb or as a noun in the phrase 'bring to a boil'.
collocations: ["boil water", "bring to a boil", "boil over", "hard-boiled egg", "boiling point"]

definition: A weapon designed to explode and cause damage; informally, it can also mean a complete failure (especially in US English) or a great success (especially in UK English).
examples: ["The historic building was destroyed by a bomb during the war.", "The new movie was a total bomb at the box office and lost millions of dollars."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'to bomb' commonly means to fail miserably (e.g., 'I bombed the test'). In British slang, 'the bomb' can mean something is excellent, whereas in US slang, 'to bomb' usually carries a negative connotation of failure.
collocations: ["bomb threat", "defuse a bomb", "bomb shelter", "to bomb an exam"]

definition: One of the hard, white parts that form the skeleton of a human or animal body.
examples: ["The dog spent the afternoon chewing on a large bone.", "He fell off his bike and broke a bone in his wrist."]
usage_notes: While usually a noun, it can also be used as a verb meaning to remove the bones from meat or fish before cooking.
collocations: ["broken bone", "bone marrow", "bone density", "bone structure", "to have a bone to pick"]

definition: A set of printed pages bound together in a cover for reading, or the act of reserving something like a room or a seat in advance.
examples: ["I just finished reading a fascinating book about space exploration.", "We need to book a table at the restaurant before we arrive."]
usage_notes: It functions as both a noun (the object you read) and a verb (meaning to reserve or make an appointment).
collocations: ["read a book", "book a flight", "book a hotel", "by the book", "comic book"]

definition: A sturdy type of shoe that covers the foot and the ankle, and sometimes part of the lower leg; in technology, it also means to start up a computer.
examples: ["She wore a pair of leather boots to protect her feet while hiking.", "It takes about thirty seconds for my laptop to boot up."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'boot' also refers to the luggage compartment of a car (called the 'trunk' in American English). As a verb, 'boot' is often paired with 'up' when referring to computers.

definition: The line that separates two countries, states, or regions, or the outer edge of an object or area.
examples: ["We had to show our passports before crossing the border into Canada.", "The garden has a beautiful flower border along the fence."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun for the boundary line or as a verb meaning to be next to something.
collocations: ["cross the border", "border control", "national border", "share a border", "border crossing"]

definition: To make someone feel tired and uninterested, usually by being dull or talking for too long about something unexciting.
examples: ["The long lecture started to bore the students after the first hour.", "I don't want to bore you with all the details of my commute."]
usage_notes: It can also be used as a noun to describe a person who is very dull or uninteresting.
collocations: ["bore someone to tears", "bore someone to death", "easily bored", "bore someone stiff"]

definition: Feeling weary and restless because you have no interest in your current activity or have nothing to do.
examples: ["I was so bored during the long meeting that I started doodling in my notebook.", "The children are bored and want to go outside to play."]
usage_notes: Be careful not to confuse 'bored' with 'boring'. Use 'bored' to describe how a person feels, and 'boring' to describe the person or thing that causes that feeling.
collocations: ["get bored", "bored to tears", "bored stiff", "easily bored", "bored with"]

definition: Not interesting or exciting; making you feel tired or impatient because there is nothing to do or see.
examples: ["The movie was so boring that I fell asleep before it ended.", "I have a very boring job filing papers all day."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'boring' with 'bored'. Use 'boring' to describe the thing or person that causes the feeling, and 'bored' to describe how a person feels.
collocations: ["boring job", "incredibly boring", "boring lecture", "find something boring", "boring routine"]

definition: To be brought into existence by birth; having started life.
examples: ["She was born in a small town in Italy.", "He was born with a natural talent for playing the piano."]
usage_notes: Almost always used in the passive voice with the verb 'to be' (e.g., 'I was born').
collocations: ["born and raised", "first-born child", "born into a family", "newly born"]

definition: To take and use something that belongs to someone else with the intention of returning it later.
examples: ["Can I borrow your pen for a second?", "She borrowed a book from the library last week."]
usage_notes: Often confused with 'lend'. You borrow something from someone (take), while someone lends something to you (give).
collocations: ["borrow money", "borrow a book", "borrow from a friend", "borrow heavily"]

definition: A person who is in charge of a worker, a team, or an entire organization.
examples: ["I need to ask my boss for a day off next week.", "She is a great boss because she always listens to her employees' ideas."]
usage_notes: While usually used for a manager at work, it can also be used as a verb ('to boss someone around') meaning to tell people what to do in an annoying way.
collocations: ["immediate boss", "new boss", "boss around", "the big boss", "tough boss"]

definition: Used to refer to two people or things together, or to indicate that each of two things is included.
examples: ["Both of my parents are teachers.", "I like both the blue shirt and the red one."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the pattern 'both... and...' to join two words or phrases. It is only used when referring to exactly two items.
collocations: ["both of them", "both sides", "both ways", "both and", "on both counts"]

definition: To annoy someone, cause them trouble, or to make an effort to do something.
examples: ["I'm sorry to bother you, but could you help me with this box?", "He didn't even bother to call and say he would be late."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the phrase 'can't be bothered' to mean someone is too lazy or tired to do something. It can be followed by an -ing verb or a to-infinitive.
collocations: ["sorry to bother you", "don't bother", "can't be bothered", "bother with", "bother to do"]

definition: A container with a narrow neck, typically made of glass or plastic, used for storing liquids.
examples: ["She drank a whole bottle of water after her workout.", "Could you help me open this bottle of juice?"]
usage_notes: It is commonly used as a noun, but it can also be a verb meaning to put liquid into a bottle.

definition: The lowest part or surface of something, or the part that is furthest down.
examples: ["There is still some water left at the bottom of the bottle.", "She lives in the apartment at the bottom of the hill."]
usage_notes: Often used with the preposition 'at' (e.g., 'at the bottom of'). It can also refer informally to a person's buttocks.
collocations: ["at the bottom of", "bottom line", "bottom shelf", "from the bottom of my heart", "touch bottom"]

definition: Certain to happen or do something; or traveling towards a particular place.
examples: ["With so little sleep, you were bound to feel tired eventually.", "The flight is bound for New York and will depart in ten minutes."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the pattern 'bound to + verb' to express certainty, or 'bound for + destination' to indicate direction.

definition: A round, deep container that is open at the top and used for holding food or liquids.
examples: ["She filled a bowl with fresh fruit.", "I usually have a bowl of oatmeal for breakfast."]
usage_notes: It can refer to both the container itself and the amount it holds (e.g., 'a bowl of soup').
collocations: ["soup bowl", "mixing bowl", "cereal bowl", "fruit bowl", "a bowl of"]

definition: A container with flat sides and a lid, usually square or rectangular, used for storing or moving items.
examples: ["He packed his old books into a large cardboard box.", "The gift was delivered in a small, wooden box."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun for the container or as a verb meaning to put something in a box or to participate in the sport of boxing.
collocations: ["cardboard box", "gift box", "lunch box", "check the box", "box office"]

definition: A male child or a young man.
examples: ["The little boy is playing with his toy car in the park.", "He has been a member of the choir since he was a young boy."]
usage_notes: While primarily used for children, it is often used informally among friends, but should be avoided when referring to adult men in professional settings.

definition: A male partner in a romantic or sexual relationship.
examples: ["She introduced her new boyfriend to her family during dinner.", "They have been boyfriend and girlfriend since they met in high school."]
usage_notes: While common in casual conversation, some people prefer the term 'partner' for long-term or more serious relationships.

definition: The organ inside the head that controls thoughts, memory, feelings, and body movements, or the intelligence that comes from it.
examples: ["The human brain uses a lot of energy even when we are resting.", "She has a great brain for solving complex math problems."]
usage_notes: It is often used in the plural 'brains' to refer to intelligence or the smart person behind a project (e.g., 'she's the brains behind the operation').
collocations: ["brain damage", "brain storm", "use your brain", "brain cell", "human brain"]

definition: A part of a tree that grows out from the main trunk, or a smaller division of a larger organization like a bank or company.
examples: ["The cat climbed high up onto a thick branch.", "Our company is opening a new branch in Chicago next month."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun for parts of trees and organizations, or as a verb meaning to divide into smaller parts or to start doing something new.

definition: A type of product manufactured by a particular company under a particular name.
examples: ["This supermarket sells both its own brand and famous national brands.", "She always buys the same brand of coffee because she loves the taste."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun or a verb (e.g., 'to brand a product'). In modern contexts, it also refers to a person's public image ('personal brand').
collocations: ["brand loyalty", "brand awareness", "brand name", "famous brand", "build a brand"]

definition: Showing no fear of dangerous or difficult things; having courage.
examples: ["The brave firefighter ran into the burning building to save the child.", "It was very brave of her to speak up against the unfair treatment."]
usage_notes: Commonly used as an adjective. The phrase 'put on a brave face' means to pretend to be happy or confident when you are actually feeling sad or scared.
collocations: ["brave soldier", "brave decision", "put on a brave face", "brave the elements", "be brave"]

definition: A common food made from dough composed of flour and water, usually baked.
examples: ["I bought a fresh loaf of bread from the bakery.", "She spread butter and jam on a slice of bread."]
usage_notes: Bread is an uncountable noun when referring to the food in general. Use 'a slice of' or 'a loaf of' to count individual units.
collocations: ["a loaf of bread", "a slice of bread", "fresh bread", "white/whole-wheat bread", "bake bread"]

definition: To separate into pieces as a result of a blow, shock, or strain, or to pause an activity for a short period of time.
examples: ["Be careful with that glass vase, or you might break it.", "Let's break for lunch and meet back here in an hour."]
usage_notes: 'Break' is an irregular verb (break, broke, broken). As a noun, it often refers to a short rest or pause.
collocations: ["take a break", "break a habit", "break the rules", "lunch break"]

definition: To stop functioning correctly (usually a machine or vehicle) or to lose emotional control and start crying.
examples: ["Our old car broke down on the way to the airport.", "She broke down in tears when she heard the news."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. It can also be used transitively to mean 'to explain or analyze something in smaller parts'.
collocations: ["car breaks down", "break down in tears", "break down the costs", "emotional breakdown", "break down barriers"]

definition: To enter a building by force, usually to commit a crime; or to wear or use something new until it becomes comfortable.
examples: ["Someone tried to break in through the back window while we were away.", "I need to break in these new leather boots before our hiking trip."]
usage_notes: When used as a noun, it is written as one word ('break-in' or 'breakin'). As a phrasal verb, it can be intransitive (e.g., 'thieves broke in') or transitive with an object (e.g., 'to break in new shoes').
collocations: ["break in new shoes", "attempt to break in", "break in a new car", "break in on a conversation"]

definition: To enter a building or vehicle by force, usually to steal something; or to successfully start working or being involved in a new career or industry.
examples: ["Someone tried to break into our house while we were on vacation.", "It took her several years of hard work to break into the film industry."]
usage_notes: When used in the context of crime, it is an intransitive phrasal verb when used without an object (e.g., 'Burglars broke in'), but requires 'into' when the location is specified (e.g., 'They broke into the car').
collocations: ["break into a house", "break into an industry", "break into tears", "break into a smile", "break into a run"]

definition: To suddenly stop doing or saying something, or to end a relationship or formal agreement.
examples: ["He broke off in mid-sentence when he realized he was being recorded.", "The company decided to break off negotiations after the latest proposal was rejected."]
usage_notes: This phrasal verb is often used in the context of relationships, conversations, or formal agreements. It can also mean to physically separate a piece from a larger whole.
collocations: ["break off an engagement", "break off diplomatic relations", "break off negotiations", "break off a piece of chocolate"]

definition: To start suddenly, especially something dangerous or unpleasant like a war, fire, or disease; also, to escape from a place like a prison.
examples: ["A fire broke out in the basement during the night.", "The prisoners managed to break out of the facility by cutting through the fence."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. When referring to skin conditions or emotions, it is often used as 'break out in' (e.g., break out in a rash).
collocations: ["break out of prison", "war breaks out", "fire breaks out", "break out in a rash", "break out in a sweat"]

definition: To end a romantic relationship, or to separate something into smaller pieces or groups.
examples: ["They decided to break up after dating for three years.", "The teacher asked the students to break up into groups of four."]
usage_notes: When referring to a relationship, use 'break up with' followed by the person. It can also describe a poor phone or radio connection when the audio is cutting out.
collocations: ["break up with someone", "break up a fight", "break up into pieces", "a bad break up"]

definition: The first meal of the day, typically eaten in the morning after waking up.
examples: ["I usually have eggs and toast for breakfast.", "What time do you usually eat breakfast?"]
usage_notes: It is often used without an article, such as in the phrases 'have breakfast' or 'at breakfast'.
collocations: ["eat breakfast", "skip breakfast", "breakfast cereal", "bed and breakfast", "big breakfast"]

definition: The front part of the chest in humans and animals, or one of the two milk-producing organs on a woman's chest.
examples: ["The doctor discussed the importance of regular breast exams for early detection.", "For dinner, we prepared seasoned chicken breast with roasted vegetables."]
usage_notes: In culinary contexts, it specifically refers to the white meat from the chest of a bird. In medical contexts, it refers to the mammary glands.

definition: The air that you take into your lungs and then let out again when you breathe.
examples: ["She took a deep breath before jumping into the swimming pool.", "I was out of breath after running up three flights of stairs."]
usage_notes: Often confused with the verb 'breathe' (pronounced /briːð/). 'Breath' is the noun and rhymes with 'death'.
collocations: ["take a breath", "deep breath", "hold your breath", "out of breath", "bad breath"]

definition: To take air into your lungs and send it out again through your nose or mouth.
examples: ["Take a moment to breathe deeply and relax.", "The air was so smoky that it was hard to breathe."]
usage_notes: Commonly confused with the noun 'breath' (pronounced /brɛθ/). 'Breathe' is the verb and has a long 'e' sound.
collocations: ["breathe deeply", "breathe in", "breathe out", "breathe a sigh of relief", "hardly breathe"]

definition: To pull air into your lungs through your nose or mouth.
examples: ["Take a moment to breathe in the fresh mountain air.", "The doctor asked me to breathe in deeply while she listened to my heart."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. The formal synonym is 'inhale'.
collocations: ["breathe in deeply", "breathe in through your nose", "breathe in fresh air", "breathe in and out"]

definition: To release air from your lungs through your mouth or nose.
examples: ["Take a deep breath in, hold it for a second, and then slowly breathe out.", "She breathed out a long sigh of relief when she heard the good news."]
usage_notes: This is a common phrasal verb. In more formal or medical contexts, the word 'exhale' is often used instead.
collocations: ["breathe out slowly", "breathe out a sigh", "breathe in and out", "breathe out through your nose"]

definition: To take air into your lungs and send it out again through your nose or mouth.
examples: ["You should try to breathe deeply to help yourself relax.", "It was so smoky in the room that it became difficult to breathe."]
usage_notes: The verb 'breathe' (with an 'e') is often confused with the noun 'breath' (without an 'e'). 'Breathe' has a long 'e' sound like 'see'.
collocations: ["breathe deeply", "breathe in", "breathe out", "struggle to breathe", "hard to breathe"]

definition: To keep animals for the purpose of producing young, or a specific type of animal within a species that has been developed by humans.
examples: ["The farmer decided to breed his best sheep to improve the wool quality.", "Golden Retrievers are a popular breed of dog known for their friendly nature."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a verb (to reproduce) or a noun (a type of animal). Figuratively, it can mean to cause or produce something, such as 'familiarity breeds contempt'.

definition: A rectangular block made of baked clay or similar material, used for building walls and other structures.
examples: ["The old factory was built entirely of red brick.", "He carefully laid each brick to build the garden wall."]
usage_notes: It is usually a countable noun when referring to individual blocks, but can be uncountable when referring to the material itself.
collocations: ["brick wall", "red brick", "lay bricks", "brick by brick", "stack of bricks"]

definition: A structure built over a river, road, or railway to allow people and vehicles to cross from one side to the other.
examples: ["The cars drove slowly across the narrow stone bridge.", "They are building a new bridge to connect the two islands."]
usage_notes: It can be used literally for physical structures or figuratively, such as 'bridging the gap' between two different ideas or groups.
collocations: ["cross a bridge", "suspension bridge", "bridge the gap", "footbridge", "build a bridge"]

definition: Lasting for only a short period of time, or using few words to explain something.
examples: ["The meeting was very brief, lasting only ten minutes.", "Please give me a brief summary of the report."]
usage_notes: It can be used as an adjective to mean 'short', or as a verb meaning 'to give someone instructions or information'.

definition: For a short period of time, or using only a few words to explain something.
examples: ["We stopped briefly in London on our way to Paris.", "She explained the situation briefly before the meeting started."]
usage_notes: It can describe both the duration of an event and the conciseness of speech or writing.

definition: Giving out or reflecting a lot of light, or describing someone who is intelligent and quick to learn.
examples: ["The sun was so bright that I had to wear sunglasses.", "She is a very bright student who always asks interesting questions."]
usage_notes: This word is commonly used to describe both physical light and mental intelligence.

definition: In a way that produces a lot of light or has strong, vivid colors.
examples: ["The sun was shining brightly through the bedroom window.", "The children were dressed in brightly colored clothes for the parade."]
usage_notes: This is an adverb commonly used to describe how something shines, how a room is lit, or how someone smiles.

definition: Exceptionally clever, talented, or impressive; it can also describe something very bright.
examples: ["She came up with a brilliant solution to the problem.", "The fireworks lit up the sky with brilliant colors."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'brilliant' is very commonly used in informal speech to mean 'great' or 'wonderful' (e.g., 'That's a brilliant idea!').

definition: To take or carry someone or something to a place or person.
examples: ["Please bring your books to class tomorrow.", "Can you bring me a glass of water?"]
usage_notes: This is an irregular verb (bring, brought, brought). It usually implies movement toward the speaker or the place where the speaker is.

definition: To return something to its original place, or to cause someone to remember something from the past.
examples: ["Could you bring back the library books tomorrow?", "That old song always brings back happy memories of my childhood."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb; you can say 'bring back the book' or 'bring the book back'.
collocations: ["bring back memories", "bring back a trend", "bring back a law", "bring back a souvenir"]

definition: To cause someone or something to lose power, to reduce the amount or level of something, or to make someone feel unhappy.
examples: ["The scandal eventually brought down the entire government.", "The store decided to bring down the prices of all winter coats."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb. You can say 'bring down the prices' or 'bring the prices down'.
collocations: ["bring down prices", "bring down a government", "bring down the house", "bring down the cost", "bring down the level"]

definition: To change the date or time of a scheduled event so that it happens earlier than originally planned.
examples: ["The meeting has been brought forward from Friday to Wednesday.", "They decided to bring the deadline forward by two weeks to ensure everything was ready."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb. You can say 'bring forward the meeting' or 'bring the meeting forward'. It is commonly used in professional and scheduling contexts.
collocations: ["bring forward a meeting", "bring forward a deadline", "bring forward a date", "bring forward a proposal"]

definition: To make a particular quality or detail more noticeable, or to produce and launch a new product for sale.
examples: ["The bright blue shirt really brings out the color of your eyes.", "The company is planning to bring out a new smartphone model next month."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb, meaning you can put the object between 'bring' and 'out' (e.g., 'bring it out').
collocations: ["bring out the best in someone", "bring out a new product", "bring out the flavor", "bring out the truth"]

definition: To mention a subject or start a discussion about something, or to care for a child until they are an adult.
examples: ["I didn't want to bring up the budget during the meeting.", "He was brought up in a small village in the countryside."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb. When referring to raising children, it is frequently used in the passive voice (e.g., 'I was brought up').
collocations: ["bring up a topic", "bring up a child", "bring up an issue", "bring up memories", "bring up a point"]

definition: Having a large distance from one side to the other; wide. It can also describe something that is general and covers many things without focusing on small details.
examples: ["The river is very broad at this point, making it difficult to swim across.", "The government has broad support from the public for these new changes."]
usage_notes: It is frequently used both for physical width and for abstract concepts like range, scope, or categories.

definition: To send out programs, information, or signals by radio, television, or the internet to a wide audience.
examples: ["The news will be broadcast live at six o'clock this evening.", "The radio station broadcasts classical music 24 hours a day."]
usage_notes: The past tense and past participle can be either 'broadcast' or 'broadcasted', though 'broadcast' is more common in formal writing.
collocations: ["live broadcast", "radio broadcast", "broadcast news", "public broadcast", "broadcast a signal"]

definition: In a general way, without focusing on specific details or small differences.
examples: ["Broadly speaking, the new law has been well-received by the public.", "The two software programs are broadly similar in how they function."]
usage_notes: Frequently used in the phrase 'broadly speaking' to indicate that a statement is a generalization.

definition: Damaged and no longer in one piece, or not functioning correctly.
examples: ["The window is broken and needs to be replaced.", "My computer is broken, so I have to use the one in the library."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe physical objects, but can also describe abstract concepts like a 'broken promise' or a 'broken heart'.

definition: A male person who has the same parents as another person.
examples: ["My older brother is a doctor.", "He has two brothers and one sister."]
usage_notes: The word can also be used informally to refer to a close male friend or a member of the same group or religion.

definition: A dark color like the shade of earth, wood, or coffee.
examples: ["The leaves turn brown in the autumn.", "She has long, dark brown hair."]
usage_notes: It can be used as an adjective to describe color or as a verb meaning to cook food until it turns brown.

definition: A tool with bristles used for cleaning, grooming hair, or applying paint; it also refers to the act of using such a tool.
examples: ["I need to buy a new brush for my hair.", "You should brush your teeth at least twice a day."]
usage_notes: It can be used as both a noun (the object) and a verb (the action). The phrasal verb 'brush up on' means to practice or improve a skill you have forgotten.
collocations: ["brush your teeth", "hair brush", "paint brush", "brush aside", "brush up on"]

definition: A thin ball of liquid containing air or gas, or a situation where someone is isolated from outside influences or reality.
examples: ["The children were blowing soap bubbles in the backyard.", "He lives in a social media bubble and rarely hears opposing viewpoints."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun or a verb. Metaphorically, 'bursting someone's bubble' means to destroy their illusion or happy dream.
collocations: ["soap bubble", "bubble bath", "burst a bubble", "economic bubble", "filter bubble"]

definition: A plan that shows how much money you have and how you will spend it over a period of time, or the total amount of money available for a specific purpose.
examples: ["The company has a very tight budget for marketing this year.", "We need to learn how to budget our monthly expenses more effectively."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun (a plan), a verb (to plan spending), or an adjective meaning 'low-cost' or 'cheap'.
collocations: ["on a budget", "tight budget", "annual budget", "budget cuts", "stay within budget"]

definition: To create something by putting parts together, especially a structure like a house or a system.
examples: ["They plan to build a new library in the city center.", "It takes time to build a strong relationship with your colleagues."]
usage_notes: Often used metaphorically for abstract things like trust, reputation, or a career.
collocations: ["build a house", "build trust", "build a career", "build a website", "build a reputation"]

definition: To gradually increase in amount, size, or strength over a period of time.
examples: ["You need to build up your strength after being sick for so long.", "Traffic usually starts to build up around 5:00 PM."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb that can be separable (e.g., 'build it up'). It is often used for abstract things like confidence or physical things like speed.
collocations: ["build up confidence", "build up speed", "build up a reputation", "build up resistance", "build up savings"]

definition: A structure with a roof and walls, such as a house, school, or office, where people live, work, or stay.
examples: ["The tallest building in the city is the new office tower.", "They are constructing a new apartment building on our street."]
usage_notes: It can refer to the physical structure (noun) or the process of constructing something (gerund).

definition: A small metal projectile that is fired from a gun or other firearm.
examples: ["The detective found a spent bullet casing near the window.", "He decided to bite the bullet and tell his boss the truth about the mistake."]
usage_notes: In business and writing, it also refers to a small symbol used to introduce items in a list (a bullet point).
collocations: ["silver bullet", "stray bullet", "bullet point", "bullet-proof vest", "fire a bullet"]

definition: A number of things of the same type fastened, growing, or grouped together, or an informal group of people.
examples: ["She bought a beautiful bunch of bananas at the market.", "A bunch of my friends are meeting up for dinner tonight."]
usage_notes: In casual English, 'a bunch of' is often used to mean 'many' or 'a lot of' with both countable nouns (a bunch of people) and sometimes uncountable nouns (a bunch of stuff).
collocations: ["a bunch of flowers", "a bunch of grapes", "a bunch of keys", "a whole bunch", "a bunch of friends"]

definition: To produce flames or heat, or to be damaged or destroyed by fire or extreme heat.
examples: ["Be careful not to burn yourself on the hot stove.", "The wood was dry enough to burn easily in the fireplace."]
usage_notes: In British English, the past tense and past participle can be 'burnt' or 'burned', whereas American English usually uses 'burned'.
collocations: ["burn calories", "burn down", "burn out", "burn a CD", "burn with passion"]

definition: To destroy something, usually a building or structure, completely by fire.
examples: ["The old barn burned down during the thunderstorm last night.", "They decided to burn down the dilapidated shed to clear the land."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. It is often used in the past tense ('burned down' or 'burnt down').
collocations: ["burn down a house", "burn down a building", "burn down to the ground", "threaten to burn down"]

definition: To be on fire, or to damage, destroy, or injure something by fire, heat, or acid.
examples: ["Be careful not to burn the toast while you are making breakfast.", "The sun can burn your skin very quickly if you do not wear sunscreen."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'burned' is the standard past tense form, while 'burnt' is often used as an adjective. In British English, 'burnt' is commonly used as both the past tense and the adjective.
collocations: ["burn down", "burn out", "burn calories", "sun burn", "burn a bridge"]

definition: To break open or apart suddenly and violently, or to move or start doing something with a lot of energy.
examples: ["The balloon burst when it hit the prickly cactus.", "He burst into the room to share the exciting news."]
usage_notes: The past tense and past participle of 'burst' is also 'burst'. Avoid saying 'bursted'.
collocations: ["burst into tears", "burst into flames", "burst out laughing", "a burst of energy", "water pipe burst"]

definition: To suddenly start doing something, such as crying, laughing, or singing, or to suddenly enter a place with force or energy.
examples: ["The audience burst into applause as soon as the performance ended.", "She burst into the room to tell us the exciting news."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with nouns like 'tears', 'laughter', or 'flames' to describe a sudden change in state.
collocations: ["burst into tears", "burst into laughter", "burst into flames", "burst into song", "burst into the room"]

definition: To suddenly start doing something, such as laughing or crying, or to suddenly say something or move out of a place.
examples: ["Everyone in the room burst out laughing after he told the joke.", "She burst out of the house and ran down the street."]
usage_notes: When used to mean starting an action, it is almost always followed by a verb ending in -ing (e.g., 'burst out crying').
collocations: ["burst out laughing", "burst out crying", "burst out singing", "burst out of the room"]

definition: To put something into the ground and cover it with earth, or to hide something deep inside or under something else.
examples: ["The dog likes to bury its bones in the backyard.", "She tried to bury her feelings and pretend that nothing was wrong."]
usage_notes: The pronunciation of 'bury' is identical to the word 'berry'. It is frequently used figuratively, such as 'burying the hatchet' (making peace).
collocations: ["bury the hatchet", "bury a treasure", "bury one's head in the sand", "bury a secret"]

definition: A large motor vehicle designed to carry many passengers, usually following a fixed route and schedule.
examples: ["I take the bus to work every morning.", "The school bus stops right in front of our house."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'bus' can also be a verb meaning to clear dirty dishes from a table in a restaurant.
collocations: ["catch a bus", "bus stop", "bus driver", "miss the bus", "take the bus"]

definition: A plant that is smaller than a tree and has many branches growing close to the ground.
examples: ["The rabbit quickly hid behind a thick green bush.", "She spent the morning trimming the rose bushes in the garden."]
usage_notes: In some countries like Australia or South Africa, 'the bush' refers to wild, uncultivated land far from towns.
collocations: ["rose bush", "thick bush", "trim the bushes", "beat around the bush", "the Australian bush"]

definition: The activity of making, buying, or selling goods or providing services in exchange for money, or a specific organization that does this.
examples: ["She decided to start her own business after working in the industry for ten years.", "Our main goal is to do business with international partners."]
usage_notes: The word 'business' is uncountable when referring to general commercial activity (e.g., 'Business is good'). It is countable when referring to a specific company (e.g., 'They own three local businesses').
collocations: ["start a business", "run a business", "business partner", "go out of business", "do business"]

definition: A man who works in business, especially one who has an important position in a company or owns a business.
examples: ["He is a successful businessman who owns several restaurants in the city.", "The young businessman traveled to Tokyo to negotiate a new contract."]
usage_notes: While 'businessman' is widely used, the gender-neutral term 'businessperson' (or 'businesspeople' in the plural) is often preferred in modern professional contexts to be inclusive.

definition: Actively doing something, having a lot of work or tasks to do, or being full of activity.
examples: ["I am too busy with my homework to go to the movies tonight.", "The streets are always very busy during the morning rush hour."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the pattern 'busy + -ing verb' (e.g., 'busy preparing dinner') or 'busy with + noun' (e.g., 'busy with work').

definition: Used to introduce a statement that contrasts with or contradicts what has just been said.
examples: ["I want to go to the party, but I am too tired.", "She studied hard but didn't pass the exam."]
usage_notes: Avoid starting too many sentences with 'but' in formal writing; instead, use transition words like 'however' or 'nevertheless'.
collocations: ["but also", "last but not least", "nothing but", "slowly but surely"]

definition: A pale yellow fatty food made by churning cream, used as a spread on bread and in cooking or baking.
examples: ["She spread some butter on her hot toast.", "Melt two tablespoons of butter in the pan before adding the onions."]
usage_notes: 'Butter' is usually an uncountable noun when referring to the food. As a verb, it means to spread butter on something or, in the idiom 'butter someone up', to flatter someone.

definition: A small, usually round object used to fasten clothes, or a part of a machine or device that you press to make it work.
examples: ["He pressed the button to call the elevator.", "I need to sew a button back onto my shirt."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'to button' means to fasten something. 'Button up' is a common phrasal verb used for clothing.
collocations: ["push a button", "press a button", "sew a button", "button up", "panic button"]

definition: To obtain something by paying money for it.
examples: ["I need to buy some groceries on my way home.", "He decided to buy a new laptop for school."]
usage_notes: This is an irregular verb: buy, bought, bought. It is often followed by 'for' when mentioning the price (e.g., 'I bought it for ten dollars').
collocations: ["buy a house", "buy groceries", "buy online", "buy a gift", "buy time"]

definition: A person who purchases something or is looking to purchase something, such as a product, service, or property.
examples: ["The real estate agent found a buyer for the house within a week.", "As a smart buyer, she always reads product reviews before spending her money."]
usage_notes: In a business context, a 'buyer' can also be a professional job title for someone who selects and purchases goods for a retail store.

definition: A preposition used to indicate the person or thing that performs an action, the method used to do something, or a deadline for an event.
examples: ["The book was written by a famous author.", "Please submit your report by Friday."]
usage_notes: Used frequently to show agency in passive voice sentences or to specify a time limit.
collocations: ["by accident", "by far", "by hand", "by the way", "by means of"]

definition: A common, informal way to say goodbye when leaving someone or ending a conversation.
examples: ["Bye! See you tomorrow at school.", "I have to go now, so bye for now!"]
usage_notes: It is a shortened, informal version of 'goodbye' used frequently in casual speech and text messages.

definition: A piece of furniture with shelves or drawers used for storing things, or a group of senior government officials who advise a leader.
examples: ["Please put the clean dishes away in the kitchen cabinet.", "The president met with his cabinet to discuss the new economic policy."]
usage_notes: In a political context, the word is often capitalized (the Cabinet) when referring to a specific government body.

definition: A strong, thick wire or bundle of wires used for carrying electricity, electronic signals, or for supporting heavy structures.
examples: ["I need a longer cable to connect my laptop to the television.", "The bridge is held up by massive steel cables."]
usage_notes: In modern contexts, 'cable' often refers to television service ('cable TV') or charging cords (e.g., 'USB cable'). It can also be used as a verb meaning to send a message or equip with cables.

definition: A sweet baked food made from a mixture of flour, sugar, eggs, and butter or oil, often decorated with frosting.
examples: ["We baked a chocolate cake for my sister's birthday party.", "Would you like a slice of cake with your cup of tea?"]
usage_notes: Countable when referring to a whole cake or individual portions, but uncountable when referring to the food substance in general (e.g., 'Do you want some cake?').
collocations: ["birthday cake", "slice of cake", "bake a cake", "chocolate cake", "piece of cake"]

definition: To find an answer or amount by using mathematical processes or logic.
examples: ["We need to calculate the total cost of the trip before we book anything.", "The computer can calculate complex equations in a fraction of a second."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by a direct object or a 'that' clause. It can also imply making a careful judgment about a situation.
collocations: ["calculate the cost", "calculate the risk", "calculate the distance", "calculate the percentage", "accurately calculate"]

definition: The process of using numbers to find an amount or result, or the result itself.
examples: ["The engineer made a quick calculation to determine the bridge's weight limit.", "According to my calculations, we should arrive at the destination by noon."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in technical contexts, but can also describe a cold, deliberate plan to achieve a goal.
collocations: ["perform a calculation", "accurate calculation", "mathematical calculation", "rough calculation", "make a calculation"]

definition: To contact someone by telephone, to speak out loud to get someone's attention, or to give a specific name to someone or something.
examples: ["I will call you as soon as I arrive at the station.", "They decided to call their new dog Buster."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a verb and a noun. In British English, people often say 'ring' or 'phone' instead of 'call'.
collocations: ["make a phone call", "call back", "call for help", "call a meeting", "call off"]

definition: To return a telephone call to someone, or to return to a place to see someone again.
examples: ["I'm in a meeting right now, so I will call you back in an hour.", "The doctor's office said they would call back with my test results tomorrow."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb. If you use a pronoun (like 'me', 'him', 'her', 'it', 'them', 'us'), it must go between 'call' and 'back' (e.g., 'call me back', not 'call back me').
collocations: ["call someone right back", "promise to call back", "call back later", "try calling back"]

definition: To publicly demand that something should happen, or to require a particular action, quality, or ingredient.
examples: ["The protesters are calling for a change in the law.", "This difficult situation calls for a lot of patience."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. When it means 'to require,' it is often used with abstract nouns like 'action' or 'patience.'
collocations: ["call for action", "call for change", "call for a meeting", "call for calm", "recipe calls for"]

definition: To cancel something that was previously planned or scheduled.
examples: ["They had to call off the outdoor concert because of the heavy rain.", "The manager decided to call off the meeting since several key team members were sick."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb. If you use a pronoun like 'it' or 'them', it must go between 'call' and 'off' (e.g., 'call it off', not 'call off it').
collocations: ["call off a meeting", "call off the wedding", "call off the search", "call off an event"]

definition: To make a phone call to someone, or to officially select someone to join a military service or a sports team.
examples: ["I'll call up the restaurant to see if they have any tables available for tonight.", "He was thrilled when he was finally called up to play for the national soccer team."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. It is separable, meaning you can put the object in the middle (e.g., 'call him up' or 'call up my friend'). When using a pronoun, it must go in the middle ('call them up', not 'call up them').
collocations: ["call up a friend", "get called up", "call up a reserve", "call up the past"]

definition: To give a name to someone or something, or to contact someone by telephone.
examples: ["They decided to call their new dog Max.", "Please call me when you arrive at the station."]
usage_notes: The word 'called' is the past tense and past participle of 'call'. It is very commonly used as an adjective meaning 'having the name of' (e.g., 'a man called John').
collocations: ["call back", "call for help", "make a phone call", "be called"]

definition: Peaceful, quiet, and free from worry, excitement, or strong emotion.
examples: ["It is important to stay calm during an emergency.", "The sea was very calm and still this morning."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective ('a calm day'), a verb meaning to make someone peaceful ('calm down'), or a noun ('the calm before the storm').

definition: To become quiet, peaceful, or less excited and angry, or to make someone else feel this way.
examples: ["Take a deep breath and try to calm down before making a decision.", "The teacher asked the excited children to calm down."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an intransitive verb (to become calm) or transitive verb (to make someone calm). Often used as a command, but telling someone to 'calm down!' when they are angry can sometimes make them feel worse.
collocations: ["calm down a bit", "try to calm down", "help someone calm down", "calm down completely"]

definition: In a quiet, peaceful, or relaxed way, without showing anger, fear, or excitement.
examples: ["She calmly explained the situation to the worried customers.", "Despite the emergency, the pilot spoke calmly over the intercom."]
usage_notes: It is an adverb, so it is used to describe how an action is performed (e.g., 'speak calmly', 'react calmly').

definition: A device used for taking photographs or recording moving images.
examples: ["She pointed her camera at the beautiful sunset and took a picture.", "Most modern smartphones have a high-quality built-in camera."]
usage_notes: The word 'camera' can refer to both traditional digital cameras and the camera lenses on smartphones. The phrase 'on camera' means being recorded or filmed.
collocations: ["digital camera", "security camera", "look at the camera", "front-facing camera", "camera lens"]

definition: A place where people live temporarily in tents or simple huts, often for vacation, outdoor activities, or military training.
examples: ["We set up camp near the river before the sun went down.", "Every summer, the children go to a sports camp to improve their skills."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun ('a camp') or a verb ('to camp' / 'to go camping'). As an adjective in informal contexts, 'camp' can also mean deliberately exaggerated or theatrical.
collocations: ["set up camp", "summer camp", "go camping", "camp site", "break camp"]

definition: A planned series of organized activities or actions intended to achieve a specific social, political, or commercial goal.
examples: ["The company launched a massive advertising campaign to promote their new smartphone.", "She volunteered for the local mayoral campaign during the election."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a noun and a verb. When used as a verb, it is often followed by 'for' (to support something) or 'against' (to oppose something).
collocations: ["launch a campaign", "advertising campaign", "political campaign", "marketing campaign", "awareness campaign"]

definition: The activity of spending a holiday living in a tent, caravan, or campervan, usually in the countryside.
examples: ["We are going camping in the national park this weekend.", "I love camping because it allows me to connect with nature."]
usage_notes: Often used with the verb 'go' (e.g., 'go camping'). The noun 'camp' refers to the place, while 'camping' is the activity itself.

definition: To be able to do something, to have the ability or power to do something, or to have permission to do something.
examples: ["She can speak three languages fluently.", "Can I borrow your pen for a moment?"]
usage_notes: As a modal verb, 'can' is followed by the base form of the verb without 'to' (e.g., 'I can swim', not 'I can to swim'). The negative form is 'cannot' or the contraction 'can't'.
collocations: ["can afford", "can hear", "can see", "can help", "as best as one can"]

definition: A cylindrical metal container used for preserving and storing food, beverages, or other liquids.
examples: ["Could you please open this can of soup for dinner?", "He threw the empty soda can into the recycling bin."]
usage_notes: In British English, this is often referred to as a 'tin' when it contains food. The verb form 'to can' means to preserve food in a jar or can.
collocations: ["can of soup", "soda can", "garbage can", "can opener", "spray can"]

definition: To decide that an organized event, meeting, or agreement will not happen.
examples: ["They had to cancel the outdoor concert because of the heavy rain.", "I need to cancel my reservation and reschedule for next week."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with 'a meeting', 'a flight', or 'a subscription'. In British English, the past tense and participle are spelled with a double 'l' (cancelled), while American English typically uses a single 'l' (canceled).
collocations: ["cancel a meeting", "cancel a flight", "cancel a subscription", "cancel an appointment", "cancel last minute"]

definition: A serious disease in which abnormal cells in the body grow and spread in an uncontrolled way.
examples: ["The doctors are hopeful that they caught the cancer early enough to treat it successfully.", "She is raising money for a charity that funds breast cancer research."]
usage_notes: Often used with verbs like 'diagnose', 'treat', or 'beat'. It can be used as an uncountable noun for the disease in general, or a countable noun when referring to specific types (e.g., 'lung cancers').

definition: A person who is competing for a job, a political office, or an award.
examples: ["The search committee is interviewing five candidates for the position.", "She is considered a leading candidate for the Nobel Peace Prize."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the preposition 'for'. In some contexts, it can also refer to a student taking an exam.

definition: A sweet food made mostly of sugar, often combined with chocolate, fruit flavors, or nuts.
examples: ["The children were given some candy after they finished their dinner.", "She bought a bag of hard candies to suck on during the long flight."]
usage_notes: In British English, this is usually called 'sweets'. 'Candy' is uncountable when referring to the food in general, but can be countable ('candies') when referring to individual pieces or different types.
collocations: ["cotton candy", "candy bar", "piece of candy", "sweet candy", "candy store"]

definition: To be unable to do something; the negative form of 'can'.
examples: ["I cannot attend the meeting tomorrow because I have a doctor's appointment.", "We cannot accept this proposal in its current form."]
usage_notes: 'Cannot' is written as a single word in standard English, unlike 'can not' which is only used in specific grammatical structures. In informal speech and writing, it is usually contracted to 'can't'.
collocations: ["cannot afford", "cannot help but", "cannot wait", "cannot guarantee", "simply cannot"]

definition: A soft, flat hat with a curved part sticking out at the front; or a protective lid or cover for a container.
examples: ["He wore a baseball cap to shield his eyes from the sun.", "Make sure you put the cap back on the bottle so the water doesn't spill."]
usage_notes: The word 'cap' can also be used as a verb meaning to limit something (e.g., 'to cap spending') or to cover the top of something.
collocations: ["baseball cap", "bottle cap", "cap on spending", "put a cap on"]

definition: Having the ability, fitness, or necessary skills to do something successfully.
examples: ["She is a highly capable manager who always gets the job done on time.", "The new software is capable of processing thousands of transactions per second."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the preposition 'of' and a gerund (verb + -ing), as in 'capable of doing something', rather than an infinitive.

definition: The maximum amount that something can contain or produce, or a person's ability to do or understand something.
examples: ["The stadium was filled to capacity for the championship game.", "She has an amazing capacity for remembering names and faces."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'for' (e.g., 'capacity for learning') or an infinitive verb (e.g., 'capacity to adapt'). In professional contexts, it can also mean a specific role or position (e.g., 'acting in an advisory capacity').
collocations: ["filled to capacity", "carrying capacity", "intellectual capacity", "limited capacity", "productive capacity"]

definition: The most important city in a country or state, usually where the government is located; it can also refer to wealth in the form of money or assets used to start a business.
examples: ["Paris is the capital of France.", "The company is trying to raise capital to fund its new tech project."]
usage_notes: Note the spelling: 'capital' with an 'a' refers to the city or money, while 'capitol' with an 'o' refers specifically to the building where a legislature meets.

definition: The person in command of a ship, aircraft, sports team, or military group.
examples: ["The captain of the ship safely guided the vessel through the rough storm.", "She was chosen as the captain of the varsity basketball team."]
usage_notes: When used as a title before a person's name, it is capitalized (e.g., 'Captain Smith'). It can also be used as a verb meaning to lead or command.
collocations: ["ship's captain", "team captain", "captain of the industry", "sea captain"]

definition: To take someone as a prisoner, or to successfully record, represent, or gain control of something.
examples: ["The photographer managed to capture the beautiful sunset just before it disappeared.", "The soldiers were ordered to capture the enemy stronghold."]
usage_notes: Often used metaphorically in business and arts (e.g., 'capture attention' or 'capture market share'), not just in physical contexts of taking prisoners.
collocations: ["capture someone's attention", "capture the moment", "capture market share", "capture the imagination"]

definition: A road vehicle with four wheels that is powered by an engine and used to carry a small number of people.
examples: ["I usually drive my car to work every morning.", "She parked her car in the garage."]
usage_notes: The word 'car' is the standard term for personal vehicles; 'automobile' is more formal or technical.
collocations: ["drive a car", "park a car", "used car", "electric car", "sports car"]

definition: A small, flat, stiff piece of paper or plastic used for writing information on, sending a message, or making payments.
examples: ["He paid for the groceries using his credit card.", "She sent me a beautiful card for my birthday."]
usage_notes: The word 'card' can refer to many different objects depending on the context, such as a playing card, a greeting card, or a plastic payment card. In modern contexts, 'to card' can also be used as an informal verb meaning to ask someone for proof of age.
collocations: ["credit card", "birthday card", "deck of cards", "business card", "id card"]

definition: A stiff, thick paper or pasteboard used for making boxes and signs.
examples: ["We need to find some large cardboard boxes for the move.", "The children made a toy castle out of cardboard."]
usage_notes: It is an uncountable noun when referring to the material itself, but can be used as a noun adjunct (like an adjective) before other nouns, as in 'cardboard box'.

definition: To feel concern, interest, or affection for someone or something; also, the process of protecting or looking after someone or something.
examples: ["She really cares about her students and wants them to succeed.", "The doctor told him to take better care of his health."]
usage_notes: Often used with the preposition 'about' when expressing concern (e.g., 'care about the environment') or with 'for' when looking after someone (e.g., 'care for an elderly relative').
collocations: ["take care of", "care about", "medical care", "customer care", "care deeply"]

definition: To look after someone or something that needs help, or to like or want something (often used in polite offers or to express dislike).
examples: ["She spent most of her life caring for her elderly parents.", "Would you care for another cup of coffee?"]
usage_notes: When it means 'to like,' it is frequently used in the negative ('I don't care for...') to express a polite dislike. In the sense of 'looking after,' it is a transitive phrasal verb.
collocations: ["care for a patient", "care for a child", "not care for something", "would you care for", "care for the environment"]

definition: An occupation or profession that a person undertakes for a significant period of their life, usually with opportunities for progress or promotion.
examples: ["She is planning to pursue a career in medicine after she graduates.", "He spent his entire career working for the same technology company."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'career' with 'carrier' (a person or thing that carries something) or 'care' (concern/worry). It is commonly used with verbs like 'pursue', 'build', or 'launch'.
collocations: ["career path", "career goals", "pursue a career", "career advancement", "change careers"]

definition: Making sure to avoid danger, mistakes, or damage by paying close attention to what you are doing.
examples: ["Please be careful with that vase; it is very fragile.", "He made a careful plan to ensure nothing would go wrong."]
usage_notes: Commonly followed by the prepositions 'with' (for objects) or 'about' (for actions/decisions). For example: 'be careful with the glass' or 'be careful about what you say'.
collocations: ["be careful", "careful planning", "careful consideration", "a careful driver", "be careful with"]

definition: In a way that shows close attention, caution, or effort to avoid mistakes, damage, or danger.
examples: ["Please listen carefully to the instructions before starting the test.", "She carefully placed the fragile glass vase on the top shelf."]
usage_notes: This is a common adverb of manner. It is typically placed after the verb it describes (e.g., 'read carefully') or before the verb for emphasis (e.g., 'carefully read').

definition: Not taking enough care or paying enough attention to what you are doing, which can lead to mistakes, damage, or hurt feelings.
examples: ["It was careless of me to leave my keys in the car.", "She made a few careless mistakes on the math exam."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'about' (e.g., 'careless about his appearance') or used in the pattern 'it is careless of someone to do something'.

definition: In a way that does not give enough attention, thought, or care to avoiding harm, mistakes, or damage.
examples: ["He carelessly tossed his keys onto the table and broke a glass vase.", "She admitted that she had carelessly filled out the application form."]
usage_notes: This is an adverb. It is often used to modify verbs of action (like 'throw', 'drive', or 'write') to show that the action was done without proper attention.

definition: A thick, heavy floor covering made of fabric or woven pile, typically covering the entire floor of a room.
examples: ["We decided to install a soft grey carpet in the bedroom to make it feel cozier.", "She spilled a glass of red wine on the living room carpet."]
usage_notes: The noun 'carpet' refers to the material or the floor covering itself. It can also be used as a verb meaning 'to cover an area with a carpet' (e.g., 'to carpet the stairs').
collocations: ["wall-to-wall carpet", "lay a carpet", "roll out the red carpet", "carpet cleaning", "shag carpet"]

definition: A long, thin, orange root vegetable that is eaten raw or cooked.
examples: ["She chopped up some carrots and celery to add to the beef soup.", "Rabbits are famous for loving to eat crunchy carrots."]
usage_notes: The word 'carrot' is a countable noun. It can also be used metaphorically in the phrase 'carrot and stick' to describe a system of offering rewards and punishments.

definition: To hold something and move it from one place to another.
examples: ["Could you help me carry these heavy bags to the car?", "She always carries a small notebook in her purse."]
usage_notes: Often followed by prepositions like 'out' (to perform a task) or 'on' (to continue doing something). Avoid confusing 'carry' with 'wear' when talking about clothing or accessories.
collocations: ["carry a bag", "carry weight", "carry out a plan", "carry on", "carry a message"]

definition: To continue doing something, or to keep moving forward despite difficulties.
examples: ["Even though it started to rain, they decided to carry on with their walk.", "Please carry on with your work while I am out of the room."]
usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'with' or a verb ending in '-ing' (e.g., 'carry on working'). In British English, it can also mean to behave in an excited, anxious, or silly way.
collocations: ["carry on a conversation", "carry on working", "carry on business", "keep calm and carry on"]

definition: To perform, complete, or put into action a task, plan, order, or threat.
examples: ["The hospital is carrying out tests to find the cause of her illness.", "The soldiers were ordered to carry out the mission immediately."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. It is transitive and separable, meaning you can say 'carry out a plan' or 'carry a plan out'. It is commonly used in formal, business, and academic contexts.
collocations: ["carry out research", "carry out an investigation", "carry out instructions", "carry out a threat", "carry out a task"]

definition: An instance, occurrence, or example of something happening; it can also refer to a container used to hold or protect things, or a matter being investigated by police or lawyers.
examples: ["In any case, we need to make a decision by tomorrow morning.", "The police are investigating a new case of identity theft."]
usage_notes: The phrase 'in case' is used to talk about precautions (e.g., 'Take an umbrella in case it rains'), whereas 'in case of' is followed by a noun (e.g., 'in case of emergency').
collocations: ["just in case", "worst-case scenario", "a court case", "in any case", "make a case for"]

definition: Money in the form of coins or paper notes, rather than checks, credit cards, or digital transfers.
examples: ["I don't have any cash on me, so I will have to pay with my credit card.", "The store offers a small discount if you pay in cash."]
usage_notes: Commonly used in the prepositional phrases 'in cash' (to pay in cash) or 'for cash'. It is an uncountable noun.
collocations: ["pay in cash", "cold hard cash", "cash flow", "petty cash", "cash register"]

definition: To choose actors for a play, movie, or show; or to throw something lightly, like a fishing line or a vote.
examples: ["The director decided to cast her as the lead actress in the upcoming film.", "He cast his fishing line into the calm waters of the lake."]
usage_notes: The past tense and past participle form of 'cast' is also 'cast' (not 'casted').
collocations: ["cast a vote", "cast a spell", "cast doubt on", "cast a shadow", "cast member"]

definition: A large, strong building built in the past by a ruler or important person to protect the people inside from attack.
examples: ["The medieval castle stood on top of the hill, overlooking the entire valley.", "We spent the afternoon exploring the ruins of an old stone castle."]
usage_notes: The letter 't' in 'castle' is silent. It is a countable noun.

definition: A small, domesticated carnivorous mammal with soft fur, a short snout, and retractile claws, often kept as a pet or for catching mice.
examples: ["My cat loves to sleep in the sun by the window.", "She fed the cat some wet food and fresh water."]
usage_notes: The word 'cat' is a highly common, everyday noun. It is also used in many common idioms, such as 'let the cat out of the bag' (to reveal a secret).
collocations: ["pet cat", "stray cat", "domestic cat", "feed the cat", "cat food"]

definition: To intercept and hold something that has been thrown, dropped, or is in motion; or to capture a person, animal, or vehicle.
examples: ["He managed to catch the ball with one hand.", "We need to run if we want to catch the 9:00 train."]
usage_notes: The past tense and past participle form is irregular: 'caught'. It is also commonly used in idioms like 'catch a cold' (to become sick) or 'catch someone's eye' (to attract attention).
collocations: ["catch a cold", "catch a bus", "catch a ball", "catch someone's attention", "catch fire"]

definition: To reach the same quality, detail, or position as someone or something that is ahead; or to talk to someone you have not seen for a while to find out what they have been doing.
examples: ["I need to run faster to catch up with the rest of the group.", "Let's meet for coffee this weekend to catch up."]
usage_notes: Often followed by 'with' (e.g., 'catch up with friends' or 'catch up with work'). It can also be used as a noun, 'catch-up', usually with the verb 'play' (e.g., 'to play catch-up').
collocations: ["catch up with friends", "catch up on sleep", "catch up on work", "play catch-up", "try to catch up"]

definition: A group of people or things that are regarded as having shared characteristics or qualities.
examples: ["The books are divided into different categories based on their genre.", "This product falls into the category of luxury goods."]
usage_notes: The preposition 'under' is often used when saying something belongs to a specific group (e.g., 'It falls under the category of...').
collocations: ["broad category", "fall into a category", "main category", "separate category", "age category"]

definition: To make something happen, especially something bad or unpleasant; or, the person, event, or thing that makes something happen.
examples: ["The heavy rain caused severe flooding in the low-lying areas of the city.", "The police are still trying to find the cause of the fire."]
usage_notes: As a verb, it is often followed by an object and a to-infinitive (e.g., 'to cause someone to do something'). As a noun, it is frequently followed by the preposition 'of'.
collocations: ["cause damage", "root cause", "cause problems", "lead cause", "cause and effect"]

definition: A small plastic disc on which music or other digital information is stored, which is read using a laser.
examples: ["I bought my favorite band's new album on CD.", "He put the CD into the player and pressed play."]
usage_notes: CD is an abbreviation for 'compact disc'. Although digital streaming has largely replaced physical media, the term is still widely understood.
collocations: ["play a CD", "CD player", "burn a CD", "music CD", "CD collection"]

definition: To stop happening or to bring something to an end.
examples: ["The company decided to cease operations after facing severe financial losses.", "The rain finally ceased, and the sun began to shine through the clouds."]
usage_notes: It is more formal than 'stop'. It can be used transitively (cease something) or intransitively, and is often followed by a gerund (cease doing) or an infinitive (cease to do).

definition: The inside upper surface of a room, or the maximum limit set for something such as prices, wages, or altitude.
examples: ["She painted the bedroom ceiling a soft shade of blue.", "The government has decided to put a ceiling on rent increases this year."]
usage_notes: In everyday language, 'ceiling' refers to the top of a room. In business, economics, or politics, it is frequently used metaphorically to mean an upper limit (e.g., 'glass ceiling', 'debt ceiling').
collocations: ["high ceiling", "glass ceiling", "debt ceiling", "hit a ceiling", "ceiling fan"]

definition: To do something enjoyable in order to show that an event, occasion, or holiday is special.
examples: ["We gathered at a local restaurant to celebrate my sister's graduation.", "How do you usually celebrate New Year's Eve in your country?"]
usage_notes: Often used as a transitive verb (celebrate something) or intransitive verb (let's celebrate!). Do not confuse with 'congratulate', which is used for praising a specific person for an achievement.
collocations: ["celebrate a birthday", "celebrate an anniversary", "celebrate a victory", "reason to celebrate"]

definition: A special social event, such as a party, created to mark an important occasion, holiday, or achievement.
examples: ["The team held a huge celebration after winning the championship game.", "We are planning a quiet family celebration for my grandmother's 80th birthday."]
usage_notes: The word is often used with the verbs 'hold', 'have', or 'throw'. It can refer to the event itself (countable) or the act of celebrating in general (uncountable).
collocations: ["birthday celebration", "cause for celebration", "victory celebration", "annual celebration", "join the celebration"]

definition: The smallest basic unit of a plant or animal, or a small room in a prison or monastery.
examples: ["The human body is made up of billions of individual cells.", "The prisoner was locked in his cell for twenty-three hours a day."]
usage_notes: The word 'cell' is also commonly used as a short form for 'cell phone' (mobile phone) in American English.

definition: A portable telephone that connects to a cellular network, allowing users to make calls, send texts, and access the internet without being connected by wires.
examples: ["I forgot my cell phone at home, so I couldn't call you.", "She checked her cell phone for any new messages."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'mobile phone' or simply 'mobile' is much more common, whereas 'cell phone' or 'cell' is standard in American English.
collocations: ["cell phone charger", "cell phone reception", "answer a cell phone", "check your cell phone"]

definition: A unit of money equal to one-hundredth of a dollar or various other currencies.
examples: ["A postage stamp used to cost only a few cents.", "She didn't have a single cent left in her wallet."]
usage_notes: Often represented by the symbol ¢. In spoken English, people often say 'pennies' when referring to one-cent coins, but 'cents' is used for prices (e.g., 'ninety-nine cents').
collocations: ["every single cent", "not a cent", "ten cents", "put in my two cents"]

definition: A unit of length in the metric system equal to one-hundredth of a meter.
examples: ["The insect was only about one centimetre long.", "Please measure the width of the paper in centimetres."]
usage_notes: This is the British English spelling. In American English, it is spelled 'centimeter'. It is often abbreviated as 'cm'.

definition: Located in the center of an area; or, of primary importance and essential to something.
examples: ["The new hotel is very central, making it easy to walk to all the main sights.", "The character's struggle for freedom is central to the novel's plot."]
