usage_notes: Often used before a noun (e.g., 'central heating', 'central location') or after a linking verb (e.g., 'The issue is central to our campaign').

definition: The middle point of an area, group, or object, or a building used for a specific activity.
examples: ["There is a fountain in the centre of the park.", "We met at the local community centre to discuss the project."]
usage_notes: 'Centre' is the standard spelling in British, Canadian, and Australian English, whereas 'center' is used in American English. It can be used as a noun, verb, or adjective.
collocations: ["town centre", "shopping centre", "centre of attention", "call centre", "medical centre"]

definition: A period of one hundred years.
examples: ["The castle was built in the twelfth century.", "The company has been in business for over a century."]
usage_notes: When referring to a specific hundred-year period, it is usually capitalized and written as 'the [Ordinal Number] Century' (e.g., 'the 21st Century').
collocations: ["turn of the century", "quarter of a century", "half a century", "for over a century", "last century"]

definition: A formal event or set of traditional acts performed on a special occasion, such as a wedding, graduation, or religious service.
examples: ["The graduation ceremony will take place in the main hall at 10 AM.", "They held a small private ceremony to celebrate their anniversary."]
usage_notes: It can refer to the formal procedure itself or the formal behavior required by such an occasion.
collocations: ["wedding ceremony", "opening ceremony", "award ceremony", "religious ceremony", "master of ceremonies"]

definition: Completely sure of something, or known to be true without any doubt.
examples: ["I am absolutely certain that I locked the front door before leaving.", "It now seems certain that the project will be delayed by a week."]
usage_notes: Often used in the pattern 'certain that [clause]' or 'certain of [something]'. It can also mean 'some' or 'particular' when placed before a noun (e.g., 'for certain reasons').
collocations: ["make certain", "pretty certain", "almost certain", "for certain", "a certain amount"]

definition: Without any doubt; definitely. It is also used as a polite way to say 'yes' or to agree to a request.
examples: ["I will certainly help you with your project tomorrow.", "\"Could you pass the salt, please?\" \"Certainly.\"", "She was certainly the best candidate for the job."]
usage_notes: Very common in both spoken and written English. When used to agree to a request, it sounds polite and helpful.

definition: An official document that proves a fact, such as your birth, a completed course of study, or a qualification.
examples: ["She received a certificate of completion after finishing the web design course.", "You need to present your birth certificate to apply for a passport."]
usage_notes: As a noun, it is pronounced with a weak ending (/kət/). As a verb (meaning to officially attest), it is pronounced with a strong ending (/keɪt/).
collocations: ["birth certificate", "gift certificate", "medical certificate", "earn a certificate", "issue a certificate"]

definition: A series of connected metal links used for holding, pulling, or decoration, or a number of similar businesses owned by the same company.
examples: ["He locked his bicycle to the fence with a heavy steel chain.", "She manages a popular chain of organic grocery stores."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun or a verb (e.g., 'to chain a bike to a post').

definition: A piece of furniture designed for one person to sit on, typically having four legs, a seat, and a backrest.
examples: ["Please take a seat in that comfortable leather chair by the window.", "We need to buy four more chairs for the dining room table."]
usage_notes: While 'chair' usually refers to the physical furniture, it can also be used as a verb meaning to lead a meeting or committee (e.g., 'She will chair the meeting').
collocations: ["armchair", "office chair", "pull up a chair", "sit in a chair", "rocking chair"]

definition: A person, especially a man, who is chosen to lead and preside over a meeting, committee, or board of directors.
examples: ["The chairman called the meeting to order at nine o'clock.", "He was appointed as the new chairman of the company's board."]
usage_notes: While 'chairman' is traditionally used, many modern organizations prefer gender-neutral terms like 'chairperson' or simply 'chair', especially when the person in the role is a woman.
collocations: ["board chairman", "acting chairman", "committee chairman", "appoint a chairman", "chairman of the board"]

definition: A woman who is in charge of a meeting, committee, or organization.
examples: ["She was appointed as the new chairwoman of the board of directors.", "The chairwoman called the meeting to order at nine o'clock."]
usage_notes: While 'chairwoman' is specifically used for a female leader, many modern organizations prefer the gender-neutral terms 'chairperson' or simply 'chair'.

definition: Something new and difficult that requires great effort and determination to succeed at.
examples: ["Learning a new language is a difficult challenge, but it is very rewarding.", "The new manager faces the challenge of improving team morale."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a noun and a verb. As a verb, it is often followed by an object and an infinitive verb (e.g., 'She challenged him to run faster').
collocations: ["face a challenge", "accept a challenge", "pose a challenge", "a major challenge", "rise to the challenge"]

definition: A large room used for formal meetings, or an enclosed space inside the body, a machine, or a plant.
examples: ["The members of parliament gathered in the debating chamber to vote on the new bill.", "The heart is divided into four distinct chambers that pump blood throughout the body."]
usage_notes: Often used in formal, political, or scientific contexts. In everyday speech, 'room' is preferred unless referring to specific technical or historical spaces.
collocations: ["chamber music", "legislative chamber", "combustion chamber", "chamber of commerce", "echo chamber"]

definition: A possibility of something happening, or an opportunity to do something.
examples: ["There is a good chance that it will rain this afternoon.", "She gave him a second chance to explain what had happened."]
usage_notes: Often used with the preposition 'of' followed by a gerund (e.g., 'a chance of winning') or with an infinitive verb (e.g., 'a chance to win').
collocations: ["by any chance", "take a chance", "second chance", "good chance", "stand a chance", "game of chance"]

definition: To make or become different, or to replace one thing with another.
examples: ["I need to change my clothes before we go out to dinner.", "The weather is going to change tomorrow, so bring an umbrella."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a verb and a noun. As a noun, it can refer to the act of becoming different, or to the coins you receive back when paying for something.
collocations: ["change your mind", "make a change", "loose change", "change plans", "climate change"]

definition: To move things or people into different positions, or to alter the arrangement of something.
examples: ["We decided to change the furniture round in the living room to make more space.", "The teacher changed the students round so they would work with different partners."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb chiefly used in British English. It is separable, meaning you can put the object between 'change' and 'round' (e.g., 'change them round'). In American English, 'change around' is more common.
collocations: ["change the furniture round", "change the seating round", "change things round", "change the order round"]

definition: To direct money, effort, or feelings towards a particular use, purpose, or path; or a passage/route through which things flow.
examples: ["She decided to channel all her energy into her new art project.", "The government is trying to find new channels for distributing aid to the affected areas."]
usage_notes: As a verb, it is often followed by the preposition 'into' (e.g., channel something into something). In British English, the past tense and participle are spelled with a double 'l' (channelled/channelling), while American English uses a single 'l' (channeled/channeling).
collocations: ["channel energy into", "distribution channel", "communication channel", "television channel", "channel resources"]

definition: One of the main sections into which a book is divided; it can also refer to a distinct period in history or a person's life.
examples: ["I just finished reading the third chapter of the novel.", "Graduating from college marked the beginning of a new chapter in her life."]
usage_notes: When referring to a specific numbered section of a book, 'chapter' is usually capitalized and not preceded by 'the' (e.g., 'Please turn to Chapter 4').
collocations: ["the next chapter", "chapter and verse", "open a new chapter", "final chapter", "local chapter"]

definition: The combination of qualities, personality traits, or moral values that make a person, group, or place unique; it can also refer to a person in a book, movie, or play, or a written symbol like a letter.
examples: ["She is a woman of strong character who always stands up for what is right.", "My favorite character in the movie was the wise old wizard."]
usage_notes: When referring to someone's personality or moral nature, 'character' is uncountable (e.g., 'a man of character'). When referring to a person in a story or a written symbol, it is countable (e.g., 'fictional characters', 'Chinese characters').
collocations: ["strong character", "main character", "fictional character", "judge of character", "Chinese character"]

definition: A quality or feature that belongs typically to a person, group, or thing and helps to identify them.
examples: ["Generosity is one of her most notable characteristics.", "The distinctive smell is characteristic of this type of flower."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun (a characteristic) or as an adjective (characteristic of someone/something). When used as an adjective, it is almost always followed by the preposition 'of'.

definition: To ask for a specific amount of money as a price for a service or goods; or to fill a device with electricity.
examples: ["The hotel does not charge for Wi-Fi.", "I need to charge my phone before we leave."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a verb and a noun. When talking about money, the pattern is 'to charge someone for something'.
collocations: ["free of charge", "charge a fee", "charge a battery", "in charge of", "take charge"]

definition: An organization set up to provide help and raise money for those in need, or the act of giving money, food, or help to people who need it.
examples: ["She donated a large portion of her savings to a local children's charity.", "The school organized a bake sale to raise money for charity."]
usage_notes: The word 'charity' can be countable when referring to an organization (e.g., 'registered charities') and uncountable when referring to the concept of giving help (e.g., 'acts of charity').
collocations: ["raise money for charity", "charity event", "donate to charity", "charitable organization", "local charity"]

definition: A visual display of information, such as a graph, diagram, or table, used to make data easier to understand.
examples: ["The sales chart shows a steady increase in revenue over the last year.", "The doctor looked at the patient's medical chart before entering the room."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun (a bar chart) or a verb (to chart your progress).
collocations: ["pie chart", "bar chart", "flow chart", "top the charts", "chart progress"]

definition: To run or follow after someone or something quickly in order to catch them.
examples: ["The dog loves to chase balls in the park.", "Police officers chased the suspect down the street."]
usage_notes: Can be used both as a verb (to chase) and as a noun (a chase). Often used figuratively, such as 'chasing a dream' or 'chasing success'.
collocations: ["chase a dream", "chase after someone", "give chase", "wild goose chase"]

definition: To force a person or animal to leave a place by running after them or making threatening movements.
examples: ["The farmer used a scarecrow to chase away the birds from his crops.", "The loud barking dog chased away the intruder."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. It can be separated by the object (e.g., 'chase the cats away' or 'chase away the cats').
collocations: ["chase away birds", "chase away intruders", "chase away fear", "chase away the darkness"]

definition: To talk with someone in a friendly, informal, and relaxed way.
examples: ["We sat in the kitchen and chatted over a cup of coffee.", "I had a quick chat with my neighbor this morning."]
usage_notes: Can be used both as a verb ('to chat') and as a noun ('to have a chat'). In modern contexts, it is also widely used for text-based communication online.
collocations: ["have a chat", "chat with friends", "online chat", "quick chat", "chat about something"]

definition: Low in price, costing very little money, or of low quality.
examples: ["The tickets were surprisingly cheap, so we decided to buy three of them.", "I don't like buying cheap shoes because they usually break after a few weeks."]
usage_notes: Be careful when using 'cheap'. While it often just means 'low-priced', it can also mean 'poor quality' or describe a person who is unwilling to spend money (stingy). To describe something that is a good value without sounding negative, use 'inexpensive' or 'affordable'.

definition: In a way that does not cost a lot of money, or in a way that is of low quality.
examples: ["The furniture was cheaply made and broke after only a few weeks.", "They managed to travel around Europe very cheaply by staying in hostels."]
usage_notes: Can describe both financial cost (positive/neutral) and poor quality (negative). It is the adverb form of 'cheap'.

definition: To act unfairly or dishonestly in order to gain an advantage, such as in a game, an exam, or a relationship.
examples: ["He was caught trying to cheat on the final exam by using his phone.", "It is unfair to cheat when playing cards with friends."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a verb ('to cheat') or as a noun to describe a person who dishonest ('a cheat'). When referring to relationships, it is usually followed by 'on' (e.g., 'cheat on someone').
collocations: ["cheat on an exam", "cheat on a test", "cheat on your partner", "cheat at cards", "cheat code"]

definition: To prevent someone from having or getting something they deserve or own, usually through trickery or dishonesty.
examples: ["The dishonest contractor tried to cheat them out of their savings.", "Don't let them cheat you out of the recognition you earned."]
usage_notes: Usually used in the pattern 'cheat someone out of something'. The preposition 'out of' is necessary when specifying what was stolen or denied.
collocations: ["cheat someone out of money", "cheat someone out of a prize", "cheat someone out of their inheritance", "cheat someone out of a chance"]

definition: To examine something in order to determine its accuracy, quality, condition, or to find out if it is safe and correct.
examples: ["Please check your work for spelling mistakes before submitting it.", "I need to check the weather forecast before we go out."]
usage_notes: Often used with the preposition 'for' (e.g., 'check for errors') or 'on' (e.g., 'check on the baby'). In British English, the paper bill in a restaurant is spelled 'bill', and the banking document is spelled 'cheque'.
collocations: ["double check", "check the time", "check in", "check out", "run a check"]

definition: To report one's arrival at a hotel, airport, or event; or to contact someone to let them know you are safe or to see how they are doing.
examples: ["Please remember to check in at the front desk as soon as you arrive at the hotel.", "I just wanted to check in with you and see how your first day of work went."]
usage_notes: When used as a verb, it is written as two words ('check in'). The noun form is written as one word or hyphenated ('check-in'). It is often followed by the prepositions 'at' (for places) or 'with' (for people).
collocations: ["check in at the hotel", "check in online", "check in with someone", "check-in desk", "flight check-in"]

definition: To register your arrival at a hotel, airport, or similar place.
examples: ["We need to check into the hotel before we go sightseeing.", "You should check into your flight online to save time at the airport."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. It is often used interchangeably with 'check in' when referring to hotels or flights.
collocations: ["check into a hotel", "check into a flight", "check into a room", "check into a hospital"]

definition: To look at or visit someone or something to make sure they are safe, healthy, or working properly.
examples: ["I'm going to check on the baby to see if she is still sleeping.", "Could you check on the roast in the oven while I answer the door?"]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb that takes an object directly after 'on' (e.g., 'check on someone/something'). It is commonly used in informal and everyday situations.
collocations: ["check on the kids", "check on a patient", "check on progress", "stop by to check on"]

definition: To look at, examine, or investigate something of interest; or to pay and leave a hotel or store.
examples: ["You should check out that new Italian restaurant downtown; the food is amazing.", "We need to check out of our hotel room before 11:00 AM."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb. When used to mean 'examine', it is separable (e.g., 'check it out'). When leaving a hotel, it is usually followed by 'of' (e.g., 'check out of the hotel').
collocations: ["check out a book", "check out of a hotel", "check out a website", "go check it out"]

definition: To examine or inspect something carefully to make sure it is correct, safe, or in good condition.
examples: ["Please check over your essay for spelling mistakes before submitting it.", "The mechanic checked over the car to ensure it was safe for the long drive."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb, meaning you can put the object in the middle (e.g., 'check the document over' or 'check over the document').
collocations: ["check over a document", "check over a report", "check over a car", "check over the details"]

definition: To investigate or see how someone is doing, or to monitor the status or progress of a situation.
examples: ["My mom called me this morning just to check up on me.", "I need to drop by the office to check up on the team's progress."]
usage_notes: This is a phrasal verb that requires an object after 'on' (e.g., 'check up on someone' or 'check up on something'). It often implies care, concern, or supervision.
collocations: ["check up on a friend", "check up on progress", "check up on the kids", "check up on a patient"]

definition: Either side of the face below the eye and above the jaw, or rude and disrespectful behavior spoken in a lighthearted or bold way.
examples: ["She kissed her daughter gently on the cheek before leaving for work.", "He had the cheek to ask for more money after doing such a poor job."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'cheek' is commonly used to mean impudence or mild disrespect (e.g., 'What a cheek!'). As a body part, it is a basic count noun.
collocations: ["rosy cheeks", "kiss on the cheek", "turn the other cheek", "cheek to cheek", "have the cheek to"]

definition: Noticeably happy and optimistic, or causing a feeling of happiness.
examples: ["She greeted everyone with a cheerful smile every morning.", "The room was painted in a cheerful bright yellow color."]
usage_notes: It can describe a person's mood, attitude, or appearance, as well as things that make people feel happy (like music or decor).

definition: In a way that shows happiness, optimism, or a positive attitude.
examples: ["She smiled cheerfully as she greeted her guests at the door.", "He cheerfully agreed to help his neighbor with the gardening."]
usage_notes: Often used to describe the manner in which someone performs an action, especially when they are willing or happy to do it.
collocations: ["smile cheerfully", "agree cheerfully", "wave cheerfully", "greet someone cheerfully", "accept cheerfully"]

definition: A solid food made from the milk of cows, goats, or sheep, produced in a wide variety of textures and flavors.
examples: ["Would you like some grated cheese on your pasta?", "This shop sells dozens of different European cheeses."]
usage_notes: Usually an uncountable noun when referring to the food substance ('some cheese'), but countable when referring to specific varieties or wheels of cheese ('artisanal cheeses').

definition: A distinct substance that is produced by or used in a reaction involving changes to atoms or molecules. It can also describe anything related to chemistry.
examples: ["The factory was accused of leaking hazardous chemicals into the river.", "The brain releases natural chemicals that make you feel happy when you exercise."]
usage_notes: 'Chemical' can be used as both a noun (e.g., 'dangerous chemicals') and an adjective (e.g., 'a chemical reaction').

definition: A scientist who studies or works with chemicals, or in British English, a person who prepares and sells medicines (a pharmacist).
examples: ["The chemist spent years analyzing the new compound in the laboratory.", "I need to go to the local chemist to pick up my prescription."]
usage_notes: In British and Australian English, 'chemist' frequently refers to a pharmacy or a pharmacist. In American English, the word almost exclusively refers to the scientist, while 'pharmacist' and 'pharmacy' (or 'drugstore') are used for medicine.
collocations: ["research chemist", "analytical chemist", "go to the chemist", "local chemist"]

definition: The scientific study of the properties, composition, and reactions of matter, or the emotional connection and attraction between two people.
examples: ["She decided to major in chemistry because she loved doing lab experiments.", "The two lead actors had incredible chemistry on screen."]
usage_notes: When referring to the subject, 'chemistry' is an uncountable noun. It can also be used figuratively to describe interpersonal relationships.

definition: A printed piece of paper from a bank that allows you to pay money to another person or business from your bank account.
examples: ["He wrote a cheque for two hundred dollars to pay the rent.", "The company sent me a refund cheque in the mail."]
usage_notes: This is the British English spelling. In American English, it is spelled 'check'.
collocations: ["write a cheque", "pay by cheque", "cash a cheque", "blank cheque"]

definition: The front part of a person's body between the neck and the stomach, or a large, strong wooden box used for storing things.
examples: ["He folded his arms across his chest and waited.", "They found an old wooden chest filled with gold coins."]
usage_notes: When referring to the body part, it is a countable noun (e.g., 'a hairy chest', 'chest pain'). It is also commonly used in compound words like 'chest of drawers'.
collocations: ["chest pain", "chest of drawers", "treasure chest", "bare chest", "chest infection"]

definition: To bite food with your teeth repeatedly to make it soft enough to swallow.
examples: ["Make sure to chew your food thoroughly before swallowing.", "The dog loves to chew on its rubber toy."]
usage_notes: Usually used as a verb. The phrasal verb 'chew up' means to damage something by biting it repeatedly.

definition: A common farm bird raised for its eggs and meat, or the meat from this bird used as food. It can also informally mean someone who is easily scared.
examples: ["We had roasted chicken and vegetables for dinner.", "The farmer feeds the chickens early every morning."]
usage_notes: 'Chicken' is uncountable when referring to the meat (e.g., 'I ate chicken') and countable when referring to the bird (e.g., 'There are three chickens'). Calling someone a 'chicken' is informal and slightly insulting.
collocations: ["fried chicken", "roast chicken", "chicken breast", "chicken soup", "too chicken to"]

definition: Most important, main, or having the highest rank in an organization or group.
examples: ["The chief reason for his success is his hard work.", "She was recently appointed as the chief of the police department."]
usage_notes: Can function as an adjective (the chief cause) or a noun (the tribal chief). In a professional context, it often appears as a title suffix, such as 'Editor-in-Chief'.

definition: A young human being who is not yet an adult, or a son or daughter of any age.
examples: ["The child was playing happily with her toys in the garden.", "As an only child, he spent a lot of time reading books."]
usage_notes: The plural form is irregular: 'children'. It is often used to refer to someone's offspring regardless of how old they are.
collocations: ["only child", "young child", "raise a child", "child care", "school-age child"]

definition: The protruding part of the face below the mouth and above the neck.
examples: ["He rubbed his chin thoughtfully while considering the question.", "She rested her chin on her hand and stared out the window."]
usage_notes: Often used in the idiom 'keep your chin up,' which means to remain positive during a difficult time.
collocations: ["double chin", "cleft chin", "rub one's chin", "keep your chin up", "pointy chin"]

definition: A small piece of something that has broken off, a thin slice of food, or a tiny electronic component used in computers.
examples: ["She noticed a small chip in the edge of her favorite coffee mug.", "The new smartphone features a much faster processing chip."]
usage_notes: In British English, 'chips' usually refers to thick-cut fried potatoes (French fries), while in American English, they are thin, crispy snacks.
collocations: ["computer chip", "potato chip", "chocolate chip", "chip away at", "blue-chip company"]

definition: A sweet, brown food made from roasted and ground cacao seeds, often sold as a bar or used as a flavor in desserts and drinks.
examples: ["I bought a bar of dark chocolate at the store.", "Would you like some hot chocolate with marshmallows?"]
usage_notes: It is used as an uncountable noun when referring to the substance and as a countable noun when referring to individual candies or types.

definition: The act of picking or deciding between two or more possibilities, or the range of things you can pick from.
examples: ["You have a choice between tea and coffee.", "She made the right choice by staying in school."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the verb 'make' (make a choice) rather than 'do'. It can also be used as an adjective meaning 'of very high quality'.
collocations: ["make a choice", "have no choice", "wide choice", "difficult choice", "by choice"]

definition: To select something or someone from a group of different options.
examples: ["You can choose any dessert from the menu.", "It was difficult to choose between the two job offers."]
usage_notes: This is an irregular verb: choose (present), chose (past), and chosen (past participle). It is often followed by 'to' and a verb, as in 'I choose to stay'.
collocations: ["choose wisely", "choose between", "carefully choose", "choose a career", "have to choose"]

definition: To cut something, such as food or wood, into smaller pieces using a sharp tool like a knife or an axe.
examples: ["Please chop the onions into small pieces for the soup.", "He spent the afternoon chopping wood for the fireplace."]
usage_notes: The phrasal verb 'chop up' is frequently used when referring to cutting something into many small bits.
collocations: ["chop wood", "chop vegetables", "chop finely", "chop down a tree", "pork chop"]

definition: To cut through the trunk of a tree or a large plant using a tool like an axe so that it falls to the ground.
examples: ["The lumberjack managed to chop down the massive oak tree in less than an hour.", "They had to chop down several old trees to make room for the new highway."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb. You can say 'chop down the tree' or 'chop the tree down'.
collocations: ["chop down a tree", "chop down a forest", "chop down a pine", "chop down a cherry tree"]

definition: To remove something by cutting it quickly and forcefully with a sharp tool like a knife or an axe.
examples: ["The chef had to chop off the ends of the carrots before cooking them.", "He used a saw to chop off the dead branches from the tree."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb, meaning you can say 'chop off the branch' or 'chop the branch off'. It often implies a single, forceful motion.
collocations: ["chop off a branch", "chop off the ends", "chop off a piece", "chop off a finger"]

definition: A building where Christians go to pray and worship, or the religious organization that meets there.
examples: ["We usually go to church on Sunday mornings.", "The wedding was held in a beautiful old stone church."]
usage_notes: When referring to the activity or service, we often say 'go to church' without an article (a/the).
collocations: ["go to church", "church service", "local church", "Catholic church", "church bells"]

definition: A thin cylinder of finely cut tobacco rolled in paper for smoking.
examples: ["He lit a cigarette and stood by the window.", "She is trying to quit smoking cigarettes for her health."]
usage_notes: Often shortened to 'cig' or 'cigarette' in casual speech. The verb used with it is typically 'to smoke' or 'to light'.
collocations: ["smoke a cigarette", "light a cigarette", "pack of cigarettes", "electronic cigarette", "cigarette butt"]

definition: A building where movies are shown on a large screen, or the film industry in general.
examples: ["We decided to go to the cinema to see the latest blockbuster.", "She has a great passion for 1950s Italian cinema."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'movie theater' or 'the movies' is more commonly used than 'cinema'.
collocations: ["go to the cinema", "cinema ticket", "independent cinema", "world cinema", "local cinema"]

definition: A perfectly round shape where every point on the outside edge is the same distance from the center.
examples: ["The children sat in a circle on the floor to listen to the story.", "Please draw a circle around the correct answer on your test."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a noun for the shape or as a verb meaning to move around something in a circular path.
collocations: ["inner circle", "vicious circle", "draw a circle", "social circle", "full circle"]

definition: A fact or condition that affects a situation, event, or person's life.
examples: ["The meeting was cancelled due to unforeseen circumstances.", "We cannot judge his actions without knowing the full circumstances of the event."]
usage_notes: It is frequently used in the plural form 'circumstances' when referring to someone's general life situation or the details of an incident.
collocations: ["under the circumstances", "unforeseen circumstances", "extenuating circumstances", "due to circumstances beyond our control"]

definition: A person who is a legal member of a particular country and has rights and protections because of it.
examples: ["She became a US citizen after living in the country for five years.", "The government has a duty to protect its citizens."]
usage_notes: Often used in legal or political contexts, but can also refer to a resident of a specific city or town.

definition: A large and important town where many people live and work.
examples: ["New York is a very busy city.", "I prefer living in a small city rather than a big one."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'the' when referring to a specific urban area or the downtown area.

definition: Relating to ordinary citizens and their concerns, rather than military or religious matters; it can also mean polite and courteous in a formal way.
examples: ["The two political rivals managed to keep their debate civil and focused on the issues.", "After years of military rule, the country finally returned to civil government."]
usage_notes: When 'civil' means polite, it often implies being barely polite enough to avoid an argument, rather than being genuinely warm or friendly.
collocations: ["civil rights", "civil war", "civil servant", "civil society", "keep it civil"]

definition: To state that something is true, typically without providing proof; or to assert ownership or a right to something.
examples: ["He claims that he saw a UFO, but nobody believes him.", "You can claim a refund if the product is damaged."]
usage_notes: Often followed by a 'that' clause (e.g., 'she claimed that...') or an infinitive verb (e.g., 'he claims to be an expert').
collocations: ["make a claim", "claim responsibility", "insurance claim", "baggage claim", "falsely claim"]

definition: To strike the palms of your hands together repeatedly, usually to show approval, appreciation, or to get someone's attention.
examples: ["The audience began to clap loudly after the final song.", "He clapped his hands to get the children's attention in the noisy room."]
usage_notes: It can be used as a verb or a noun. When used for thunder, it refers to a single, sudden loud noise.
collocations: ["clap your hands", "clap loudly", "a clap of thunder", "give someone a clap"]

definition: A group of students who are taught together, or a period of time during which students are taught.
examples: ["I have an English class at nine o'clock in the morning.", "She missed the biology class yesterday because she was sick."]
usage_notes: The word 'class' can refer to the group of people (e.g., 'The class was quiet') or the lesson itself (e.g., 'Class starts in five minutes'). In British English, it can also refer to social status.
collocations: ["take a class", "attend class", "skip class", "first class", "working class"]

definition: Having a high, lasting quality that remains popular, fashionable, or respected for a long time; also used to describe a typical or perfect example of something.
examples: ["She wore a classic black dress that will never go out of style.", "That was a classic mistake of leaving your keys inside the car."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'classic' with 'classical'. 'Classic' refers to high quality, timelessness, or a typical example, while 'classical' usually refers to traditional culture, history, or music (e.g., classical music, classical antiquity).
collocations: ["classic example", "classic design", "classic style", "a classic movie", "classic car"]

definition: A room in a school, college, or university where classes are taught.
examples: ["The teacher asked the students to quiet down as she entered the classroom.", "Our new classroom is equipped with a modern interactive whiteboard."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun adjunct (a noun acting as an adjective) to describe things related to school environments, such as 'classroom activities' or 'classroom management'.
collocations: ["classroom discussion", "classroom environment", "in the classroom", "classroom teacher", "virtual classroom"]

definition: Free from dirt, marks, or stains; to remove dirt or unwanted substances from something.
examples: ["Please make sure your hands are clean before you eat dinner.", "I need to clean my room because it is very messy."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective ('clean hands') or a verb ('to clean the house'). It is often paired with particles to form phrasal verbs like 'clean up'.
collocations: ["clean water", "clean energy", "keep it clean", "clean up", "squeaky clean"]

definition: To make a place or person neat and tidy by removing dirt, trash, or unwanted items.
examples: ["We need to clean up the kitchen after cooking dinner.", "The city organized a community event to clean up the local park."]
usage_notes: This is a separable phrasal verb, meaning you can say 'clean the room up' or 'clean up the room.' If using a pronoun, it must go in the middle: 'clean it up.'
collocations: ["clean up the mess", "clean up after yourself", "clean up the room", "clean up the environment", "clean up your act"]

definition: Easy to see, hear, or understand; free from darkness, confusion, or obstacles.
examples: ["The instructions were very clear, so I finished the task quickly.", "It was a beautiful, clear day with no clouds in the sky."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective, a verb (e.g., 'to clear the table'), or an adverb (e.g., 'loud and clear'). A common mistake is confusing 'clear' with 'clean'; 'clear' means transparent or easy to understand, while 'clean' means free from dirt.
collocations: ["clear understanding", "crystal clear", "clear sky", "make it clear", "clear evidence"]

definition: In a way that is easy to see, hear, or understand, or used to show that something is obvious.
examples: ["The teacher explained the rules clearly so that everyone understood.", "Clearly, we need to find a better way to solve this problem."]
usage_notes: It can be used as an adverb of manner (to describe how something is done) or as a sentence adverb to indicate that the speaker thinks a fact is obvious.

definition: A person whose job is to keep records, handle paperwork, or assist customers in a store or office.
examples: ["The store clerk helped me find the right size shoes.", "She works as a filing clerk for a law firm downtown."]
usage_notes: In US English, it is pronounced /klɜːrk/. In British English, it is often pronounced /klɑːk/. It can be used as a noun or as a verb meaning to work as a clerk.

definition: Quick to understand, learn, and devise ideas; intelligent and creative in solving problems.
examples: ["She came up with a clever solution to the difficult math problem.", "The dog is very clever and can perform several tricks."]
usage_notes: While 'clever' is generally positive, it can sometimes carry a negative connotation of being sneaky, cunning, or superficial rather than deeply wise.

definition: To press a button on a computer mouse or a similar device to perform an action, or to make a short, sharp sound.
examples: ["Click the link at the bottom of the page to download the file.", "I heard a click when the key turned in the lock."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'on' when referring to digital interfaces. It can also be used figuratively to mean that two people get along well immediately.
collocations: ["click a button", "double-click", "click on a link", "click into place", "right-click"]

definition: A person or organization that uses the professional services or advice of another person or company.
examples: ["The lawyer met with her client to discuss the details of the case.", "Our company is always looking for new ways to improve client satisfaction."]
usage_notes: While 'customer' is used for someone who buys goods or simple services (like in a supermarket), 'client' implies a ongoing professional relationship involving advice or customized services (like with lawyers, accountants, or designers).
collocations: ["prospective client", "corporate client", "attract clients", "client relationship", "serve a client"]

definition: The general weather conditions of a particular region over a long period of time, or the general opinion and feeling of a situation.
examples: ["The Mediterranean climate is known for warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters.", "The current economic climate makes it difficult for small businesses to survive."]
usage_notes: Can refer to literal weather patterns (natural climate) or metaphorically to a social, political, or economic atmosphere.

definition: To go up something towards the top, often using your hands and feet.
examples: ["We decided to climb the mountain early in the morning.", "The cat managed to climb up the tall oak tree."]
usage_notes: The letter 'b' at the end of 'climb' is silent. It can be used as both a verb and a noun.
collocations: ["climb a mountain", "climb the stairs", "climb up", "steep climb"]

definition: The sport or activity of scaling rocks, mountains, or artificial walls using hands and feet.
examples: ["We went climbing in the national park over the weekend.", "Indoor climbing has become a very popular way to stay fit."]
usage_notes: The 'b' in 'climbing' is silent. It can function as a noun (gerund) or as an adjective (e.g., 'climbing gear').

definition: A device used for measuring and showing the time, typically found on a wall or a table.
examples: ["The clock on the wall says it is almost noon.", "I need to set my alarm clock for 7:00 AM."]
usage_notes: A 'clock' is usually stationary (on a wall or desk), while a 'watch' is worn on the wrist.
collocations: ["alarm clock", "wall clock", "set the clock", "around the clock", "digital clock"]

definition: Located a short distance away in space or time; or having a strong, affectionate relationship with someone.
examples: ["My best friend lives very close to my house.", "We have been close friends since elementary school."]
usage_notes: Note the pronunciation difference: the adjective 'close' ends in an /s/ sound, while the verb 'close' (to shut) ends in a /z/ sound.
collocations: ["close friend", "close relative", "close proximity", "pay close attention", "a close call"]

definition: Near in distance, time, amount, or relationship.
examples: ["Our new apartment is very close to the train station.", "She is very close to her older sister and talks to her every day."]
usage_notes: When 'close' means 'near', it is pronounced with an /s/ sound at the end, not a /z/ sound. It is followed by the preposition 'to'.
collocations: ["close to home", "close to tears", "close to the edge", "close to perfection"]

definition: Not open; blocked to prevent entry, or not operating and open to the public at the current time.
examples: ["The museum is closed on Mondays for maintenance.", "Please keep the door closed so the cold air doesn't escape."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'closed' (the adjective/past participle) with 'close' (the verb or the adjective meaning near). For example, say 'The shop is closed,' not 'The shop is close.'
collocations: ["closed door", "closed for the holidays", "remain closed", "closed to the public"]

definition: In a careful, thorough manner, or in a way that is very near in distance, time, or relationship.
examples: ["The police are watching the situation very closely.", "The two events are closely linked to each other."]
usage_notes: Often follows verbs like watch, monitor, follow, listen, or resemble. Do not confuse with the adjective 'close'.
collocations: ["watch closely", "work closely with", "closely related", "closely linked", "follow closely"]

definition: A small room or cupboard used for storing things, especially clothes.
examples: ["She hung her new winter coat in the bedroom closet.", "The hallway closet is full of old board games and blankets."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'closet' is the standard word for a built-in wardrobe. In British English, 'wardrobe' or 'cupboard' is more commonly used, while 'closet' often refers to a small, private room or is used in the idiomatic phrase 'in the closet' (meaning keeping a secret, especially about one's sexuality).
collocations: ["walk-in closet", "closet space", "hallway closet", "clean out a closet", "skeleton in the closet"]

definition: A material made by weaving or knitting fibers together, such as cotton, wool, or silk, used for making clothes or covering surfaces.
examples: ["She used a soft cloth to wipe the dust off the wooden table.", "The tailor selected a high-quality wool cloth for the new suit."]
usage_notes: Do not confuse 'cloth' (the material) with 'clothes' (the items you wear). 'Cloth' is often uncountable when referring to the material in general, but countable when referring to a specific piece used for a task.
collocations: ["a piece of cloth", "damp cloth", "cotton cloth", "table cloth", "soft cloth"]

definition: Items worn on the body, such as shirts, pants, dresses, and coats, to protect or cover it.
examples: ["She bought some new clothes for her upcoming job interview.", "I need to wash my dirty clothes this weekend."]
usage_notes: The word 'clothes' is always plural and has no singular form (you cannot say 'a clothe'). To refer to a single item, use 'a piece of clothing' or 'an item of clothing'. The 'th' sound is often silent in casual speech, making it sound exactly like 'close'.
collocations: ["wear clothes", "change clothes", "casual clothes", "designer clothes", "a change of clothes"]

definition: Items such as shirts, pants, and dresses that people wear to cover their bodies.
examples: ["You should pack warm clothing if you are traveling to Canada in winter.", "The store sells high-quality outdoor clothing and gear."]
usage_notes: 'Clothing' is an uncountable (mass) noun, so it does not have a plural form like 'clothings'. To count individual items, use phrases like 'an item of clothing' or 'a piece of clothing'.
collocations: ["warm clothing", "protective clothing", "an item of clothing", "casual clothing", "clothing store"]

definition: A white or gray mass of tiny water drops floating in the sky, or a remote digital network used to store and access data over the internet.
examples: ["Dark clouds gathered in the sky right before it started to rain.", "I backed up all my photos to the cloud so I wouldn't lose them."]
usage_notes: Can be used as a noun or a verb (e.g., 'to cloud someone's judgment'). In technology, it is usually preceded by 'the' (e.g., 'stored in the cloud').
collocations: ["dark cloud", "cloud cover", "cloud storage", "in the cloud", "cloud computing"]

definition: An organization for people who share a common interest, or a place where people meet to socialize, dance, and listen to music.
examples: ["I decided to join the local photography club to meet new people.", "The group went to a dance club downtown to celebrate her birthday."]
usage_notes: The word can also refer to a heavy stick used as a weapon or a specific tool used in sports like golf.
collocations: ["join a club", "night club", "golf club", "book club", "health club"]

definition: A hard, black or dark brown rock found underground that can be burned as a fuel to produce heat or electricity.
examples: ["The power plant burns coal to generate electricity for the city.", "Miners extracted thousands of tons of coal from the underground mine.", "In the winter, they used to burn coal in the fireplace to keep the house warm."]
usage_notes: It is an uncountable noun when referring to the material as fuel (e.g., 'a supply of coal'). The plural form 'coals' refers to individual glowing pieces of burning coal.
collocations: ["coal mine", "burn coal", "coal power", "lump of coal", "coal industry"]

definition: The land next to or near the ocean or sea.
examples: ["We drove along the Pacific coast and stopped to take pictures of the ocean.", "Many people like to visit the coast during the warm summer months."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'coast' means to move without using power (e.g., riding a bike downhill) or to make progress with little effort.
collocations: ["along the coast", "east coast", "west coast", "coastal area", "rocky coast"]

definition: A piece of clothing worn over other clothes to keep warm or dry, usually having long sleeves and opening down the front.
examples: ["Don't forget to put on your warm coat before going outside in the snow.", "She hung her winter coat on the rack by the door."]
usage_notes: 'Coat' usually refers to heavier outerwear (like a winter coat or raincoat), while 'jacket' refers to a shorter or lighter layer.

definition: A system of words, letters, figures, or symbols used to represent others, especially for secrecy, or the instructions written for a computer program.
examples: ["She learned how to write computer code in high school.", "You need to enter a four-digit security code to open the door."]
usage_notes: When referring to computer programming instructions, 'code' is an uncountable noun (e.g., 'lines of code', not 'many codes').

definition: A popular hot brown drink made from the roasted and ground seeds (coffee beans) of a tropical plant.
examples: ["I always start my morning with a hot cup of coffee.", "Would you like some coffee or tea with your dessert?"]
usage_notes: It can be used as an uncountable noun for the liquid (e.g., 'I drink coffee') or as a countable noun when ordering a cup (e.g., 'Two coffees, please').
collocations: ["make coffee", "cup of coffee", "black coffee", "coffee shop", "strong coffee"]

definition: A small, flat, round piece of metal used as money, or to invent a new word or phrase.
examples: ["She dropped a few coins into the vending machine.", "The scientist managed to coin a new phrase to describe the phenomenon."]
usage_notes: As a verb, 'coin' usually means to create a new word or expression (e.g., 'to coin a phrase'). As a noun, it refers to physical metal currency.
collocations: ["flip a coin", "gold coin", "coin a phrase", "rare coins"]

definition: Having a low temperature, or feeling a lack of warmth.
examples: ["It is very cold outside, so make sure to wear a heavy jacket.", "I poured myself a glass of cold water after running."]
usage_notes: Can be used as an adjective (cold weather) or a noun (to catch a cold).
collocations: ["cold weather", "cold water", "freezing cold", "catch a cold", "cold hands"]

definition: In a way that lacks warmth, emotion, or friendliness.
examples: ["She stared at him coldly and refused to answer his question.", "'I don't care what you do,' he said coldly."]
usage_notes: Usually describes how someone speaks, looks, or acts towards another person when they are showing disapproval or indifference.

definition: To fall down or fall apart suddenly, or to fail completely in structure, health, or an economic system.
examples: ["The old roof collapsed under the weight of the heavy snow.", "He was so exhausted after running the marathon that he almost collapsed."]
usage_notes: Can be used as both a verb and a noun. Often used with the preposition 'into' (e.g., 'collapse into a chair').

definition: A person that you work with, especially in a professional setting or skilled job.
examples: ["I discussed the new project proposal with my colleagues at work.", "She has a great relationship with her former colleagues from the law firm."]
usage_notes: Mainly used in professional contexts. For informal workplaces, people often use 'coworker' instead.

definition: To bring things together from different places, or to gather items of a specific type as a hobby.
examples: ["She likes to collect rare stamps from all over the world.", "Please collect your belongings before leaving the train."]
usage_notes: It is often followed by 'from' when picking up something or someone (e.g., 'collect the children from school'). In informal US English, 'pick up' is often used instead.

definition: A group of objects or things that have been gathered together, often because they are similar or interesting.
examples: ["She has an impressive collection of rare stamps from around the world.", "The museum is displaying a new collection of modern artwork this month."]
usage_notes: Often used with the preposition 'of' followed by a plural noun (e.g., 'a collection of books').
collocations: ["art collection", "private collection", "a vast collection", "build a collection", "data collection"]

definition: An educational institution that provides higher education and awards academic degrees, or a division within a university.
examples: ["She plans to go to college after she graduates from high school.", "He studied business administration at a local community college."]
usage_notes: In American English, 'going to college' generally refers to attending university-level education. In British English, 'college' often refers to a place for higher school-level education (ages 16-18) or a specific constituent part of a university.
collocations: ["attend college", "go to college", "college student", "college degree", "college campus"]

definition: The visual quality of an object that you see when light reflects off it, such as red, blue, green, or yellow.
examples: ["What is your favorite color?", "The leaves change color in the autumn."]
usage_notes: 'Color' is the standard spelling in American English, while 'colour' is used in British and other international varieties of English.

definition: The visual property of things that results from the light they reflect, transmit, or emit, such as red, blue, green, or yellow.
examples: ["What is your favorite color?", "The leaves change color in the autumn."]
usage_notes: 'Coloured' is the British/Commonwealth past tense or adjective form of 'colour'. In US English, it is spelled 'color'. Note that using 'colored' to refer to people is considered offensive in modern English.

definition: A tall vertical structure used as a building support or decoration, or a vertical section of text or numbers on a page or spreadsheet.
examples: ["The spreadsheet has one column for expenses and another for income.", "Ancient Greek temples are famous for their large stone columns."]

collocations: ["newspaper column", "spreadsheet column", "column of numbers", "stone column", "opinion column"]

definition: A joining or merging of different things, qualities, or people to form a single unit.

usage_notes: Often followed by the preposition 'of' (e.g., 'a combination of X and Y'). Also refers to the series of numbers or letters used to open a lock.
collocations: ["winning combination", "in combination with", "perfect combination", "color combination", "lock combination"]

definition: To join or bring two or more things together to form a single unit or whole.

definition: To move toward or arrive at a particular place, person, or position.

definition: To have your origin or birthplace in a particular place, or to be produced or obtained from a specific source.

collocations: ["come from a family", "come from behind", "come from nowhere", "come from far away", "come from experience"]

definition: To succeed or happen as planned, or to give a particular impression to others.

collocations: ["come off well", "come off badly", "come off as confident", "come off as rude", "come off without a hitch"]

definition: An informal phrasal verb used to encourage someone to do something, to tell someone to hurry up, or to express disbelief.

definition: To be published or released, to become available to the public, or to become known.

definition: To regain consciousness, or to change your opinion and agree with something you previously opposed.

definition: To regain consciousness after being unconscious, fainted, or asleep, or to reach a particular state, amount, or total.
